https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22010.Title: World Guidance: World Modeling in Condition Space for Action Generation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.22010.Summary: The "World Guidance" (WoG) framework from ByteDance Seed and The University of Hong Kong enhances Vision-Language-Action models by leveraging a compact "condition space" derived from future observations for precise action generation. This approach overcomes the trade-off between efficient future representation and fine-grained control, achieving an average 69.4% success rate on Google Robot tasks in simulation and demonstrating robust generalization across real-world out-of-distribution scenarios and effective learning from diverse human and UMI datasets.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle to effectively leverage future observation modeling for action generation.
A fundamental "redundancy-precision trade-off" exists, where rich future representations are redundant, but compact latent spaces lack fine-grained detail.
This trade-off leads to inefficiencies in pretraining, limits scalability, and hinders real-world performance for precise manipulation tasks.
Method: Introduces World Guidance (WoG), a novel two-stage predictive framework for VLA models.
Compresses future observations into a compact, action-relevant "condition space" using frozen vision models and a trainable Q-Former-based encoder.
Integrates these conditions directly into the action inference pipeline during Stage I and trains the VLM to predict them internally for self-guided inference in Stage II.
Results: Achieved an average 69.4% success rate on Google Robot tasks in simulation, outperforming baselines like π0-FAST (60.5%) by a significant margin.

Demonstrated robust generalization in real-world out-of-distribution settings, with minimal performance degradation for tasks like "Pick and Place" under background changes (60% to 55%) and novel objects (60% to 40%).
Effectively scaled by integrating unannotated human and UMI data, boosting real-world "Pick and Place" success rates from 60% to 85% and "Fold the Towel" from 60% to 80% with UMI data.
Takeaways: An implicit "condition space" can effectively distill action-relevant features from future observations, balancing computational efficiency with the precision needed for fine-grained control.
A two-stage training curriculum, initially using explicit future guidance and then learning internal condition prediction, enables robust and self-guided VLA models.
Leveraging frozen foundation models for future observation encoding helps preserve generalization capabilities from upstream visual priors, making the condition space invariant to visual nuisances.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18224.Title: SimVLA: A Simple VLA Baseline for Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18224.Summary: A streamlined Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baseline, SimVLA, demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in robotic manipulation, achieving an average 98.6% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark with a compact 0.5B parameter model. This performance is attributed to a modular architecture and rigorous standardization of training details, outperforming larger, more complex VLA models.
Problem: Performance attribution in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models is obscured by increasing architectural complexity, varied pretraining, and diverse optimization schedules.
The lack of standardized training practices impedes reproducibility and fair comparisons across different VLA models.
There is a prevalent assumption that advanced robotic manipulation capabilities necessitate ever-increasing architectural complexity in VLA designs.
Method: SimVLA adopts a modular architecture, strictly decoupling a pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) for perception from a lightweight Transformer-based action head for continuous control.
Continuous action generation is modeled using conditional flow matching, which learns a deterministic vector field to transform Gaussian noise into desired action chunks efficiently.
The approach meticulously standardizes training and inference recipes, including data handling, optimization dynamics, action representation, and VLM backbone fine-tuning strategies.
Results: SimVLA achieves an average 98.6% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, surpassing multi-billion-parameter models like OpenVLA-OFT (97.1%) and MemoryVLA (96.7%) with a 0.5B parameter backbone.
It exhibits strong zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-PRO, achieving superior semantic and task robustness, with a 10% improvement over baselines on Goal and Long suites.

The model demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on WidowX robot tasks (95.8% average success) and competitive results on Google Robot tasks (76.1% average success), showcasing efficient real-robot transfer capabilities.
Takeaways: Meticulous standardization of training and inference details, referred to as "silent drivers," is more impactful on VLA model performance than architectural complexity alone.
A minimalist architectural design, when rigorously trained, can achieve state-of-the-art performance in robotic manipulation, effectively challenging the necessity of multi-billion-parameter models.
Decoupling the vision-language backbone from the action head creates a modular and adaptable system, allowing for easy integration of future Vision-Language Model (VLM) advancements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15922.Title: World Action Models are Zero-shot Policies
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.15922.Summary: DreamZero, a 14B World Action Model (WAM) developed by NVIDIA, enables zero-shot robot policies by jointly predicting future video states and actions from diverse data. It achieves an average task progress of 39.5% on unseen tasks and demonstrates 42% relative improvement in cross-embodiment transfer using video-only demonstrations, all while maintaining real-time control at 7Hz through significant optimization.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle with generalizing to unseen physical motions in novel environments due to limited spatiotemporal priors from static image-text pretraining.
Learning generalist robot policies traditionally requires extensive, repetitive, task-specific demonstrations, which is inefficient and scales poorly to diverse, real-world scenarios.
Inefficient cross-embodiment transfer, often requiring new action-labeled data for each robot platform or human demonstration.
Method: Introduces DreamZero, a 14B World Action Model (WAM) that uses an autoregressive diffusion transformer backbone to jointly predict future video frames and robot actions.
Leverages a pretrained video diffusion backbone and flow-matching objective to learn world physics and spatiotemporal dynamics from diverse robot data.
Implements DreamZero-Flash with asynchronous execution and optimizations like decoupled noise schedules to achieve real-time closed-loop control at 7Hz.
Results: Achieved 62.2% average task progress on seen tasks in unseen environments, outperforming state-of-the-art pretrained VLAs (27.4%).
Demonstrated 39.5% average task progress on 10 entirely unseen tasks, markedly higher than VLA baselines (16.3%).
Enabled 42% relative improvement in unseen task performance for cross-embodiment transfer using only 10-20 minutes of video-only demonstrations from other robots or humans.
DreamZero-Flash achieved real-time control at 7Hz (150ms inference) with 74% task progress on table bussing, recovering most of the performance of 4-step DreamZero (83%).
Takeaways: Jointly predicting future world states (video) and actions with a video diffusion model provides powerful spatiotemporal priors, enabling zero-shot generalization to unseen physical motions and environments.
Generalist policies can be learned effectively from diverse, non-repetitive robot data, reducing the reliance on laborious, repetitive demonstrations.
Cross-embodiment transfer is highly efficient with WAMs, allowing learning from video-only demonstrations and few-shot adaptation to new robot platforms, crucial for scaling with human video data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13710.Title: HBVLA: Pushing 1-Bit Post-Training Quantization for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.13710.Summary: HBVLA introduces a 1-bit post-training quantization framework for Vision-Language-Action models, enabling their robust deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms. It achieves this by intelligently partitioning and spectrally quantizing weights, maintaining near full-precision performance with marginal degradation in simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.
Problem: Large parameter counts and high memory requirements of VLA models prevent their deployment on resource-constrained robotic platforms.
Direct application of 1-bit binarization methods designed for LLMs or VLMs to VLA models leads to severe policy degradation due to amplified quantization errors in continuous action spaces.
Identifying critical weights in VLAs for aggressive quantization is challenging due to issues like the "dual dominance problem" in saliency estimation and modality mixing in weight distributions.
Method: A policy-aware weight partitioning strategy uses a rectified Hessian, derived from a block-wise gradient backpropagation, to identify and protect weights critical for action generation.

Non-salient weights undergo a sparse orthogonal transform (permutation) to reorder columns, minimizing high-frequency noise before being quantized in the Haar domain using group-wise 1-bit binarization with a shared mean.
Salient weights are quantized on the residual, using a column-wise Haar transform and group-wise 1-bit binarization, then combined with the non-salient reconstruction.
Results: HBVLA consistently achieved higher success rates on the LIBERO (70.0% for OpenVLA, 90.3% for OpenVLA-OFT) and SIMPLER (70.0% for CogACT) benchmarks, showing significantly smaller performance degradation (e.g., 6.5% on OpenVLA) compared to other 1-bit PTQ methods.

Real-world evaluation on Mobile ALOHA with a dual-arm cobot demonstrated only marginal success rate decreases for HBVLA-quantized models, maintaining strong performance (e.g., 83.3% for Pick and Place) where other baselines failed due to oscillations.

The proposed policy-aware Hessian effectively identified task-critical weights, reducing quantization error and improving success rates (e.g., 10.3% degradation vs. 12.5% for standard Hessian) compared to generic saliency estimation methods.
Takeaways: VLA model components show differential sensitivity to quantization, with action heads and projectors being the most sensitive, while vision encoders are more robust.
Standard Hessian-based saliency identification methods are inadequate for VLAs due to the "dual dominance problem," requiring a policy-aware rectified Hessian to prioritize action-critical signals.

Applying a sparse orthogonal transform to VLA weights before Haar decomposition helps narrow the distribution gap for 1-bit quantization by reducing high-frequency energy caused by intermingled modalities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12063.Title: VLAW: Iterative Co-Improvement of Vision-Language-Action Policy and World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12063.Summary: The VLAW framework iteratively co-improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies and action-conditioned world models for robot manipulation. It leverages limited real-world interaction to ground the world model, which then generates abundant synthetic data to boost policy performance, achieving a 39.2% absolute success rate increase on contact-rich tasks.
Problem: Collecting sufficient real-world interaction data for post-training VLA models is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, limiting their scalability.

Existing learned world models often lack physical fidelity, exhibiting over-optimism (trained on successful demonstrations) and struggling to accurately model diverse physical interactions, including failure cases.
Continuously improving VLA policies in the real world is challenging due to the data scarcity bottleneck and the difficulty of optimizing expressive policies without explicit action likelihoods.
Method: VLAW introduces an iterative co-improvement framework that alternately refines a VLA policy and an action-conditioned world model.

A pre-trained world model is fine-tuned using a small, fixed budget of real-world online policy rollouts (Dreal), crucially including failure cases, to improve its physical fidelity and reduce over-optimism.

The improved world model then generates a large amount of synthetic trajectories, which are automatically filtered for success by a vision-language reward model, providing high-quality data to post-train the VLA policy.
Results: The world model, post-trained with online rollouts, demonstrated substantial improvements in video prediction quality (e.g., FVD reduced from 225.13 to 64.12) and accurately modeled interaction outcomes, effectively mitigating over-optimism.

VLAW achieved a 39.2% absolute success rate improvement, increasing the mean success rate of the VLA policy from 0.46 to 0.868 on challenging contact-rich manipulation tasks, outperforming baselines that do not use world models.

Training with world model-generated synthetic data contributed 11.6% absolute success rate improvement, highlighting the significant value of scalable, high-quality synthetic data for policy enhancement.
Takeaways: Limited real-world interaction, when strategically used to include diverse outcomes like failures, can effectively ground a pre-trained world model, leading to significantly higher physical fidelity.

High-fidelity synthetic data, generated by a grounded world model and filtered by an accurate reward model, provides a scalable and effective alternative to expensive real-world data for improving VLA policies.

An iterative feedback loop between policy exploration (generating new real-world data) and world model refinement (generating better synthetic data) enables continuous and scalable performance improvement for robot learning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12062.Title: HoloBrain-0 Technical Report
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.12062.Summary: HoloBrain-0, a vision-language-action (VLA) foundation model by Horizon Robotics, introduces an integrated framework for robotic manipulation that incorporates explicit robot embodiment priors and a full-stack open-source ecosystem, RoboOrchard. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks with a lightweight 0.2B-parameter variant demonstrating comparable capabilities to larger models, enabling efficient on-device deployment for real-time control.
Problem: VLA agents often lack robust generalization to out-of-distribution states, visual perturbations, and physical variations in real-world environments.
Large foundation models typically incur significant inference latency, hindering their practical deployment for real-time robot control due to high computational demands.
Acquiring and curating large volumes of high-quality, expert-level robotic demonstrations for complex, long-horizon tasks is prohibitively expensive and inefficient.
Method: HoloBrain-0 employs an end-to-end VLA architecture that explicitly integrates robot embodiment priors, such as multi-view camera parameters and kinematic descriptions, to enhance 3D spatial reasoning.

The framework includes lightweight model variants (e.g., 0.2B parameters) and introduces SimpleRTC for smooth asynchronous inference, combined with a Teacher Forcing training strategy to ensure robust, low-latency on-device deployment.
A two-stage 'pre-train then post-train' data strategy is utilized, featuring an iterative, test-driven approach for quality-focused data curation, particularly for dexterous and long-horizon tasks.
Results: The lightweight 0.2B-parameter HoloBrain-0-GD achieved a 90.8% success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and a 74.0% average score on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, outperforming larger existing VLA models.

HoloBrain-0 models surpassed the π0.5 baseline by average success rates of 5.65% to 8.02% across 10 real-world tasks, with improvements of 25% and 30% on challenging cloth and box folding tasks respectively.

The SimpleRTC and Teacher Forcing strategies enabled smooth asynchronous inference, eliminating inference pauses and achieving fluid control for complex dynamic tasks with negligible impact on efficiency.
Takeaways: Explicitly embedding robot embodiment priors into VLA architectures significantly enhances 3D spatial reasoning and facilitates robust generalization across diverse robotic platforms.

Designing VLA models with a focus on efficiency, such as lightweight variants and optimized inference strategies, is crucial for bridging the gap between research and practical, real-time robot deployment.

An iterative, test-driven data curation methodology that focuses on proactive state expansion and targeted failure recovery can substantially reduce data requirements for complex, long-horizon tasks while maintaining high performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11236.Title: ABot-M0: VLA Foundation Model for Robotic Manipulation with Action Manifold Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11236.Summary: Researchers from Alibaba Group's AMAP CV Lab developed ABot-M0, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation model that leverages a systematically harmonized dataset of over 6 million trajectories and a novel Action Manifold Learning paradigm to achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse robotic manipulation benchmarks, including an average 98.6% success rate on LIBERO.
Problem: General-purpose embodied agents face barriers including insufficient data scale, lack of standardization across datasets, and misaligned pre-training paradigms for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.
Embodied intelligence remains fragmented, with robot policies rarely transferring across different hardware morphologies.
Existing VLA models often use visual encoders from VLMs that prioritize semantic recognition over the 3D structure and physical dynamics crucial for robot manipulation.
Method: Constructed UniACT-dataset by harmonizing and standardizing over 6 million trajectories from six public datasets, unifying action representations and enabling dual-arm training.

Introduced Action Manifold Learning (AML), a paradigm that directly predicts clean action sequences instead of noise or velocity, based on the hypothesis that effective actions reside on a low-dimensional manifold.
Developed a modular perception mechanism that integrates VLM semantics with explicit geometric priors from plug-and-play 3D modules (VGGT, Qwen-Image-Edit) via cross-attention.
Results: Achieved an average success rate of 98.6% on the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming strong baselines like Diffusion Policy and OpenVLA.
Demonstrated robust zero-shot generalization with an 80.5% success rate on LIBERO-Plus, significantly surpassing OpenVLA-OFT (69.6%) and UniVLA (42.9%).

Set a new state-of-the-art with a 58.3% success rate on RoboCasa GR1 tabletop tasks, outperforming previous noise-prediction methods like GR00T-N1.6 (47.6%), validating the superiority of Action Manifold Learning.
Takeaways: Effective robot actions reside on a low-dimensional, smooth manifold, allowing for more stable and efficient learning through direct action prediction (AML).

Systematic data harmonization, including unified action representation (delta actions, EEF frame, rotation vectors) and a pad-to-dual-arm strategy, is critical for achieving cross-embodiment and cross-task generalization.
Integrating 3D spatial priors through modular, external components effectively augments VLM semantics, enhancing precision in manipulation tasks without modifying the core VLM backbone.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10098.Title: VLA-JEPA: Enhancing Vision-Language-Action Model with Latent World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10098.Summary: VLA-JEPA enhances Vision-Language-Action models for robotic control by integrating a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) and a latent world model. This framework learns robust dynamics abstractions from human videos and robot data, achieving state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-world manipulation benchmarks with improved generalization and robustness to out-of-distribution conditions.
Problem: Existing latent action learning in VLA models often results in representations biased by pixel-level variations rather than action-relevant state changes.
Current methods are vulnerable to noisy motion and irrelevant background changes in real-world videos, which hinder the learning of meaningful dynamics.
Information leakage from future observations during training can lead to latent actions that are semantically empty and ineffective for control.
Many prior VLA pipelines rely on complex, multi-stage training procedures, increasing their overall complexity and fragility.
Method: VLA-JEPA integrates a JEPA-style latent world model to learn robust dynamics abstractions by predicting future latent representations instead of pixels, inherently filtering low-level noise.
It employs a 'leakage-free state prediction' mechanism where future frames are used only for supervision targets, ensuring latent actions capture true transitional dynamics without shortcuts.
The framework introduces learnable tokens for state transitions and embodied actions, conditioned by a Qwen3-VL backbone and utilizing a flow-matching action head for trajectory generation.
A unified two-stage pretraining pipeline combines action-free human videos and action-labeled robot data, simplifying the training process compared to multi-stage approaches.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on in-distribution (LIBERO, 97.2% average success) and out-of-distribution (LIBERO-Plus, 79.5% average success) simulation benchmarks, demonstrating superior generalization and robustness.
Showcased improved real-to-sim transfer capabilities on SimplerEnv, achieving the highest average success rate (65.2%) on Google Robot tasks.
Attained SOTA performance in real-world table-top manipulation tasks, producing more stable execution and exhibiting emergent skills like repeated grasping, attributed to exposure to human videos.

Ablation studies confirmed substantial performance gains from human video pretraining and the unified training paradigm, with attention visualizations validating the leakage-free design's focus on relevant regions.
Takeaways: Leveraging JEPA principles for latent state prediction allows the model to learn semantic abstractions of dynamics that are robust to pixel-level noise and irrelevant visual disturbances.
A carefully designed leakage-free world model is essential for learning meaningful latent actions that encode genuine state transitions rather than merely encoding future observations.
Pretraining on a combination of diverse human videos and robot data significantly enhances policy robustness, generalization, and can enable the emergence of useful real-world skills.

A unified, joint optimization of world modeling and action prediction objectives streamlines the training process and improves the quality of learned action representations by focusing on operation-relevant regions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22153.Title: DynamicVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22153.Summary: DynamicVLA, from S-Lab at Nanyang Technological University, introduces a compact 0.4B parameter vision-language-action model alongside the Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, enabling robots to robustly manipulate moving objects in real-world scenarios. The model achieved an average 47.06% success rate on the DOM simulation benchmark, notably outperforming prior baselines, and demonstrated consistent performance on physical robots.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily focus on static manipulation, struggling with the complexities of dynamic objects in real-world environments.
High inference latency in current VLA models creates a "perception–execution gap," leading to outdated actions and task failures when objects are in continuous motion.
There is a lack of large-scale, standardized datasets and benchmarks specifically designed for evaluating VLA models in dynamic object manipulation tasks.
Method: Developed DynamicVLA, a compact 0.4-billion-parameter VLA model leveraging a convolutional vision encoder (FastViT) and a truncated language backbone for improved efficiency and speed.

Introduced two execution mechanisms: "Continuous Inference" to pipeline inference and execution, and "Latent-aware Action Streaming" to explicitly manage temporal misalignment by prioritizing the most recent action predictions.

Created the Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark, a large-scale dataset with 200K synthetic and 2K real-world episodes, collected via automated pipelines to provide diverse dynamic tasks for evaluation.
Results: DynamicVLA achieved an average success rate of 47.06% on the DOM simulation benchmark, significantly surpassing the best baseline (GR00T-N1.5 at 13.05%) and reducing task completion time to 8.53 seconds.
In real-world evaluations, DynamicVLA consistently outperformed baselines across various dynamic tasks on Franka and PiPER robots, achieving success rates ranging from 50.0% to 78.3%.

Ablation studies confirmed the crucial role of Continuous Inference (increasing SR by 10.95%) and Latent-aware Action Streaming (increasing SR by 7.34%) in mitigating latency and temporal misalignment, respectively.
Takeaways: Minimizing inference latency and explicitly addressing temporal misalignment are critical factors for achieving robust and responsive dynamic object manipulation with VLA models.

Compact model architectures (0.4B parameters) can effectively achieve high performance in dynamic tasks when paired with efficient execution mechanisms, demonstrating that large parameter counts are not always necessary.

Automated data collection, including a "real-world simulator" approach for physical robots, is essential for building scalable and diverse datasets for dynamic robotic tasks, bridging the sim-to-real gap.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21998.Title: Causal World Modeling for Robot Control
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.21998.Summary: Robbyant Technology researchers developed LingBot-VA, an autoregressive diffusion framework for robot control that unifies video prediction and action inference. The system enhances performance on long-horizon, precision, and deformable object manipulation tasks in real-world and simulated environments, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmarks like RoboTwin 2.0 (avg 92.9% Easy) and LIBERO (avg 98.5%).
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies suffer from representation entanglement, leading to suboptimal generalization and sample inefficiency.
Prior world models for robotics face limitations in closed-loop control, including a reactivity gap, limited long-term memory, and causality violations.
Challenges in achieving data-efficient, generalizable, and precise long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.
Method: Introduces LingBot-VA, an autoregressive diffusion framework that unifies video and action tokens in a shared continuous latent space, processed by a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture.
Employs a closed-loop rollout mechanism that decomposes learning into visual dynamics prediction and inverse dynamics, using real-time observation feedback and KV-caching for persistent memory.

Deploys an asynchronous inference pipeline with a Forward Dynamics Model (FDM)-grounded step and noisy history augmentation to achieve real-time, robust control by overlapping computation and execution.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on RoboTwin 2.0 (avg. 92.9% Easy, 91.6% Hard) and LIBERO benchmarks (avg. 98.5% across suites), demonstrating improved success rates on long-horizon and complex tasks.
Outperformed strong baselines in real-world tasks involving long-horizon planning, precision manipulation, and deformable objects, with significantly higher progress scores.

Exhibited superior sample efficiency, achieving comparable or better performance with significantly fewer task-specific demonstrations, and strong generalization to novel objects and spatial configurations.
Takeaways: Unifying visual dynamics prediction and action inference within a single causal autoregressive diffusion process in a continuous latent space improves robot learning by disentangling visual reasoning from action prediction.
Integrating continuous real-world observation feedback and persistent memory through an autoregressive loop is crucial for robust, adaptive, and long-horizon control.

An asynchronous inference pipeline, enhanced by FDM-grounding, can overcome the computational demands of large generative models to enable real-time robotic deployment without performance degradation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18692.Title: A Pragmatic VLA Foundation Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18692.Summary: The LingBot-VLA foundation model empirically demonstrates that real-world VLA performance consistently scales with increasing pre-training data up to 20,000 hours without saturation. It achieves improved performance on 100 real-world manipulation tasks across multiple robotic platforms and exhibits enhanced training efficiency and data-efficient adaptation.
Problem: There was a lack of comprehensive empirical studies on how real-robot performance of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models scales with increasingly massive pre-training datasets.

The VLA community lacked a highly optimized training codebase capable of efficiently conducting large-scale scaling evaluations on multi-node clusters due to I/O bottlenecks and communication overheads.
Existing VLA evaluation methodologies often struggle to provide robust, large-scale real-world assessments across diverse robotic platforms and numerous tasks.
Method: Developed LingBot-VLA, a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture integrating a pre-trained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as its semantic backbone and using Flow Matching for continuous action modeling.
Assembled a large-scale pre-training dataset of approximately 20,000 hours of real-world teleoperated manipulation data from 9 distinct dual-arm robot embodiments.
Implemented systemic training optimizations including Hybrid Sharded Data Parallel, FlexAttention, and operator fusion via `torch.compile` to enhance throughput and scalability.
Results: LingBot-VLA with depth achieved an average Success Rate (SR) improvement of 4.28% and a Progress Score (PS) increase of 7.76% over the \u03c0_0.5 baseline on the GM-100 real-world benchmark.

The optimized codebase achieved a throughput of 261 samples per second with an 8-GPU setup, representing a 1.5x to 2.8x speedup over existing VLA-oriented codebases and exhibiting near-linear scaling up to 256 GPUs.

Demonstrated superior data efficiency in post-training, outperforming \u03c0_0.5 even with 80 demonstrations per task compared to \u03c0_0.5's full 130 demonstrations, with the performance gap widening as data increased.
Takeaways: Real-world VLA performance consistently improves as pre-training data volume scales from 3,000 to 20,000 hours, showing no saturation and indicating continued benefits from larger datasets.
Integrating spatial awareness through a vision distillation approach with depth information enhances VLA models' success rates and progress scores in both real-world and simulated environments.
An optimized training codebase significantly improves efficiency, delivering substantial throughput speedups and near-linear scaling for large-scale VLA model development.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16163.Title: Cosmos Policy: Fine-Tuning Video Models for Visuomotor Control and Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.16163.Summary: Researchers from NVIDIA and Stanford University fine-tune a large, pretrained latent video diffusion model, Cosmos-Predict2, into a unified robot policy for visuomotor control and planning. This method achieves state-of-the-art average success rates of 98.5% on LIBERO, 67.1% on RoboCasa, and 93.6% on ALOHA, demonstrating enhanced data efficiency and robustness for complex manipulation tasks.
Problem: Adapting large foundation models for robotics often requires complex multi-stage training pipelines or custom architectural modifications.
Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models, typically trained on static image-text data, often lack the dynamic spatiotemporal priors essential for robust robot control.
Traditional robot learning systems frequently employ separate, loosely coupled modules for policy, world modeling, and value estimation, which can increase system complexity.
Method: A large, pretrained latent video diffusion model (Cosmos-Predict2) is fine-tuned in a single stage, without architectural changes, to function as a unified robot policy, world model, and value function.

Diverse modalities such as robot proprioception, action chunks, state values, and multi-camera images are encoded as "latent frames" and injected directly into the video model's existing latent diffusion sequence.

A joint training scheme on robot demonstration and collected rollout data enables simultaneous learning of actions, future states, and expected rewards, leveraging auxiliary targets to enhance performance.
Results: Achieved new state-of-the-art average success rates: 98.5% on LIBERO, 67.1% on RoboCasa (with significantly fewer demonstrations), and 93.6% on real-world ALOHA bimanual tasks, outperforming leading baselines.

Ablation studies confirmed that the pretrained video model backbone improved performance by 3.9% on LIBERO and significantly more on real-world tasks, validating the importance of rich spatiotemporal priors.

Model-based planning, utilizing the learned world model and value function, yielded a 12.5-point average score increase on the most challenging ALOHA tasks, demonstrating effective guidance for decision-making even with limited rollout data.
Takeaways: Pretrained video generation models inherently learn strong spatiotemporal priors from dynamic internet videos, which are crucial for robust low-level visuomotor control in robotics.

A simple single-stage fine-tuning approach with latent frame injection is sufficient to adapt a powerful video foundation model into a multi-functional robot policy without the need for bespoke architectural modifications.

Unifying the policy, world model, and value function within a single, pretrained video model architecture creates a more coherent and effective system for both direct control and model-based planning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11421.Title: The Great March 100: 100 Detail-oriented Tasks for Evaluating Embodied AI Agents
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11421.Summary: The Great March 100 (GM-100) benchmark provides a collection of 100 systematically designed, detail-oriented tasks for evaluating embodied AI agents, addressing limitations in current evaluation approaches. Experiments demonstrate that existing Vision-Language-Action models achieve low success rates on these challenging tasks, though a strong inverse correlation is observed between action prediction error and physical task completion.
Problem: Existing robot learning datasets suffer from a lack of task diversity, primarily focusing on a narrow range of common actions, leading to biased model training.
Complex, multi-step, or rare 'long-tail' interactions crucial for versatile embodied agents are often underrepresented in current benchmarks.
The absence of standardized evaluation tasks across different studies hinders objective comparison and assessment of progress in embodied AI.
Method: Developed a systematic task design framework leveraging insights from human-object interaction primitives and 'how-level affordances', deliberately avoiding biases from perceived real-world utility.
Utilized a large language model (Qwen3) to generate and refine 100 detail-oriented tasks, followed by LLM-based executability scoring and human expert filtering to ensure feasibility and diversity.
Collected over 13,000 teleoperated trajectories for the GM-100 tasks on two distinct robotic platforms (Agilex Cobot Magic and Dobot Xtrainer) to provide a diverse dataset.
Results: The 100 GM-100 tasks are feasible for human operators but prove highly challenging for current VLA models, with the best-performing model (π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​) achieving an average Success Rate of only 24.9% on the Xtrainer platform.
GM-100 effectively differentiates the capabilities of various VLA models, with π0.5\pi_{0.5}π0.5​ consistently outperforming Diffusion Policy and π0\pi_0π0​ across nearly all evaluated tasks.

A strong inverse correlation was observed between normalized action prediction error (MSE) and Partial Success Rate (PSR), indicating that models with lower prediction errors achieve higher physical task completion rates.
Takeaways: Current robot learning benchmarks overemphasize common actions, resulting in models with significant biases and limited generalization capabilities.

A principled approach to task design, integrating human-object interaction knowledge and low-level manipulation understanding, is essential for creating truly challenging and comprehensive benchmarks.

High-precision action modeling is a prerequisite for robust physical interaction in complex tasks, as evidenced by a strong inverse correlation between action prediction error and real-world task success.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11404.Title: ACoT-VLA: Action Chain-of-Thought for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11404.Summary: A framework introduces Action Chain-of-Thought (ACoT) for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, enabling robots to reason directly in the action space by leveraging both explicit motion trajectories and implicit action priors. This approach enhances task success rates and robustness across diverse robotic manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world deployments.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models suffer from a "semantic-kinematic gap," as their reasoning in abstract vision-language spaces provides only indirect guidance for precise physical actions.

Language Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Visual CoT/World Model approaches, while improving generalization, still rely on semantic or visual intermediaries that are not directly optimized for low-level robot control.

Pre-trained Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbones, primarily designed for understanding and question-answering, lack the granular knowledge of the action space essential for truly grounded robotic policy learning.
Method: The ACoT-VLA framework introduces Action Chain-of-Thought (ACoT), formulating the reasoning process as a structured sequence of coarse action intents directly in the action space.

An Explicit Action Reasoner (EAR) generates kinematically plausible reference action trajectories as explicit guidance, while an Implicit Action Reasoner (IAR) extracts latent action priors from the Vision-Language Model's internal representations.
An Action-Guided Prediction (AGP) head integrates these explicit and implicit action guidances to condition the final policy learning, effectively bridging the semantic-kinematic gap.
Results: ACoT-VLA achieved a 98.5% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 1.6% and demonstrating enhanced robustness in long-horizon tasks.

The framework exhibited substantial robustness against distribution shifts on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark (84.1% avg success), improving performance by up to 16.3% under robot initial-state perturbations.

Real-world deployment on AgiBot G1 and AgileX platforms confirmed consistently higher average success rates (e.g., 66.7% vs. 61.0% for π0.5) across various manipulation tasks, validating practical applicability.
Takeaways: The most effective form of reasoning for generalist robot policies occurs directly in the action space, providing "kinematically coherent guidance" superior to abstract language or visual sub-goals.
Combining explicit, coarse-grained action trajectories (from EAR) with implicit, latent action-related semantics (from IAR) synergistically enhances robotic policy learning and robustness.
Even VLM backbones, primarily trained for semantic understanding, contain extractable implicit action priors in their internal representations that are valuable for grounding robot actions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24653.Title: RoboMIND 2.0: A Multimodal, Bimanual Mobile Manipulation Dataset for Generalizable Embodied Intelligence
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24653.Summary: RoboMIND 2.0 introduces a large-scale, multimodal dataset comprising 310K bimanual and mobile manipulation trajectories collected from six diverse robot embodiments, including tactile sensing and a high-fidelity digital twin. The accompanying MIND-2 dual-system framework, optimized with offline reinforcement learning, enhances generalizable embodied intelligence and improves performance on long-horizon, multi-robot collaborative tasks.
Problem: Existing robotic manipulation datasets are limited in scale, diversity (e.g., single-arm, fixed-base, single-embodiment), and multimodal richness (e.g., lacking tactile feedback), hindering the training of generalizable policies.
Data scarcity and limited diversity impede the development of robust policies for complex bimanual, mobile, and long-horizon tasks.
A significant gap exists in bridging the sim-to-real performance for robot learning due to insufficient high-fidelity simulated data and assets.
Method: Constructed RoboMIND 2.0, a dataset featuring 310K dual-arm trajectories from six heterogeneous robot platforms, covering 759 tasks, 129 skills, and 1,139 objects, including tactile feedback and mobile manipulation.
Developed a high-fidelity digital twin with open-source USD assets and a 20K-trajectory simulated dataset collected in Isaac Sim for effective sim-to-real transfer.

Proposed MIND-2, a hierarchical dual-system framework, combining a high-level VLM planner (MIND-2-VLM) and a low-level Vision-Language-Action executor (MIND-2-VLA) optimized via Implicit Q-Learning (IQL).
Results: The MIND-2 system with IQL achieved the highest success rates (up to 1.0) on multi-robot collaborative tasks, outperforming direct VLA fine-tuning and single-task imitation learning methods.

State-of-the-art VLA models like XR-1, when trained on RoboMIND 2.0, demonstrated strong cross-embodiment and object-level generalization capabilities, consistently performing well across diverse robot platforms and novel objects.
Integration of tactile sensing led to improved success rates for VLA models, with XR-1 showing more pronounced gains in tasks requiring fine-grained physical interaction.
Takeaways: Multimodal data, particularly the inclusion of tactile feedback, consistently enhances the success rates and robustness of VLA models in contact-rich and precision-demanding manipulation tasks.

A hierarchical dual-system approach (MIND-2), combining a semantic planner with an offline RL-trained VLA executor, effectively addresses long-horizon mobile manipulation and multi-robot collaborative tasks.
Co-training with a mix of real and high-fidelity simulated data significantly improves real-world robot performance, with increased simulation data further enhancing results for challenging tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24125.Title: Unified Embodied VLM Reasoning with Robotic Action via Autoregressive Discretized Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.24125.Summary: AgiBot Research and the Shanghai Innovation Institute developed GenieReasoner, a system that integrates Vision-Language Model reasoning with precise robotic action via autoregressive discretized pre-training. This system achieved an 82.72% score on the new ERIQ embodied reasoning benchmark and demonstrated superior real-world task success rates across diverse robotic platforms by resolving the reasoning-precision trade-off.
Problem: Ambiguity in diagnosing robotic task failures, making it unclear whether issues stem from high-level reasoning deficits or low-level execution errors.
The persistent "reasoning-precision trade-off" in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, where achieving broad semantic generalization often compromises high-precision physical control, and vice-versa.

Limitations in current action discretization methods (e.g., simple binning, VQ-VAE, FAST) which either lack precision or stability, and continuous control methods which suffer from optimization conflicts when co-trained with VLM backbones.
Method: Introduced the Embodied Reasoning Intelligence Quotient (ERIQ), a large-scale benchmark with 6,052 embodied question-answer pairs, to quantitatively assess VLM embodied reasoning independently of physical action.
Developed FACT (Flow-matching Action Tokenizer) to discretize continuous robotic actions into compact tokens while preserving high-fidelity reconstruction through a novel flow-matching decoder.

Proposed GenieReasoner, a unified autoregressive framework that uses FACT-tokenized actions to jointly optimize multimodal reasoning and precise low-level control within a shared representation space, leveraging a three-stage training recipe.
Results: GenieReasoner achieved an average score of 82.72% on the ERIQ benchmark, representing an absolute improvement of 41% over baseline VLMs, particularly excelling in action understanding and human intention comprehension.

FACT demonstrated substantially lower Mean Squared Error in action reconstruction compared to baselines, showing an order of magnitude improvement in fidelity, which is critical for precise motor control.

In real-world experiments on AgiBot and ARX platforms, GenieReasoner consistently outperformed state-of-the-art discrete and continuous VLA baselines across all complexity settings, resolving the reasoning-precision trade-off and exhibiting robust generalization in complex tasks.
Takeaways: There is a strong positive correlation between VLM embodied reasoning capabilities (as measured by ERIQ scores) and end-to-end VLA generalization performance in robotic manipulation tasks.

Flow-matching provides a highly effective and stable method for converting continuous actions into discrete tokens, achieving significantly higher reconstruction fidelity and compactness compared to existing action tokenization methods.

A multi-stage training strategy, including joint pre-training with diverse VQA and action data, followed by post-training focused on embodied VQA and action data, is crucial for unifying reasoning and action alignment while preserving general VLM capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.22414.Title: Emergence of Human to Robot Transfer in Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.22414.Summary: Researchers from Physical Intelligence and Georgia Institute of Technology demonstrate that human-to-robot skill transfer emerges in Vision-Language-Action models when sufficiently pre-trained on diverse robot data, treating human video demonstrations as another embodiment. This approach significantly improves robot performance on novel scenes, objects, and tasks, for instance, boosting egg sorting accuracy from 57% to 78% by leveraging human data.
Problem: Leveraging human video data for robot control is challenging due to a significant domain gap in embodiment, viewpoint, kinematics, and action spaces.
Prior methods for human-to-robot transfer often require manual engineering, indirect learning, or explicit alignment, limiting their generality and scalability.
Collecting large quantities of diverse robot teleoperation data is expensive and time-consuming, hindering the development of generalist robot policies.
Method: A simple co-training recipe, named "pi0.5\\pi_{0.5}pi0.5​ + ego", integrates embodied human video data directly into a pre-trained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model.
Humans are treated as another embodiment, applying the same low-level action and high-level subtask prediction objectives used for robot data, without explicit kinematic or visual alignment.
A scalable human data collection pipeline was designed using head-worn and optional wrist-mounted cameras to capture egocentric demonstrations, processed with 6D pose and 3D hand keypoint estimation.
Results: The approach nearly doubled success rates on scene generalization tasks (e.g., Spice: 32% to 71%; Dresser: 25% to 50%) by learning from human demonstrations in novel environments.
For task generalization, robot performance on sorting eggs by color increased from 57% (robot-only baseline) to 78% accuracy with human co-training.
Ablation studies confirmed that transferring both high-level subtask predictions and low-level actions from human data is essential for optimal mobile manipulation performance.
Takeaways: Human-to-robot transfer is an emergent property, scaling with the diversity and size of the VLA's pre-training data, akin to emergent abilities in large language models.
Diverse pre-training leads to the formation of embodiment-agnostic latent representations, enabling the VLA model to inherently bridge the human-robot domain gap.
Human data serves as a scalable and efficient source of knowledge, providing comparable effectiveness to target robot data for certain generalization tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15692.Title: mimic-video: Video-Action Models for Generalizable Robot Control Beyond VLAs
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.15692.Summary: The mimic-video framework introduces Video-Action Models (VAMs) for robotic manipulation by leveraging generative, pre-trained video models to learn dynamic priors. It achieves a 10x improvement in sample efficiency and 2x faster convergence compared to existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, demonstrating strong generalization in simulation and a 93% success rate on real-world bimanual tasks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely on static image-text pre-training, which lacks explicit information about physical dynamics, causality, and procedural knowledge necessary for robot control.
Learning physical dynamics for robot control with VLAs requires extensive and expensive robot demonstration data, leading to a significant data-efficiency bottleneck.
Prior attempts to integrate video into VLAs often convert rich video data into sparse representations, losing fine-grained dynamic information crucial for complex manipulation.
Method: Propose mimic-video, a Video-Action Model (VAM) that combines a language-conditioned generative video backbone (Cosmos-Predict2) with a lightweight action decoder, both trained using Conditional Flow Matching.
The action decoder conditions on intermediate, *partially denoised* latent states from the video backbone to infer actions, avoiding computationally expensive full video generation at inference time.

Training decouples the finetuning of the video backbone on robotics data from the training of the action decoder, which is performed from scratch with a *frozen* backbone to separate planning from control.
Results: Achieved superior average success rates on benchmarks like SIMPLER-Bridge (56.3% with "τv" tuning) and LIBERO (93.9%), outperforming existing state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action models.
In real-world dexterous bimanual manipulation, the framework achieved high success rates of 72.0% for "Package Sorting" and 93.0% for "Measuring Tape Stowing" with minimal demonstration data.

The method demonstrated a 10x improvement in sample efficiency and 2x faster convergence for the action decoder compared to VLA-conditioned decoders, reaching maximum success rates with only 10% of the training data.
Takeaways: Grounding robot policies in generative video models, which learn dynamic priors from large-scale video data, significantly enhances sample efficiency and convergence speed compared to Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.

Effective policy learning does not require full video reconstruction; using intermediate, partially denoised, or even purely noisy latent states (e.g., at "τv = 1") from the video model during inference is sufficient and often optimal, simplifying real-time control.

Decoupling complex visual planning (offloaded to the frozen video backbone) from low-level action control (learned by a lightweight action decoder) leads to a more efficient and robust robot learning system.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14666.Title: EVOLVE-VLA: Test-Time Training from Environment Feedback for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14666.Summary: EVOLVE-VLA introduces a framework for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to continuously adapt and improve from environmental interaction during test time, using a learned progress estimator as a reward signal. It yields a +6.5% absolute gain in average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, significantly enhancing performance in low-data settings and enabling cross-task adaptation.
Problem: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for VLA models requires extensive, labor-intensive expert demonstrations (hundreds per task), limiting scalability.
SFT-trained policies are brittle, rigidly memorizing trajectories and struggling to generalize, recover from errors, or adapt to novel deployment conditions.
Existing reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning for VLAs often relies on oracle reward functions, which are unavailable in real-world test-time deployment scenarios.
Method: Introduced a test-time training (TTT) framework that enables VLA models to continuously adapt through online reinforcement learning (Group Relative Policy Optimization).
Replaced unavailable oracle rewards with a learned task progress estimator, providing dense, continuous feedback for policy improvement.
Implemented mechanisms, including an accumulative progress estimation and a progressive horizon extension strategy, to mitigate the inherent noise of the learned reward signals.
Results: Achieved a +6.5% absolute gain in average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, raising the OpenVLA-OFT baseline from 89.2% to 95.8%, with an 8.6% gain on challenging long-horizon tasks.
Demonstrated substantial improvements in low-data regimes, boosting a 1-shot pre-trained VLA from 43.6% to 61.3% success rate (+17.7%).
Pioneered cross-task generalization through test-time adaptation, achieving a 20.8% success rate on unseen tasks with zero task-specific demonstrations, breaking the 0% barrier.
Takeaways: Vision-Language-Action models can achieve robust adaptation and performance improvements through autonomous learning from environmental feedback during test time, reducing reliance on extensive expert demonstrations.

A carefully designed learned task progress estimator can effectively serve as a dense, continuous reward signal, enabling reinforcement learning in real-world scenarios where oracle rewards are absent.

Mitigating the noise and temporal credit assignment challenges of learned reward functions through accumulative estimation and progressive horizon extension is crucial for stable and effective online learning in complex, long-horizon tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13030.Title: Motus: A Unified Latent Action World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13030.Summary: Motus, a unified latent action world model from Tsinghua University, Peking University, and Horizon Robotics, integrates five embodied AI capabilities into a single generative framework. It leverages latent actions from optical flow to learn from diverse, unlabeled visual data, achieving an 88.66% success rate in clean simulation and demonstrating strong generalization on real-world dual-arm robots.
Problem: Current embodied AI systems are fragmented, modeling cognitive functions like perception, imagination, and action generation in isolated components, hindering holistic learning.
Difficulty in leveraging vast, heterogeneous datasets (internet videos, human demos) for robot learning due to varying action spaces across embodiments and scarcity of explicit action labels.
Existing unified models often lack comprehensive integration of all key distributions or robust vision-language and physical interaction knowledge from pre-trained foundation models.
Method: A Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture unifies Vision-Language Understanding (VLM), Video Generation (VGM), and an Action Expert through Tri-model Joint Attention, allowing joint modeling of five key embodied AI distributions.
Introduces latent actions, derived from optical flow and compressed by a VAE, to represent general motion patterns, enabling learning from large-scale, heterogeneous, and often unlabeled video data.

Employs a three-phase pretraining-finetuning pipeline on a six-layer data pyramid to progressively learn visual dynamics, action representations with latent actions, and specialize for target robotic embodiments.
Results: Achieved an average success rate of 88.66% in clean simulation and 87.02% in randomized simulation on RoboTwin 2.0, surpassing baselines like \u03c00.5 by over 45% and X-VLA by over 15%.

Demonstrated robust generalization on real-world dual-arm robots (AC-One and Agilex-Aloha-2), with average partial success rates of 63.22% and 59.30%, respectively, representing improvements of +48.43% and +10.7% over the \u03c00.5 baseline.
Ablation studies confirmed that the full multi-stage pretraining with latent actions contributed a 10.02% increase in success rate over training from scratch in randomized simulation.
Takeaways: Tri-model Joint Attention within a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture effectively integrates specialized generative and understanding experts while preventing task interference.
Latent actions, derived from optical flow, provide a universal and embodiment-agnostic representation for motion, allowing scalable pretraining of action experts from unlabeled visual data.

A progressive, multi-stage training pipeline, building upon pre-trained foundation models and leveraging a six-layer data pyramid, enables robust generalization across diverse robotic tasks and embodiments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00975.Title: MM-ACT: Learn from Multimodal Parallel Generation to Act
https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.00975.Summary: MM-ACT introduces a unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that integrates text, image, and robot actions into a shared token space, enabling efficient parallel generation for real-time robotic control. This framework achieves state-of-the-art performance with an average 96.3% success rate on LIBERO simulation tasks and improved generalization to out-of-domain manipulation.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack explicit physical dynamics, limiting their ability to generate precise temporal actions despite strong semantic understanding.
Current unified VLA approaches suffer from slow inference speeds due to autoregressive generation or architectural complexities arising from hybrid decoding strategies.
Hybrid VLA models frequently encounter objective misalignment issues when combining different generation paradigms (e.g., autoregressive text with diffusion-based action heads).
Method: MM-ACT integrates text, image, and robot states/actions into a unified discrete token space, processed by a single Transformer-based mask token predictor with bidirectional attention.
It employs a "Context-Shared Multimodal Learning" paradigm, where task planning (text) and future image prediction (image) jointly supervise and enhance action generation from a shared context.
The model utilizes a one-step parallel decoding strategy for action generation, enabling low-latency, real-time robot control at high frequencies (up to 40 Hz).
Results: MM-ACT achieved an average 96.3% success rate on LIBERO simulation tasks, outperforming all baselines, and secured a 72.0% average success rate in real-world Franka robot experiments.
The model demonstrated improved out-of-domain generalization on RoboTwin2.0 with a 52.38% average success rate across bimanual tasks in unseen settings.

The one-step parallel decoding strategy for action generation achieves real-time inference (0.22s for an 8-chunk action) without compromising effectiveness, which is crucial for practical robotic deployment.
Takeaways: Jointly supervising task planning and future image prediction from a shared context significantly boosts action generation performance, with unified text-image-action training providing a +9.25% gain on RoboTwin2.0.
A unified token space with parallel decoding across all modalities simplifies VLA model architecture and substantially improves efficiency for real-time robotic control.

Different modalities exhibit distinct training dynamics (e.g., text overfitting faster than image), highlighting the necessity for careful loss weighting and scheduling in multimodal training pipelines.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18960.Title: AVA-VLA: Improving Vision-Language-Action models with Active Visual Attention
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18960.Summary: Researchers from LiAuto Inc. developed the AVA-VLA framework, reformulating Vision-Language-Action models from a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process perspective, which allows for dynamic visual attention based on historical context. The system achieves state-of-the-art success rates on robot manipulation benchmarks and demonstrates robust real-world performance on a dual-arm robot.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models treat robotic tasks as Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), processing visual inputs independently at each timestep.
This history-agnostic design struggles with dynamic environments and partial observations, leading to inefficient visual attention and poor generalization.

Prior attempts to incorporate historical information primarily focused on model efficiency (e.g., token pruning) rather than fundamentally enhancing visual processing for improved generalization quality.
Method: The framework reformulates the VLA problem as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), using a recurrent state to approximate the agent's belief state from past observations and actions.

An Active Visual Attention (AVA) module dynamically modulates visual processing by leveraging the recurrent state to identify and prioritize task-relevant visual tokens through a cross-attention mechanism.
The recurrent state also initializes the learnable action placeholder embedding, integrating historical context directly into the action generation path.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art overall success rates on the LIBERO and CALVIN simulation benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization, particularly on challenging sequential tasks.
Demonstrated robust sim-to-real transferability, achieving the highest average performance across four challenging real-world tasks on a dual-arm Mobile ALOHA robot.
Ablation studies confirmed that both the Active Visual Attention (AVA) module and the state-based initialization strategy individually and synergistically contribute to performance gains.
Takeaways: Explicitly integrating temporal context through a recurrent state and active visual attention fundamentally enhances VLA models' ability to filter redundant information and focus on task-relevant visual regions.
A POMDP formulation, approximated via a recurrent state, provides a more principled theoretical basis for VLA models in dynamic, partially observable robotic manipulation tasks.

The AVA module not only improves performance but also enables significant visual token reduction (e.g., 70% pruning) while maintaining competitive results, suggesting a pathway for more efficient VLA inference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18810.Title: MergeVLA: Cross-Skill Model Merging Toward a Generalist Vision-Language-Action Agent
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.18810.Summary: MergeVLA is a framework designed to overcome the challenge of merging independently fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which previously failed due to structural specializations. The framework achieves robust multi-skill, multi-embodiment, and multi-environment generalization, demonstrating up to a 90.2% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark and successful application on a real robotic arm.
Problem: Directly applying established model merging techniques to independently fine-tuned Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models results in near-zero success rates, indicating fundamental incompatibilities.

VLA models exhibit destructive Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) parameter interference and architectural incompatibility in their action experts, particularly due to self-attention and task-specific specialization in deeper layers.
Evaluating merged VLA models in mixed-task settings is challenging, as it requires dynamic task identification at inference time without explicit supervision.
Method: MergeVLA introduces a merging-oriented VLA architecture featuring sparsely activated LoRA adapters with task-specific binary masking to stabilize VLM merging by selectively activating beneficial parameters.

The action expert is redesigned by removing self-attention layers and replacing the `tanh` gating function with `sigmoid` to reduce task-specific dependencies, while deeper 'expert head' blocks remain unmerged for each task.

A training-free test-time task router is implemented, which infers task relevance by projecting initial observation hidden states onto value-based principal components of the action expert to dynamically select appropriate skill components.
Results: MergeVLA achieved an average success rate of 90.2% on the LIBERO cross-skill benchmark, representing a significant improvement over direct merging methods that resulted in 0% success.

The framework demonstrated enhanced robustness on LIBERO-Plus, maintaining an average success rate of 62.5% for merged models under distribution shifts, outperforming other VLA models' single-task performance in shifted conditions.

MergeVLA successfully generalized across different robotic embodiments and tasks on RoboTwin and performed equivalently to single-task models on a real SO-101 robotic arm, achieving a 90.0% average success rate for multi-skill tasks.
Takeaways: VLA model non-mergeability is primarily caused by divergent LoRA updates in the VLM backbone and architectural coupling in action experts, where task-specific information propagates widely across layers.
Sparsely activating LoRA parameters through task-specific masking can effectively preserve pretrained visual-language representations and mitigate cross-task interference during merging.

Removing self-attention from the action expert forces reliance on robust VLM features, making shallow layers more amenable to merging, while deep layers (expert heads) remain task-specialized and should be retained individually.

Value projection matrices from the action expert provide stable and discriminative signals for test-time task routing, enabling dynamic selection of skill components based on input features without additional training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17502.Title: RynnVLA-002: A Unified Vision-Language-Action and World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17502.Summary: Researchers from DAMO Academy, Alibaba Group, developed RynnVLA-002, a unified vision-language-action (VLA) and world model that integrates environmental dynamics learning with action planning. It achieved high success rates on simulation and real-world robot tasks, often outperforming extensively pretrained baselines without requiring large-scale pretraining itself.
Problem: Existing VLA models lack internal understanding of action dynamics, imagination (predicting future states), and explicit knowledge of physical interactions.
Traditional world models, despite their predictive power, cannot directly generate actions, creating a functional gap for direct robot control.
Autoregressive discrete action generation in VLA models suffered from error accumulation and poor generalization on limited real-world robotic data, leading to slow and non-smooth inference.
Method: RynnVLA-002 unifies VLA and world model capabilities into a single autoregressive framework, initialized from a Large Language Model (Chameleon), learning environmental dynamics and action planning jointly.
It employs a novel attention masking strategy for discrete action generation, ensuring each action relies only on visual and textual inputs to mitigate error propagation.
A compact continuous Action Transformer head generates entire action chunks in parallel using learnable queries, providing smoother trajectories, faster inference, and improved generalization.
Results: Achieved 97.4% success rate with continuous actions on the LIBERO benchmark, matching or exceeding strong baselines without relying on large-scale pretraining.
Demonstrated competitive real-world performance on LeRobot SO100 tasks, with superior robustness in cluttered multi-target environments (e.g., over 80% success in 'Place the block' task).
World model pretraining improved grasping performance, and ablation studies confirmed that the integrated world model significantly improved overall real-world task success rates.
Takeaways: VLA and world models exhibit mutual enhancement: VLA's visual understanding improves world model's generation, while world model's dynamics understanding refines VLA's action generation.
Integrating world model training data is crucial for robust real-world robotic tasks, boosting success rates by 50% in ablation studies.

The continuous Action Transformer design significantly accelerates VLA training convergence, improves final success rates, and offers more efficient and smoother action execution compared to discrete autoregressive methods.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17441.Title: RoboCOIN: An Open-Sourced Bimanual Robotic Data COllection for INtegrated Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.17441.Summary: RoboCOIN is introduced as an open-source, multi-embodiment dataset for bimanual robotic manipulation, developed by researchers from BAAI and various institutions, providing over 180,000 demonstrations across diverse platforms. Its hierarchical annotations and CoRobot data quality framework enhance VLA model performance on complex bimanual tasks, with up to a 23% increase in success rates.
Problem: A scarcity of large-scale, diverse, and richly structured datasets for bimanual robotic manipulation hindered the development of generalist policies.
Hardware heterogeneity across numerous robotic platforms presented challenges for unified data collection and model training.
Existing datasets lacked deep structural understanding beyond raw action trajectories, limiting advanced reasoning and generalization capabilities in robot learning models.
Method: Developed RoboCOIN, an open-sourced dataset comprising over 180,000 bimanual demonstrations collected from 15 distinct robotic platforms across 421 tasks.
Introduced a 'hierarchical capability pyramid' for multi-level annotations (trajectory-level concepts, segment-level subtasks, frame-level kinematics) to enable structured robot learning.

Created CoRobot, an integrated data processing framework, which includes the Robot Trajectory Markup Language (RTML) for quality control and a semi-automatic annotation toolchain for efficient data management.
Results: The hierarchical annotation scheme improved VLA model success rates on a half-humanoid robot, raising simple task success from 80% to 90% and complex task success from 20% to 70%.
RTML filtering identified and removed 35.3% of low-quality trajectories, with grasping failures (52.7%) and velocity violations (46.2%) being the most common issues in human teleoperation.

Training the GR00T-N1.5 model with RTML-filtered data (GR00T-Fine) resulted in a 16% performance gain, and further augmenting with high-quality segments (GR00T-Mine) achieved a total 23% improvement over unfiltered data.
Takeaways: Hierarchical Annotation Integration (HAI) substantially boosts VLA model performance, increasing success rates for complex bimanual tasks from 20% to 70% by providing layered contextual information.
Rigorous data quality control via RTML is critical, filtering out an average of 35.3% of low-quality trajectories and leading to a significant 16% to 23% improvement in robotic policy performance.

The combination of multi-embodiment data, structured annotations, and a robust data processing framework offers a foundational resource for developing more generalist and dexterous bimanual robotic policies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15605.Title: SRPO: Self-Referential Policy Optimization for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15605.Summary: SRPO (Self-Referential Policy Optimization) enhances Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation by addressing reward sparsity, generating dense, progress-wise rewards using the model's own successful trajectories and latent world representations from V-JEPA 2. The method achieved a 99.2% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, a 103% relative improvement over its one-shot SFT baseline, and demonstrated strong generalization on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark.
Problem: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation rely heavily on expert demonstrations, leading to demonstration bias and limited generalization to novel situations.
Acquiring diverse and high-quality expert demonstrations is expensive, time-consuming, and often impractical for a wide range of tasks and environments, hindering scalability.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training in VLA domains faces severe reward sparsity, as agents typically receive only binary success/failure feedback, leading to inefficient learning from failed trajectories and high computational costs.
Method: SRPO introduces a self-referential paradigm that leverages the model's own successful trajectories within the current training batch to generate dense, progress-wise rewards for all trajectories, including failures.
It extracts robust latent world representations for trajectories using a pre-trained large-scale video-pretrained latent world model (V-JEPA 2), which captures transferable behavioral patterns.

Successful trajectory representations are clustered to form stable reference points, and failed trajectories are assigned a reward based on their behavioral similarity (L2 distance) to the closest successful cluster center.
Results: SRPO achieved a new state-of-the-art success rate of 99.2% on the LIBERO benchmark, representing a 103% relative improvement over its initial one-shot Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) baseline, reaching this performance in just 200 RL steps.

The method demonstrated substantial robustness and generalization on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark (featuring seven perturbation dimensions), achieving a 167% performance improvement over its one-shot SFT base model and surpassing full-shot SFT policies.

Qualitative and quantitative analysis showed that SRPO's latent world representation-based reward provides smoother, more monotonic progress curves compared to pixel-level and ImageBind methods, leading to more stable and efficient training across various metrics like Spearman Correlation (0.998) and Monotonicity (0.992).
Takeaways: Dense, progress-wise reward signals can be automatically generated for VLA-RL without external expert demonstrations or manual engineering by referencing a model's own successful trajectories.

Latent world representations from pre-trained world models provide a task-agnostic and robust metric for measuring behavioral progress, enabling effective reward shaping that is transferable across environments and less sensitive to perceptual variations than pixel-level methods.

Integrating this self-referential reward mechanism into a policy optimization framework allows VLA models to efficiently learn from previously uninformative failed trajectories, accelerating training and fostering exploration beyond initial demonstration data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14759.Title: $π^{*}_{0.6}$: a VLA That Learns From Experience
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14759.Summary: A general-purpose reinforcement learning method, RECAP, improves the robustness and throughput of large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models like π*0.6 through real-world deployment experience. This approach doubles task throughput and halves failure rates on complex tasks such as espresso making and diverse laundry folding, achieving practically useful levels of robotic performance.
Problem: Imitation Learning-based VLA models suffer from compounding errors and are limited by demonstration data, preventing them from achieving true skill mastery.
Scaling real-world reinforcement learning to large, high-capacity Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for complex, long-horizon tasks is challenging.
Integrating diverse data sources, including initial demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and human interventions, into a unified and scalable self-improvement process for robots is difficult.
Method: Introduces RECAP (RL with Experience and Corrections via Advantage-conditioned Policies), an iterative training method for VLA models instantiated with π*0.6.
Employs an iterative loop of data collection (autonomous rollouts and human interventions), value function re-training, and advantage-conditioned policy re-training.
Utilizes a novel policy extraction method based on advantage conditioning (similar to classifier-free guidance) that integrates a binarized advantage indicator as a text input for flow-matching VLAs.
Results: RECAP consistently doubled throughput and halved failure rates on complex real-world tasks, including diverse laundry folding and espresso making, with final success rates exceeding 90% on most tasks.
The π*0.6 model demonstrated practical robustness, performing tasks like espresso making for 13 hours without human intervention and assembling boxes in a factory setting.

The advantage-conditioned policy extraction method outperformed other RL approaches like Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) in terms of task throughput on a laundry task.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning can substantially improve the real-world robustness and throughput of large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, moving beyond the inherent limitations of imitation learning.

Advantage-conditioned policy extraction offers a scalable and effective mechanism for integrating RL with expressive flow-matching VLA architectures, circumventing the challenges of traditional policy gradient methods.

An iterative training loop that seamlessly integrates heterogeneous data sources (demonstrations, autonomous experience, and human interventions) is critical for practical, data-efficient robot self-improvement.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14148.Title: AsyncVLA: Asynchronous Flow Matching for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14148.Summary: AsyncVLA introduces an asynchronous flow matching framework for Vision-Language-Action models, allowing robots to dynamically self-correct continuous actions based on a confidence rater. This approach significantly boosts task success rates and robustness across various robotic manipulation benchmarks, including LIBERO, WidowX, and Google Robot.
Problem: Existing VLA models, particularly those based on synchronous Flow Matching (SFM), use rigid and uniform time schedules for continuous action generation, lacking context awareness and asynchronous self-correction.
A single inaccurate action prediction in SFM models can rapidly cascade into unrecoverable errors in long-horizon or precision-demanding robotic tasks.
Previous self-correction methods in VLA models primarily focused on discrete action token generation, leaving a gap for robust self-correction in continuous action spaces.
