Method: The framework proposes Asynchronous Flow Matching (AFM) where an initial action chunk is generated by SFM, followed by a confidence-driven self-correction phase.
A dedicated confidence rater evaluates each SFM-generated action token and masks low-confidence actions for regeneration, leveraging unmasked high-confidence actions as context.
A unified training procedure allows a single model to operate in both SFM and AFM modes, treating SFM as a fully-masked case, which also enables efficient KV-cache reutilization during inference.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art average success rates across various benchmarks, including 97.4% on LIBERO, 70.8% on WidowX, and 74.9% (visual matching) on Google Robot.
Ablation studies confirmed the critical roles of asynchronous flow matching, the confidence rater, and unified training, showing substantial performance degradation upon their removal.

Demonstrated enhanced training data efficiency with faster convergence and lower final training loss in limited data settings, while maintaining efficient inference through significant KV-cache reutilization for the AFM phase.
Takeaways: Temporal asynchrony in action generation is crucial for enabling robust self-correction in continuous action spaces, moving beyond the limitations of rigid synchronous approaches.
An introspective confidence rater can effectively identify and guide the selective re-generation of erroneous action tokens, improving overall task reliability.
A unified training scheme not only enhances model coherence across synchronous and asynchronous operations but also implicitly acts as data augmentation, improving data efficiency.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05275.Title: TwinVLA: Data-Efficient Bimanual Manipulation with Twin Single-Arm Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.05275.Summary: TWINVLA presents a framework for data-efficient bimanual robotic manipulation by composing two pre-trained single-arm Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. This approach achieves performance comparable to or exceeding existing bimanual systems while drastically reducing the need for bimanual demonstration data and computational resources.
Problem: High-quality, large-scale datasets specifically for bimanual robotic manipulation are scarce, making it challenging to train effective policies.

Current state-of-the-art bimanual VLA models rely on thousands of hours of proprietary bimanual demonstrations and immense computational resources for pre-training, limiting accessibility and reproducibility.
Existing bimanual control methods often involve specialized architectures or monolithic VLA models, both of which struggle with data efficiency and generalization.
Method: The framework duplicates two instances of a pre-trained single-arm VLA (SingleVLA) and integrates them into a bimanual system, selectively replicating the VLM backbone while sharing the vision encoder and action head.
A Joint Attention mechanism enables efficient coordination between the two replicated VLM backbones, allowing cross-arm information flow via shared self-attention layers with a causal mask.

Shared inputs (language, ego-centric image) are processed using a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) mechanism, and attention re-weighting is applied to shared modality tokens to preserve pre-trained knowledge during fine-tuning.
Results: TWINVLA demonstrated superior data and compute efficiency, requiring ~50 episodes of bimanual fine-tuning data and ~25 H100 GPU-days, significantly less than baselines like RDT-1B (thousands of hours and GPU-days).
On real-world bimanual tasks, TWINVLA achieved an average success rate of 76% on the Anubis robot, outperforming RDT-1B (45%) and closely approaching π0 (80%), which uses vastly more resources.

The system consistently outperformed RDT-1B in simulation benchmarks (e.g., 75.8% vs 61.6% on Tabletop-Sim Easy) and showed improved language following capabilities, while ablation studies confirmed the critical role of each architectural component.
Takeaways: Complex bimanual skills can be learned efficiently by leveraging and coordinating knowledge from pre-trained single-arm VLA models, rather than requiring extensive bimanual pre-training from scratch.
A modular architecture with lightweight coordination mechanisms (e.g., Joint Attention) offers a data- and compute-efficient alternative to monolithic VLA models for bimanual control.

Techniques like attention re-weighting and MoE integration are critical for effectively transferring and preserving pre-trained knowledge in a new, more complex architecture while optimizing resource usage.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13626.Title: LIBERO-Plus: In-depth Robustness Analysis of Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13626.Summary: Researchers from Fudan University and collaborators developed LIBERO-Plus, a diagnostic benchmark that systematically evaluates the robustness of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models across seven perturbation dimensions. This framework reveals that VLA models exhibit brittle generalization despite achieving high performance on traditional benchmarks.
Problem: VLA models achieve high success rates on standard benchmarks in controlled simulations, but these metrics often conceal deficiencies in real-world applicability.

Current evaluation methodologies focus on aggregate success rates under static, ideal conditions, failing to capture policy stability and reliability under realistic environmental and task variations.
Models struggle to maintain performance with minor variations, exhibiting interpolation rather than true generalization to diverse, dynamic environments.
Method: Introduces LIBERO-Plus, a comprehensive and fine-grained robustness evaluation framework for VLA models implemented in a simulated environment.

Evaluates models across seven distinct perturbation dimensions (e.g., objects layout, camera viewpoints, language instructions, sensor noise) and 21 sub-dimensions, stratified into five difficulty levels.
Utilizes automated task generation to create large, diverse training and test samples, enabling systematic vulnerability analysis and the construction of a generalization-oriented training dataset.
Results: VLA models demonstrate 'brittle generalization,' with performance drops from over 95% to below 30% under modest camera viewpoint or robot initial state perturbations.
Models exhibit 'language ignorance,' often failing to follow modified instructions and relying on visual context, with success rates dropping to nearly zero in goal replacement tasks.

Fine-tuning models on the diverse, generalized dataset constructed for LIBERO-Plus substantially enhances robustness, with the post-trained OpenVLA-OFT achieving 79.6% overall success and 92.8% camera view robustness, significantly outperforming baselines.
Takeaways: Current VLA models often rely on superficial cues like positional memorization or frequently ignore language instructions, rather than demonstrating deep multimodal understanding.

A 'negative compositionality gap' indicates that performance degradation from multiple simultaneous perturbations is often greater than the sum of individual effects, exposing critical entanglements in learned representations.

The inclusion of a first-person wrist camera significantly enhances robustness, particularly to illumination changes, by providing close-range geometric and contact cues that are invariant to lighting.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13054.Title: VLA-0: Building State-of-the-Art VLAs with Zero Modification
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13054.Summary: NVIDIA researchers introduce VLA-0, a Vision-Language-Action model that achieves state-of-the-art robotic manipulation by directly representing robot actions as numerical text strings and fine-tuning an unmodified Vision-Language Model. This minimalist design outperforms more complex or extensively pretrained alternatives in both simulation and real-world tasks.
Problem: Existing VLA models introduce complexity through architectural modifications, specialized action heads, or vocabulary alterations, leading to trade-offs like restricted action resolution or compromised language understanding.

The purest form of representing robot actions directly as text using a VLM's native capabilities for low-level control has largely been unexplored, despite its potential for simplicity and arbitrary action resolution.
Achieving high-fidelity action generation for embodied agents while preserving the foundational knowledge of powerful pre-trained Vision-Language Models remains a challenge.
Method: VLA-0 utilizes an unmodified, off-the-shelf Qwen-VL-2.5-3B Vision-Language Model, avoiding new tokens, vocabulary changes, or additional neural network layers.
Robot actions are represented as continuous values normalized to an integer range and generated directly as space-separated numerical text strings by the VLM's native text generation capability.
The approach incorporates a novel masked action augmentation during training and an action ensembling technique during inference to enhance robustness and performance.
Results: VLA-0 achieves an average success rate of 94.7% on the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming all existing non-pretrained VLA methods and securing an average rank of 1.0.
It demonstrates highly competitive performance against models pretrained on vast robotic datasets, achieving the second-best average rank (2.8) among all evaluated models.
In real-world evaluations on an SO-100 robot, VLA-0 surpasses a strong pretrained baseline (SmolVLA) by an average of 12.5 points in success rate across four manipulation tasks.
Takeaways: Directly representing continuous robot actions as numerical text strings and leveraging a VLM's native text generation, without any architectural modifications, can achieve state-of-the-art performance.

Preserving the integrity of the underlying Vision-Language Model by avoiding architectural changes can unlock latent capabilities for effective action generation and potentially enhance generalization.
Simple training and inference strategies, such as masked action augmentation and action ensembling, are crucial for extracting high performance from this minimalist VLA design.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10274.Title: X-VLA: Soft-Prompted Transformer as Scalable Cross-Embodiment Vision-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.10274.Summary: X-VLA introduces a soft-prompted Transformer architecture designed to address data heterogeneity in large-scale robotics datasets, enabling a scalable Vision-Language-Action model. This model achieves state-of-the-art results across numerous simulation and real-world robot benchmarks, demonstrating robust adaptation with minimal fine-tuning.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle with the inherent heterogeneity in large-scale robotics datasets, stemming from diverse robot embodiments, action spaces, and data collection strategies.
This heterogeneity causes severe distributional shifts and semantic misalignments, leading to unstable pretraining and suboptimal adaptation performance across different robotic platforms.
Prior VLA methods primarily tackle action space heterogeneity with separate decoders, often overlooking other critical sources of variation that limit generalizability and scalability.
Method: X-VLA employs a novel soft-prompt mechanism where unique, learnable embeddings are assigned to each hardware configuration, implicitly encoding embodiment-specific knowledge for heterogeneity-aware guidance.

The architecture is a flow-matching-based VLA framework built upon standard Transformer encoders, integrating a pretrained VLM encoder (Florence-Large) for the main vision-language stream and a shared backbone for auxiliary views.

A customized two-phase training recipe involves pretraining the backbone and soft prompts with a flow-matching objective, followed by parameter-efficient domain adaptation using prompt warm-up and joint policy fine-tuning (LoRA).
Results: X-VLA-0.9B achieved new state-of-the-art results across 5 out of 6 major simulation benchmarks (Libero, Simpler, VLABench, RoboTwin-2.0, NAVSIM) and consistently outperformed baselines on three real-world robotic platforms (WidowX, Agilex, AIRBOT).
The model demonstrated dexterous manipulation capabilities on challenging tasks like bi-manual cloth-folding, achieving nearly 100% success rate on the new "Soft-Fold" dataset.

Parameter-Efficient Fine-tuning (PEFT), tuning only 1% (9M) of the model's parameters, yielded competitive success rates (e.g., 93% on Libero) comparable to fully fine-tuned 3B parameter models, showcasing remarkable data and parameter efficiency.
Takeaways: The soft prompt mechanism effectively absorbs embodiment-specific variations, allowing the core VLA backbone to learn a more generalist, embodiment-agnostic control policy.

X-VLA exhibits strong, unsaturated scaling behavior across model capacity, data diversity, and data volume, with pretraining validation error strongly correlating with improved downstream adaptation performance.

Learned soft prompts show meaningful clustering aligned with hardware configurations and provide strong transfer benefits during adaptation, indicating effective encoding of domain-specific knowledge.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24948.Title: RehearseVLA: Simulated Post-Training for VLAs with Physically-Consistent World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24948.Summary: A simulated post-training framework, RehearseVLA, enhances Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by employing a physically-consistent world model and a VLM-guided instant reflector. The approach yields higher success rates for VLA policies in data-scarce conditions and transfers effectively to real-world robotic tasks.
Problem: VLA models, reliant on imitation learning, struggle with data scarcity, requiring costly and often unsafe large-scale real-world demonstrations.
Reinforcement learning (RL) for VLA post-training is hindered by high real-world interaction costs, non-resettable environments, and the "sim-to-real" gap in traditional simulators.
Current VLA approaches lack robust task completion detection, leading to redundant actions that can disrupt achieved goal states and reduce overall task success.
Method: Proposes RehearseVLA, a framework for VLA post-training that uses a low-cost, world model-based virtual simulator to replace real-world interactions for reinforcement learning.
Develops a physically-consistent world simulator that generates action-conditioned future observations by injecting geometry-aware features (VGGT, CLIP) into a U-Net diffusion network.
Implements a VLM-guided instant reflector, a semantics-aware reward mechanism that provides continuous reward signals and dynamically terminates actions upon task success.
Results: Achieved an average 79.6% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark with only five expert demonstrations per task, surpassing supervised fine-tuning baselines like OpenVLA-OFT (74.85%).
Demonstrated effective transfer to real-world tasks, improving success rates (e.g., from 20% for baseline to 30% for RehearseVLA on "clean table").
The VLM-guided instant reflector's dynamic termination mechanism improved average success rates (74.9% vs. 63.05% for OpenVLA-OFT without termination) by preventing redundant post-success actions.
Takeaways: Training the world simulator with a diverse dataset, including autonomously explored successful and failed trajectories, is crucial for improving its fidelity and the robustness of VLA training.
Integrating geometry-aware features (VGGT and CLIP) into the world model's generation process is essential for synthesizing physically plausible and temporally consistent visual observations.

A continuous, trainable reward head in the instant reflector, rather than sparse binary rewards or VLM-based classification, provides more reliable advantage estimates, improving RL sample efficiency and stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22643.Title: VLA-Reasoner: Empowering Vision-Language-Action Models with Reasoning via Online Monte Carlo Tree Search
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.22643.Summary: VLA-Reasoner enhances Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models with test-time reasoning through online Monte Carlo Tree Search, simulating future states to select optimal actions. This framework improves VLA performance in long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks, demonstrating an absolute 19% increase in real-world success rates for OpenVLA and consistent gains in simulated environments.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models make short-sighted next-action predictions, neglecting long-horizon sequential dependencies.
This leads to incremental deviations that accumulate over time, causing task failures in complex, multi-step robotic manipulation.
Limitations in accuracy and exploration make VLAs fragile when encountering distribution shifts in real-world environments.
Method: VLA-Reasoner is introduced as a plug-in framework that empowers off-the-shelf VLAs with foresight via online Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) during test time.
It employs a learned world model to simulate future states and action trajectories, while Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) efficiently generates plausible action candidates.
A vision-based value network provides dense feedback for evaluating intermediate, model-generated states, guiding the MCTS towards optimal actions.
Results: In simulation, VLA-Reasoner improved OpenVLA-SFT's average success rate by an absolute 5% on the LIBERO benchmark and enhanced Octo-Small and SpatialVLA by an average of 9.8% and 7.8% respectively on SimplerEnv.

In real-world experiments, the framework boosted OpenVLA's average success rate by an absolute 19% (from 22% to 41%) and increased π0-FAST's by 10% (from 64% to 74%) across five challenging manipulation tasks.

Ablation studies confirmed that KDE-based action sampling (91.5% success) outperformed Gaussian noise sampling (85.0%), and image-based value estimation (91.5%) was more effective than token-based approaches (87.0%).
Takeaways: Integrating a test-time MCTS can effectively mitigate the accumulation of short-sighted errors in VLAs by allowing the model to reason about future action consequences.

Efficient action sampling via KDE, implicitly reflecting smoothed expert behaviors, and accurate image-based value estimation are critical for practical online tree search in high-dimensional action spaces.
Blending the VLA's immediate prediction with the MCTS-reasoned action, with a moderate injection strength, achieves superior performance by balancing generalist capabilities with focused foresight.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18644.Title: Do You Need Proprioceptive States in Visuomotor Policies?
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.18644.Summary: Robotic visuomotor policies achieve dramatically improved spatial generalization by removing proprioceptive state inputs. This approach leverages a relative end-effector action space and comprehensive egocentric vision to enable robust task performance across varied spatial configurations, while also enhancing data efficiency and cross-embodiment adaptation.
Problem: Existing visuomotor policies, reliant on proprioceptive states, show limited spatial generalization, struggling with variations in object placement or robot starting positions.
Proprioceptive states encourage policies to overfit by memorizing specific training trajectories, preventing the learning of a generalizable visual understanding.
Addressing generalization issues in state-based policies typically requires extensive and costly data collection across numerous spatial configurations.
Method: Introduces "State-free Policies" by completely omitting proprioceptive state inputs from the visuomotor policy.
Employs a relative end-effector (EEF) action space, allowing actions to be invariant to the robot's absolute pose and dependent only on visual observations.
Utilizes dual wide-angle wrist-cameras to ensure full, egocentric visual observation of the task environment, critical for policies relying solely on visual cues.
Results: State-free Policies achieved up to 98% height generalization and 58% horizontal generalization success rates for manipulation tasks, compared to 0% for state-based policies.
The method consistently improved spatial generalization across 5 real-world tasks, multiple robot embodiments, and various policy architectures (π0, ACT, Diffusion Policy).
Demonstrated enhanced data efficiency for in-domain tasks and faster cross-embodiment adaptation, requiring less fine-tuning data for new robot platforms.
Takeaways: Proprioceptive states, while seemingly beneficial, can act as a "shortcut" that limits a policy's ability to generalize spatially.
A relative end-effector action space is crucial for enabling spatial invariance in vision-only policies, ensuring consistent actions despite absolute pose changes.
Comprehensive egocentric vision from wide-angle wrist cameras can be more effective for spatial generalization than traditional world-centric overhead cameras, especially in out-of-domain scenarios.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09674.Title: SimpleVLA-RL: Scaling VLA Training via Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09674.Summary: SimpleVLA-RL is a reinforcement learning framework designed to improve Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by using outcome-based rewards and an efficient online training approach. This method significantly enhances model performance, generalization, and data efficiency in robotic manipulation tasks while also enabling the discovery of novel manipulation strategies.
Problem: VLA model training suffers from data scarcity and high costs associated with acquiring extensive, high-quality human-operated robotic trajectories for Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT).
SFT-trained VLA models often exhibit poor generalization to new, unseen tasks, objects, or environmental configurations.
Prior VLA-RL methods frequently relied on complex hand-crafted process rewards or intricate reward modeling, which limits their scalability and broad applicability.
Method: The research developed SimpleVLA-RL, an efficient online reinforcement learning framework for VLA models, by extending the `veRL` framework for LLMs and adapting the `Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)` algorithm.
It employs a scalable, sparse binary outcome-based reward (1 for task success, 0 for failure) that is propagated uniformly across trajectories, simplifying reward design.

The framework integrates VLA-specific adaptations, including token-based action generation, closed-loop multi-round environment interaction, and parallel multi-environment rendering for faster trajectory sampling.
Results: SimpleVLA-RL achieved state-of-the-art performance on the LIBERO benchmark, boosting the average success rate from 91% to 99.1% and improving LIBERO-Long tasks by 12%.
It demonstrated robust data efficiency, increasing success rates from 48.9% (One-Trajectory SFT) to 96.9% on LIBERO tasks after RL training, approaching the performance of full-data SFT+RL.
The policies trained in simulation showed strong sim-to-real transfer, improving real-world success rates on RoboTwin2.0 tasks from 17.5% (SFT-only) to 38.5% on average.
The RL-trained policy discovered novel "pushcut" strategies in tasks like "move can pot," replacing the demonstrated grasp-and-place behaviors with more efficient pushing actions.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning with sparse, outcome-based rewards can drastically reduce the reliance on extensive demonstration data for VLA models, achieving near state-of-the-art performance with significantly fewer demonstrations.
RL training substantially enhances VLA models' generalization capabilities across spatial, object, and task variations, mitigating catastrophic forgetting observed in SFT-only methods.
RL can drive the discovery of emergent, more efficient behaviors (e.g., "pushcut" strategies) that were not present in human demonstrations, indicating optimization beyond pure imitation.
The effectiveness of VLA-RL is strongly correlated with the initial competence of the SFT-tuned base model; stronger initial priors lead to greater performance improvements after RL.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09372.Title: VLA-Adapter: An Effective Paradigm for Tiny-Scale Vision-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09372.Summary: Researchers from Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Westlake University, and Zhejiang University, along with the OpenHelix Team, introduce VLA-Adapter, an efficient method to bridge vision-language representations to robotic actions. The approach enables state-of-the-art level performance with a tiny-scale 0.5B parameter backbone without robotic data pre-training, achieving a 97.3% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark and providing a 3x faster inference speed (219.2 Hz) than comparable methods.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models incur high training and inference costs, relying on large, multi-billion parameter Vision-Language Models (VLMs).
Extensive pre-training on robotic datasets is often required, leading to slow fine-tuning and high GPU memory consumption.
These factors limit the accessibility, real-time control capabilities, and deployment of VLA models on resource-constrained hardware.
Method: VLA-Adapter introduces a lightweight Policy network that efficiently bridges vision-language (VL) representations to action (A) by optimizing the multimodal conditions it receives from the VLM.
It systematically analyzes and integrates both all-layer raw VLM features and all-layer ActionQuery features using a novel Bridge Attention module within the Policy network.
A learnable injection ratio is incorporated into the Bridge Attention to selectively inject relevant information from raw features, ensuring optimal information transfer to the action space.
Results: VLA-Adapter achieved a 97.3% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark with a 0.5B parameter VLM backbone, matching or exceeding the performance of many 7B+ parameter models.
It demonstrated superior efficiency, achieving an inference throughput of 219.2 Hz (approximately 3 times faster than OpenVLA-OFT) and the fastest reported latency of 0.0365 seconds.
The model exhibited strong zero-shot generalization on the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark with a 4.42 average task length and successfully performed complex tasks in real-world robotic experiments.
Takeaways: Middle-layer raw latent features from the VLM are more effective for action generation than deep-layer ones, as they better balance multimodal integration with rich detail.
Deep-layer ActionQuery latents prove to be more effective, aggregating richer multimodal details from scratch for action prediction.

A learnable injection ratio for raw features in conjunction with direct use of ActionQuery features allows the Policy to effectively absorb and utilize essential multimodal information, enhancing performance and stability.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06951.Title: F1: A Vision-Language-Action Model Bridging Understanding and Generation to Actions
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06951.Summary: F₁, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, integrates explicit visual foresight into its decision-making process, moving beyond purely reactive control. This approach yields enhanced robustness in dynamic environments and improved generalization across a range of real-world and simulated robotic manipulation tasks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models largely depend on reactive state-to-action mappings.
This reactive paradigm leads to short-sighted behaviors and poor robustness in dynamic scenes, struggling with generalization and long-horizon tasks.
Existing approaches lacked an explicit mechanism to reason about future states or temporal evolution, hindering adaptability in complex environments.
Method: F₁ introduces a Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) architecture with dedicated Understanding, Generation, and Action experts.
It integrates explicit goal-conditioned visual foresight into decision-making, reframing action generation as a foresight-guided inverse dynamics problem.
A three-stage progressive training recipe is employed, involving generation-understanding alignment, full model pretraining on large datasets, and task-specific adaptation.
Results: F₁ achieved an 82.2% average success rate across 9 real-world Genie robot tasks, surpassing `π₀`'s 65.2%, and demonstrated a 93.3% success rate on the challenging 'Handover (R2H)' task compared to `π₀`'s 40%.

The model showed a 66.7% overall success rate for continuous dual-arm dynamic grasping on a novel robot in moving belt scenarios and sustained meaningful success across a 10-step long-horizon task, where `π₀` failed after basic grasps.

Ablation studies confirmed that removing the generation expert significantly dropped performance by 17.2% in simulation and similarly in real-world tasks, validating the critical role of visual foresight.
Takeaways: Explicitly generating and using goal-conditioned visual foresight allows VLA models to move beyond reactive control, enabling proactive planning and significantly improving robustness in dynamic scenes.
Even with imperfect pixel-level visual foresight, the 'actionable guidance' provided by anticipated future states is sufficient to greatly enhance downstream robotic control accuracy and reliability.

A progressive, multi-stage training approach, leveraging both pretrained multimodal understanding and large-scale robotics data, is crucial for developing stable, generalizable, and transferable visuomotor policies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04996.Title: FLOWER: Democratizing Generalist Robot Policies with Efficient Vision-Language-Action Flow Policies
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04996.Summary: FLOWER presents an efficient Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy for generalist robotics, achieving competitive or superior performance on 190 tasks across 10 benchmarks. It accomplishes this with a 99% reduction in pretraining compute and significantly lower memory requirements compared to prior large models, by incorporating intermediate modality fusion and a cross-action space Flow Transformer.
Problem: Existing generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies are computationally prohibitive, demanding multi-billion parameters, massive pretraining compute (e.g., tens of thousands of GPU hours), and high VRAM.
The high resource requirements of current VLAs create significant barriers to entry for diverse research communities and restrict practical real-world deployment on commodity hardware.
Current VLA architectures struggle to effectively balance rich semantic understanding from large pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with efficient and accurate action generation.
Method: Develops an efficient 950M parameter VLA policy using intermediate modality fusion, which prunes VLM layers and conditions the Flow Transformer on intermediate VLM embeddings for semantic richness with reduced overhead.

Introduces a cross-action space Flow Transformer leveraging Action-Space Global-AdaLN-Zero to efficiently handle heterogeneous action spaces with 20% fewer parameters, augmented by LoRA adapters for fine-grained modulation.
Utilizes Rectified Flow for action generation, enabling high-quality action sequences with fewer denoising steps and improved inference efficiency, crucial for low-latency control.
Results: FLOWER achieved a new State-of-the-Art (SoTA) performance of 4.53 average sequence length on the CALVIN ABC benchmark, surpassing OpenVLA and ",0.

The policy demonstrated a 99% reduction in pretraining compute, requiring only 200 GPU hours compared to tens of thousands for models like OpenVLA and RDT-1B, while achieving competitive performance across 190 tasks.

In real-world evaluations, FLOWER doubled the average success rate of the second-best baseline (OpenVLA) across 20 distinct tasks (61% vs. 31%) and showed robust generalization to novel objects and challenging environmental conditions.
Takeaways: Intermediate modality fusion provides an optimal balance between VLM semantic richness and computational efficiency for robotic manipulation, outperforming early and late fusion strategies.

The novel Action-Space Global-AdaLN-Zero mechanism can significantly reduce the parameter count of the transformer head while maintaining performance, by sharing modulation weights across layers for action-type conditioning.

Pre-trained Vision-Language Models emphasizing object detection and visual grounding, such as Florence-2-L, are more effective as backbones for robotic manipulation tasks compared to general reasoning models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00576.Title: Galaxea Open-World Dataset and G0 Dual-System VLA Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.00576.Summary: The Galaxea Team introduces a 500-hour Open-World Dataset collected in diverse real-world environments with a consistent robotic embodiment, alongside G0, a dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model. This work demonstrates that single-embodiment pre-training on high-quality, in-domain data is critical for achieving robust action execution and few-shot learning for complex mobile manipulation tasks.
Problem: A severe scarcity of large-scale, high-quality, and diverse robot behavior data collected in authentic, unstructured human environments.
Existing robot datasets often feature controlled settings, insufficient environmental richness, or inconsistencies across heterogeneous embodiments, creating a "domain gap" for real-world deployment.
Unclear understanding of optimal pre-training strategies for VLA models, particularly the effectiveness and interplay of cross-embodiment versus single-embodiment data for specific robot platforms.
Method: Introduction of the Galaxea Open-World Dataset, comprising 500 hours of high-fidelity data from a single robot embodiment (Galaxea R1 Lite) across 50 diverse real-world scenes with fine-grained subtask language annotations.
Development of G0, a dual-system framework where G0-VLM (System 2) handles high-level task planning and G0-VLA (System 1) performs real-time, fine-grained action execution asynchronously.
A robust 3-stage training curriculum for G0-VLA: cross-embodiment pre-training, single-embodiment pre-training on the Galaxea dataset, and task-specific post-training.
Results: The full G0 model, utilizing both cross-embodiment and single-embodiment pre-training, achieved the highest average progress scores across diverse tabletop and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks.

Models with Stage-2 (single-embodiment) pre-training demonstrated superior language following, action consistency, and whole-body control, and significantly outperformed other models in few-shot transfer scenarios.

The fine-tuned G0-VLM significantly surpassed baseline VLM models by over 50% in instruction accuracy for generating subtask sequences, validating its role as an effective task planner for robotic applications.
Takeaways: High-quality, single-embodiment pre-training on in-domain data is indispensable for strong VLA performance, significantly enhancing language following, action consistency, whole-body control, and few-shot transfer capabilities.
Cross-embodiment pre-training alone provides limited benefits and can even degrade performance for embodiment-specific skills when a large embodiment gap exists between source and target robots.

Domain-specific fine-tuning of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) is crucial for robotic task planning, enabling significantly higher instruction accuracy and better alignment with executable action primitives.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19236.Title: MemoryVLA: Perceptual-Cognitive Memory in Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19236.Summary: Researchers from Tsinghua University and Dexmal developed MemoryVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model for robotic manipulation that integrates a bio-inspired dual-memory system. This system allows robots to leverage both short-term perceptual details and long-term cognitive semantics, achieving up to a +26 percentage point gain on real-world long-horizon temporal tasks compared to prior VLA models.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic manipulation primarily rely on instantaneous observations, neglecting temporal context.

This leads to poor performance in long-horizon, temporally dependent, and non-Markovian tasks where past events are crucial for decision-making (e.g., tracking progress or avoiding redundant actions).
Existing temporal modeling attempts often suffer from computational inefficiency (frame concatenation), loss of fine-grained detail (latent propagation), or superficial reasoning (chain-of-thought).
Method: A Cognition-Memory-Action framework (MemoryVLA) is introduced, inspired by the human dual-memory system, integrating vision-language processing with structured memory.
A Perceptual–Cognitive Memory Bank (PCMB) is designed to store both low-level perceptual details and high-level cognitive semantics over extended horizons.

The PCMB features mechanisms for retrieving decision-relevant historical context, adaptively fusing it with current observations via a gate mechanism, and consolidating new experiences to maintain a compact memory.
Results: MemoryVLA achieved an average success rate of 71.9% on SimplerEnv-Bridge, outperforming the CogACT-Large baseline by +14.6 percentage points.

On real-world long-horizon temporal tasks, it demonstrated an 83% success score, marking a substantial +26 percentage point gain over CogACT and significant improvements on tasks like "Seq. Push Buttons" (+43).

The model showed strong robustness and generalization across various out-of-distribution conditions and introduced minimal inference overhead (+3.6% latency, +0.8 GB GPU memory) compared to a baseline.
Takeaways: Adopting a dual-memory system (working and episodic-like memory) allows VLA models to effectively manage both immediate and long-term temporal information for complex tasks.
Explicitly distinguishing and storing perceptual details and cognitive semantics enables a more comprehensive understanding of task progress and context over time.
Adaptive gate fusion dynamically balances the influence of current observations and retrieved historical context, while redundancy-aware consolidation efficiently manages memory capacity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18269.Title: FlowVLA: Visual Chain of Thought-based Motion Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18269.Summary: Researchers at HKUST(GZ) and Shanghai Jiao Tong University developed FlowVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that incorporates a "Visual Chain of Thought" to explicitly reason about motion dynamics via optical flow before generating future frames. This approach yields physically coherent predictions, state-of-the-art performance in complex robot manipulation tasks, and significantly improved sample efficiency.
Problem: Existing VLA world models based on direct next-frame prediction often produce blurry, inconsistent, or physically implausible long-horizon visual forecasts, dubbed the "pixel-copying trap."
A "domain gap" exists between passive observational knowledge acquired during pre-training and the active, action-oriented knowledge needed for policy learning, leading to inefficient fine-tuning.
Direct pixel-space regression for world modeling is an ill-posed objective that hinders the acquisition of robust physical reasoning in VLA models.
Method: Introduces the "Visual Chain of Thought" (Visual CoT) paradigm, which compels the model to first reason about motion dynamics (predict `f_t`) and then generate the future frame (`v_t+1`) based on this predicted motion, formulated as `v_t "\u2192" f_t "\u2192" v_t+1`.
Develops FlowVLA, an autoregressive Transformer model that materializes this paradigm by predicting an intermediate optical flow field (`f_t`) as a concrete representation of motion.

Utilizes a unified tokenization strategy where 2-channel optical flow fields are converted into 3-channel RGB-like "flow maps" and processed by the exact same VQ-GAN tokenizer as standard RGB frames, ensuring architectural simplicity and parameter efficiency.
Results: FlowVLA achieved state-of-the-art performance on robotics benchmarks, with an average success rate of 88.1% on LIBERO and 74.0% on SimplerEnv, showing superior robustness to visual domain shifts.
In real-robot experiments on the AgileX Cobot, FlowVLA obtained an average success rate of 44.0%, outperforming baselines, particularly in complex bimanual manipulation tasks.

The model demonstrated superior sample efficiency, reaching baseline peak performance with one-third of training steps (2k vs. 6k) in full-data regimes and achieving 55% higher peak success rates in low-data regimes (50% data).
Takeaways: Explicitly modeling motion dynamics (optical flow) as an intermediate step within a causal chain significantly improves the physical plausibility and semantic consistency of future visual predictions compared to direct next-frame prediction.
The Visual CoT paradigm acts as a powerful inductive bias, dramatically boosting sample efficiency during policy fine-tuning and enabling more effective learning, especially in low-data regimes.

A unified architectural approach, where a single autoregressive Transformer processes both visual appearance and motion tokens from a shared latent space, fosters deep cross-modal representations while maintaining simplicity.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10333.Title: ReconVLA: Reconstructive Vision-Language-Action Model as Effective Robot Perceiver
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10333.Summary: ReconVLA introduces a reconstructive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that enhances visual attention grounding by implicitly training the VLA to reconstruct the "gaze region" of the manipulated object in a latent space. This approach achieves a 3.95 average subtask length on the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark and demonstrates improved generalization to unseen objects in real-world robotic manipulation.
Problem: Robotic Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models suffer from dispersed visual attention, hindering precise object interaction.
This lack of precise visual grounding causes inaccurate manipulation, struggles with long-horizon tasks, and poor generalization to novel environments.
Existing visual grounding paradigms (explicit or Chain-of-Thought) often rely on external models or are challenging to train effectively, failing to fundamentally improve VLA's intrinsic attention.
Method: A reconstructive learning framework is integrated into a VLA model, training it to perform latent visual reconstruction of the "gaze region" (target object).
A lightweight diffusion transformer denoiser, conditioned on the VLA's internal visual tokens, learns to predict noise added to latent "scene tokens" derived from the gaze region.

A large-scale visual pretraining dataset, automatically annotated with gaze regions via Grounding DINO, is used to enhance the VLA's generative capabilities and generalization to diverse manipulation tasks.
Results: ReconVLA achieved the highest average subtask completion length of 3.95 on the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark, surpassing other grounding paradigms.
Visualizations demonstrated concentrated attention on target objects, translating to a 79.5% success rate for "stack block" compared to 59.3% for the baseline.
Real-world experiments showed superior generalization, with ReconVLA successfully manipulating unseen objects where other Vision-Language-Action models failed.
Takeaways: Implicit visual grounding, achieved by training the VLA to reconstruct the task-relevant "gaze region," effectively refines the model's internal attention.
This reconstructive learning paradigm inherently forces the VLA to encode precise visual information, improving fine-grained perception for manipulation tasks.

Pretraining the VLA on a large, diverse dataset of robot trajectories with automatically annotated gaze regions is essential for building robust visual generation capabilities and enhancing generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07917.Title: MolmoAct: Action Reasoning Models that can Reason in Space
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.07917.Summary: MolmoAct introduces a class of Action Reasoning Models that integrate depth-aware perception tokens and visual reasoning traces into a three-stage pipeline to enhance robotic manipulation. This approach yields state-of-the-art performance across simulation and real-world benchmarks, improves out-of-distribution generalization, and allows for intuitive visual steering.
Problem: Existing robotic foundation models, particularly Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, often lack adaptability, robustness, and opaque decision-making when transferring across tasks, scenes, or robot embodiments.

Current VLA models struggle with a lack of 3D spatial understanding, relying purely on RGB images, and suffer from information loss when distilling complex 3D trajectories into high-level linguistic descriptions for planning.
The brittleness and ambiguity of language-only steering make precise control difficult and are sensitive to out-of-distribution phrasing.
Method: A three-stage autoregressive pipeline predicts depth-aware perception tokens, mid-level spatial plans as visual reasoning traces, and then low-level robot actions, grounding reasoning in explicit spatial understanding.
Action tokenization discretizes continuous action dimensions into byte-level BPE symbols, preserving ordinal structure and reducing training time significantly.

A new steerability mechanism allows users to draw visual reasoning traces directly on camera images, which are then used to condition the model's action predictions, providing precise and unambiguous control.
Results: MolmoAct-7B-D achieved an 86.6% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark and demonstrated superior adaptation efficiency, with an average of +10% task progression over π0-FAST on real-world single-arm tasks and +22.7% on bimanual tasks.

The model showed strong out-of-distribution generalization, achieving 72.1% success on SimplerEnv variant-aggregation tasks (7.8% higher than RT-2-X) and a 23.3% average improvement in task progression over π0-FAST across real-world OOD conditions.
Visual trace steering achieved a 75% success rate, representing a 33% improvement compared to steering with open-ended natural language instructions, demonstrating enhanced precision and robustness.
Takeaways: Integrating explicit spatial reasoning through depth perception tokens and visual reasoning traces overcomes limitations of purely linguistic Chain-of-Thought approaches for precise 3D manipulation.
Structured intermediate representations, like visual reasoning traces, enable both greater explainability of robot behavior and intuitive, precise user steerability.

A carefully curated MolmoAct Dataset, designed for mid-training, alongside efficient action tokenization, is crucial for improving general manipulation performance and spatial reasoning in real-world household settings.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00795.Title: Video Generators are Robot Policies
https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.00795.Summary: A "Video Policy" framework developed by Columbia University and Toyota Research Institute leverages video generation as a proxy for robot policy acquisition, demonstrating improved generalization and sample efficiency in visuomotor learning, including state-of-the-art results with as few as 50 human demonstrations per task.
Problem: Existing visuomotor policies struggle with poor generalization to novel situations, such as unseen objects, backgrounds, or new tasks, due to perceptual or behavioral distribution shifts.
Learning robust visuomotor policies typically requires large volumes of expensive and labor-intensive human demonstration data.
Current methods underutilize the powerful implicit priors about object movement and physical interactions present in large-scale video generative models.
Method: The "Video Policy" framework employs a modular design consisting of a Video U-Net (fine-tuned SVD) for synthesizing future robot roll-out videos conditioned on language descriptions.
An Action U-Net is introduced, which predicts robot actions by conditioning on intermediate hidden embeddings extracted from the decoder layers of the Video U-Net.
A two-stage training process is used: first fine-tuning the Video U-Net for video prediction, then training the Action U-Net while preventing gradients from propagating back to the Video U-Net.
Results: Video Policy achieved state-of-the-art average success rates on the RoboCasa and Libero10 benchmarks, notably outperforming baselines with only 50 human demonstrations per task.
The method demonstrated strong generalization in real-world manipulation tasks, adapting robustly to unseen objects, varying object locations, and novel backgrounds.
Ablation studies confirmed that the two-stage training and fine-tuning the video model on robot demonstration videos are critical for high performance and generalization across tasks.
Takeaways: Video generative models can effectively serve as a robust proxy for robot policies, allowing for intrinsic linking of visual task understanding with executable actions.

The two-stage training methodology with gradient stopping is crucial, enabling the video generator to focus on coherent visual behavior while the action decoder efficiently translates visual cues into commands.

Leveraging action-free video data to pre-train the video generation model significantly enhances generalization capabilities, allowing the policy to adapt to tasks with minimal or no direct action supervision.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16815.Title: ThinkAct: Vision-Language-Action Reasoning via Reinforced Visual Latent Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.16815.Summary: A dual-system framework named ThinkAct enables Multimodal Large Language Models to perform long-horizon planning and guide robotic actions through reinforced visual latent planning. This approach achieves success rates up to 15.5% higher than baselines on SimplerEnv robot manipulation tasks and demonstrates emergent capabilities like few-shot adaptation and self-correction.
Problem: End-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack explicit reasoning, limiting their ability to handle complex instructions and long-horizon tasks.
Supervised chain-of-thought (CoT) methods for VLA require expensive, high-quality reasoning annotations, hindering scalability and generalization.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) for MLLM reasoning in embodied tasks typically uses abstract, QA-style rewards that lack direct grounding in physical actions and visual outcomes.
Method: A dual-system framework integrates a 'slow thinking' Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) for high-level planning and a 'fast control' action model for low-level execution.
The MLLM is fine-tuned using reinforced visual latent planning, employing novel action-aligned rewards that measure visual goal completion and trajectory consistency.
MLLM reasoning is compressed into a compact 'visual plan latent' which explicitly conditions the downstream action model, effectively bridging high-level deliberation and low-level control.
Results: ThinkAct achieved improved success rates on robot manipulation benchmarks, including a 15.5% increase over its base policy on SimplerEnv Google-VM split and an 84.4% overall success rate on LIBERO, outperforming CoT-VLA and OpenVLA.
It demonstrated higher accuracy on embodied reasoning tasks, achieving 48.2% on EgoPlan-Bench2 and a BLEU score of 59.8 on RoboVQA, surpassing competitive MLLMs like GPT-4V and fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL.

The framework exhibited emergent capabilities such as few-shot adaptation to novel skills with limited demonstrations and the ability to self-correct from execution errors by detecting failures and generating revised plans.
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning with action-aligned visual feedback effectively grounds MLLM reasoning in embodied tasks, enabling robust long-horizon planning.
Compressing complex MLLM reasoning into a visual plan latent provides a crucial interface for explicitly steering and enhancing downstream action execution.
A dual-system architecture with asynchronous reasoning and acting can elicit emergent capabilities such as few-shot adaptation to new tasks and self-correction from execution failures.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09160.Title: Tactile-VLA: Unlocking Vision-Language-Action Model's Physical Knowledge for Tactile Generalization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09160.Summary: TACTILE-VLA integrates tactile sensing into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, enabling robots to interpret force-related language and apply common-sense grasp forces for contact-rich tasks. This framework demonstrates generalization to novel objects and environments, along with adaptive reasoning for physical failure recovery.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily rely on visual feedback, limiting their ability to ground decisions in fine-grained physical interactions, especially in contact-rich scenarios.
VLAs struggle with tasks requiring precise force control, such as grasping fragile objects or delicate insertion, often failing due to insufficient or ambiguous visual information.
Existing tactile sensing efforts in robotics often lack the language-driven generalization and world knowledge offered by modern VLA models.
Method: A multi-modal transformer architecture fuses vision, language, and tactile inputs into a deeply integrated representation, leveraging a pre-trained VLM backbone.
A force-aware action expert generates augmented action vectors specifying both target position and target contact force, coupled with a hybrid position-force controller for adaptive force regulation.

A Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning module, finetuned on failure events, enables the model to diagnose physical interaction problems from tactile feedback and autonomously generate corrective instructions.
Results: TACTILE-VLA achieved superior success rates in tactile-relevant instruction following, such as 90% in the Charger task compared to 40-25% for baselines, and successfully generalized force adverbs to unseen contexts (e.g., 'harder' applied 2.94N vs 'hard' 2.57N).

The model demonstrated strong common-sense generalization in tabletop grasping, inferring and applying appropriate forces for various out-of-domain objects (e.g., 90% success for OOD fragile paper box without damage).

TACTILE-VLA-CoT achieved 80% zero-shot success in the challenging blackboard wiping task by autonomously adapting applied force from an initial 3.5N to 6.7N after diagnosing insufficient force, while baselines largely failed (0-15%).
Takeaways: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) implicitly retain a latent, semantic understanding of physical interaction that can be activated and leveraged through tactile sensing with minimal demonstrations.

Directly incorporating force targets into the action space and training with a Conditional Flow Matching objective enables the model to effectively map linguistic nuances to corresponding physical force magnitudes.
Tactile-involved Chain-of-Thought reasoning allows for robust adaptation to novel, physically distinct scenarios by diagnosing failures and adjusting force-based strategies autonomously.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04447.Title: DreamVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model Dreamed with Comprehensive World Knowledge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04447.Summary: DreamVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model from a collaboration including Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Tsinghua University, enhances robot manipulation by forecasting comprehensive future world knowledge, including dynamic regions, depth, and semantics. It achieves this by integrating these predictions into a unified transformer, leading to improved generalization and higher success rates across various robotic tasks while maintaining efficient inference.
Problem: Existing VLA models primarily use direct observation-to-action mapping, lacking the 'closed-loop forecasting' capability for future states that humans possess.
Prior future state prediction methods suffer from inefficiency due to redundant pixel information and often lack explicit 3D spatial or high-level semantic knowledge.
Current robot policies struggle with generalization in novel or complex scenarios due to an inability to explicitly reason about future environmental changes.
Method: DreamVLA introduces a novel VLA framework that predicts compact, task-relevant world knowledge (dynamic regions, depth maps, and high-level semantic features) instead of full future frames.

It employs a unified transformer architecture with a block-wise structured attention mechanism and disentangled queries to process multimodal inputs and separately predict future dynamic, depth, and semantic knowledge.
Actions are generated via a denoising diffusion transformer conditioned on the predicted world embedding, allowing the model to skip pixel-level reconstruction during inference for efficiency.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN ABC-D benchmark with an average task length of 4.44 and an impressive 92.6% average score on the LIBERO benchmark suites.

Demonstrated a 76.7% overall average success rate in real-world manipulation tasks using a Franka Panda arm, significantly outperforming strong baselines like Diffusion Policy (50.8%) and Octo-Base (45.0%).

Ablation studies confirmed that dynamic region prediction, the structured attention mechanism, and disentangled queries are critical components, with their removal leading to notable performance degradation.
Takeaways: Forecasting compact, motion-centric dynamic regions is crucial for action semantics, providing the greatest performance gain compared to other knowledge types or full optical flow prediction.

Disentangling different types of future world knowledge (dynamic, depth, semantics) using structured attention and separate queries is essential for preventing information leakage and achieving robust reasoning.

Predicting future world knowledge, rather than merely reconstructing current observations, provides a richer, action-oriented signal that significantly improves learning effectiveness and task generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22242.Title: 4D-VLA: Spatiotemporal Vision-Language-Action Pretraining with Cross-Scene Calibration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22242.Summary: The 4D-VLA framework enhances vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining by integrating 3D coordinate embeddings and multi-frame historical context to resolve issues of ambiguous robot positioning and latent state. This approach achieves a 12.1% higher average success rate compared to OpenVLA on LIBERO benchmarks and demonstrates robust generalization across diverse simulated and real-world robotic tasks.
Problem: Existing VLA pretraining paradigms often suffer from "coordinate system chaos," where single-image inputs lack sufficient spatial context to infer a robot's precise position and orientation, leading to dispersed action distributions.

Models experience "state chaos" when single frames provide insufficient temporal or contextual cues, resulting in ambiguity for actions, such as symmetric trajectories or visually similar observations requiring different movements.
The limitations of incomplete inputs hinder the efficient pretraining and broad generalization of VLA models across diverse robotic tasks and viewpoints.
Method: Integrates 3D coordinate information derived from depth data and camera poses into "spatial vision tokens," explicitly grounding visual features in a 3D space to resolve coordinate system ambiguity.

Incorporates temporal dynamics by using an adaptive "memory bank sampling" (MBS) strategy to select informative historical frames, augmented with learnable temporal positional encodings, to mitigate state chaos.

Utilizes a large pretrained vision-language model (InternVL-4B) as a backbone, fine-tuned with a composite loss function including translation, rotation, grip, and directional terms for robust action prediction.
Results: 4D-VLA achieves an average 12.1% higher success rate than OpenVLA on LIBERO simulation benchmarks, including a 25.4% improvement on challenging long-horizon tasks (LIBERO-LONG).

On the novel MV-Bench, 4D-VLA demonstrates superior spatial understanding, achieving an 81.0% success rate in in-view settings (28.8% higher than OpenVLA) and strong generalization with 73.8% in cross-view settings.

Real-world evaluations using a Franka arm show the full 4D-VLA model achieving an 85.63% average success rate, significantly outperforming OpenVLA (27.70%) in tasks requiring precise placement, instruction following, and robustness to distractors.
Takeaways: Explicitly fusing 3D spatial coordinates with visual features, rather than relying solely on 2D images, is critical for achieving precise spatial grounding and mitigating coordinate system chaos in robot control.
Adaptive sampling of historical frames provides a more efficient and effective way to capture temporal context and disambiguate actions compared to uniform sampling or single-frame inputs.

Combining both 3D spatial information and multi-frame temporal context (4D representation) in a VLA pretraining framework leads to significantly improved generalization and robustness in complex robotic manipulation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21539.Title: WorldVLA: Towards Autoregressive Action World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.21539.Summary: Researchers from DAMO Academy, Hupan Lab, and Zhejiang University developed WorldVLA, an autoregressive framework that unifies robot action generation and environmental state forecasting. This approach integrates vision, language, and action modeling with a world model, yielding superior performance on robotic manipulation tasks and improving both action execution and future state prediction.
Problem: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate actions but often lack a deep understanding of how actions influence environmental physics and future states.
Traditional world models predict future visual states based on actions but cannot directly generate actions for robotic control.

Autoregressive generation of action sequences (action chunks) often suffers from performance degradation due to error propagation from earlier predictions and limited action generalization in pre-trained MLLMs.
Method: WorldVLA unifies action generation and world state forecasting into a single, autoregressive framework built upon a Vision-Language Model backbone, initialized from Chameleon.
It employs distinct tokenizers for images, text, and continuous robot actions, converting them into a shared discrete token space for unified processing within the LLM.

A novel attention mask strategy is introduced for action chunk generation, ensuring that each action within a chunk is conditioned only on visual and textual inputs, effectively masking out previously generated actions to prevent error propagation.
Results: WorldVLA achieved an average grasping success rate of 81.8% on the LIBERO benchmark with 512x512 resolution, surpassing discrete OpenVLA's 76.5% success rate.
Integrating the world model data during training consistently boosted the action model's performance, increasing average success rates (e.g., from 62.8% to 67.2% without action chunking).
The proposed action attention masking strategy improved grasping success rate from 54.0% (naive chunking) to 76.6% (with proposed mask), demonstrating its efficacy in addressing error propagation.
Takeaways: Integrating a world model component into a VLA architecture leads to a mutual enhancement, where the world model's understanding of physics guides action generation and the action model's refined understanding improves world state prediction.
Higher image resolution (e.g., 512x512 pixels) significantly improves performance in precise robotic manipulation tasks, leveraging the capabilities of the underlying multimodal LLM backbone.

The specialized attention mask is crucial for enabling robust and efficient autoregressive action chunk generation, mitigating the performance degradation typically associated with naive sequential prediction.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19850.Title: Unified Vision-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19850.Summary: UniVLA introduces a unified vision-language-action (VLA) model that processes all modalities as discrete tokens within a shared autoregressive Transformer. This framework achieves state-of-the-art results on robotic manipulation benchmarks like CALVIN, LIBERO (95.5% average success rate), and SimplerEnv by leveraging a world model trained on large-scale action-free video data.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often rely on a language-centric paradigm and late-fusion strategies, limiting deep cross-modal integration.
Prior VLA approaches struggle to capture temporal and causal dependencies within the perception-action loop, particularly for complex, long-horizon tasks.
The scarcity and high cost of collecting action-annotated robotic demonstration data restrict the scalability and generalizability of policy learning.
Method: UniVLA develops a unified multimodal model that represents vision, language, and action as discrete tokens within a shared vocabulary, processed by an 8.5 billion parameter autoregressive Transformer.

A two-stage training paradigm is employed: 1) post-training a world model on large-scale action-free video datasets to learn environment dynamics by predicting future visual content, and 2) fine-tuning for policy learning using action-annotated data.
The model frames embodied planning as sequence modeling, where observations and actions are causally interleaved, leveraging the autoregressive nature to capture temporal dependencies.
Results: UniVLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN benchmark and sets new SOTA across all LIBERO suites with an average success rate of 95.5%, improving LIBERO-Long to 94.0%.
World model post-training provides substantial performance gains, enabling higher success rates on CALVIN using only 10% of the fine-tuning data and faster convergence.

The model demonstrates multimodal capabilities beyond policy learning, including spatial reasoning via text output and future state prediction via visual output, with promising preliminary results in autonomous driving.
Takeaways: Unifying vision, language, and action into a single token-based, autoregressive framework enables tighter cross-modal integration and learning of temporal and causal dynamics.
Training a world model on abundant action-free video data significantly improves downstream policy learning efficiency and generalization, addressing robot data scarcity.
Visual prediction capabilities, even during fine-tuning, naturally integrate world model learning into policy learning, leading to performance improvements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19816.Title: CronusVLA: Towards Efficient and Robust Manipulation via Multi-Frame Vision-Language-Action Modeling
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19816.Summary: Researchers from Shanghai AI Lab and collaborating institutions introduce CronusVLA, an efficient framework that extends single-frame Vision-Language-Action models to leverage multi-frame observations for robust robotic manipulation. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse tasks in simulation and real-world, significantly improving resilience against visual disturbances while maintaining fast inference speeds.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily operate within a single-frame paradigm, failing to fully utilize temporal information critical for understanding motion cues and resolving state ambiguities.
Directly extending large-scale VLA models to a multi-frame paradigm incurs prohibitive computational overhead and inference latency due to the quadratic scaling of self-attention with input tokens.

Current robotic manipulation benchmarks often lack comprehensive evaluation for 'observational robustness,' leaving a gap in assessing how VLA models perform under real-world visual disturbances like blur, noise, or occlusions.
Method: A two-stage framework: initial single-frame VLA pretraining to establish a strong vision-language foundation, followed by efficient multi-frame post-training on high-quality datasets.

Introduces continuous 'learnable features' from the VLA backbone and 'feature chunking' with a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue to aggregate multi-frame historical information while reusing previously computed VLM features, ensuring fast inference.

Employs a DiT-based cross-frame decoder with a feature modulator to dynamically balance current and past frame contributions, and a multi-frame regularization technique using stop-gradients to efficiently update the VLA backbone without disrupting single-frame perception.
Developed SimplerEnv-OR, a novel benchmark with 24 types of temporal and spatial observational disturbances across over 120 severity levels, to quantitatively assess and compare model robustness.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art average success rates of 70.9% on SimplerEnv Google Robot and WidowX Robot tasks, and 97.0% on the LIBERO benchmark, showing significant improvements (e.g., 40.3% over OpenVLA on LIBERO long-horizon tasks).

Demonstrated superior observational robustness on the SimplerEnv-OR benchmark, consistently outperforming prior methods under various temporal and spatial disturbances, with high R-Scores (e.g., 96.2 R-Score for Sparse 1:3 disturbances).

Maintained fast inference speeds (e.g., 8.7 Hz for the 7B model with 7 frames), addressing the computational challenges of multi-frame processing and making advanced temporal modeling practical for real-time robotic control.
Takeaways: Efficient integration of multi-frame temporal information is crucial for enhancing the performance, fluidity, and robustness of robotic manipulation, moving beyond the limitations of instantaneous single-frame perception.

Decoupling single-frame perception from multi-frame temporal modeling allows for leveraging powerful pre-trained VLM backbones while achieving significant computational efficiency during multi-frame inference.

Rigorous evaluation of observational robustness against diverse disturbances is essential for bridging the gap between laboratory performance and the reliable deployment of VLA models in complex, unpredictable real-world environments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18088.Title: RoboTwin 2.0: A Scalable Data Generator and Benchmark with Strong Domain Randomization for Robust Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.18088.Summary: RoboTwin 2.0 introduces a scalable simulation framework and benchmark designed to generate high-quality, domain-randomized data for robust bimanual robotic manipulation, addressing limitations in existing synthetic datasets. Policies trained with RoboTwin 2.0 data achieved a 24.4% improvement in real-world success rates for few-shot learning and 21.0% for zero-shot generalization on unseen backgrounds.
Problem: The prohibitive cost and complexity of collecting large-scale, high-quality real-world datasets for bimanual robotic tasks.
Existing synthetic datasets often lack automated quality control, leading to execution failures or suboptimal grasps that hinder policy learning.
Current simulation environments employ superficial domain randomization, oversimplifying real-world complexities and limiting robust sim-to-real transfer.
Method: An automated expert data generation pipeline leveraging multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and closed-loop simulation-in-the-loop feedback to synthesize and refine high-quality task execution code.
Comprehensive domain randomization systematically applied across five dimensions: scene clutter, background textures, lighting variations, tabletop heights, and diverse language instructions.
Embodiment-aware grasp adaptation mechanisms that account for heterogeneous dual-arm kinematics, generating robot-specific action candidates and manipulation strategies.
Results: Automated expert code generation achieved an average success rate of 71.3% with multimodal feedback, alongside reduced token costs for code refinement.
Policies trained with RoboTwin 2.0's domain-randomized data showed relative improvements of up to 31.9% in average success rate for generalization on unseen, randomized conditions in simulation.

Real-world experiments demonstrated policies augmented with RoboTwin 2.0 data achieved a 24.4% improvement in average real-world success rate in few-shot scenarios and 21.0% in zero-shot generalization on unseen backgrounds.
Takeaways: Multimodal feedback from a vision-language model, combined with execution logs, substantially improves the reliability and success rate of MLLM-generated robotic task code.

Extensive and systematic domain randomization across visual, physical, and linguistic factors is critical for training policies that exhibit strong robustness and generalization to real-world complexities.

Accounting for robot-specific kinematic differences through embodiment-aware grasp adaptation is essential for efficient manipulation across diverse robotic platforms, especially those with fewer degrees of freedom.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08440.Title: TGRPO :Fine-tuning Vision-Language-Action Model via Trajectory-wise Group Relative Policy Optimization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.08440.Summary: The TGRPO framework introduces a critic-free online reinforcement learning approach to fine-tune Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, utilizing Large Language Models for automated dense reward generation and a dual-level group relative policy optimization. This method achieved an 80.7% average success rate on the LIBERO benchmark, notably improving long-horizon task performance by 8.1% compared to standard supervised fine-tuning.
Problem: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, typically fine-tuned with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), often struggle with learning from failures and adapting to out-of-distribution scenarios due to an "action memorization" approach.

Applying reinforcement learning (RL) to complex, long-horizon robotic tasks is challenged by sparse rewards, high variance and instability during optimization, and the computational burden of training separate value networks (critics).
Method: Leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to automatically decompose natural language task descriptions into sub-stages and construct fine-grained, multi-stage dense reward functions using key object and end-effector pose information.

Proposes Trajectory-wise Group Relative Policy Optimization (TGRPO), a critic-free online RL framework that samples parallel trajectories and computes dual-level relative advantages (step-level and trajectory-level) for robust policy updates.
Fuses the step-level and trajectory-level advantages to provide a comprehensive optimization signal, updating the VLA model's LoRA weights without requiring a separate value network.
Results: TGRPO achieved an average success rate of 80.7% across the LIBERO benchmark, outperforming OpenVLA-SFT (76.5%) and other RL-based fine-tuning methods like DPO (76.2%) and GRAPE (80.2%).

The framework demonstrated particularly strong performance on the challenging LIBERO-Long suite, securing a 59.2% success rate, an 8.1% improvement over SFT, highlighting its efficacy for complex, long-horizon tasks.

Ablation studies confirmed that both trajectory-level and step-level relative advantages are essential for TGRPO's stability, with optimal performance achieved using specific advantage weightings (α1=0.3,α2=0.7\alpha_1=0.3, \alpha_2=0.7α1​=0.3,α2​=0.7) and a group size of 4.
Takeaways: Large Language Models can effectively automate the creation of dense, multi-stage reward functions for complex robotic tasks, mitigating the sparse reward problem without extensive manual engineering.

Combining relative advantages at both the trajectory and step levels provides a stable and comprehensive optimization signal, effectively balancing global task progress with local action contributions in long-horizon tasks.

Critic-free relative advantage estimation, derived from parallel trajectory sampling, offers a robust and efficient alternative to traditional value-based methods, reducing variance and simplifying the reinforcement learning pipeline.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01844.Title: SmolVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model for Affordable and Efficient Robotics
https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01844.Summary: Hugging Face researchers develop SmolVLA, a 450-million parameter vision-language-action model that achieves competitive robotic manipulation performance using 7x less memory and 40% faster training than larger VLA models like π0 (3.3B parameters), demonstrating 78.3% success rate on real-world SO-100 tasks compared to 61.7% for π0 and introducing an asynchronous inference stack that enables 30% faster task completion (9.7s vs 13.75s) by decoupling action prediction from execution, while being trained exclusively on community-contributed datasets totaling fewer than 30,000 episodes and deployable on consumer-grade hardware including CPUs.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action models require billions of parameters and extensive computational resources, making them inaccessible to smaller research groups and preventing deployment on affordable robotic platforms
State-of-the-art VLA models rely on proprietary or large-scale academic datasets, limiting reproducibility and community participation in robotics research
Method: Develop a compact VLA architecture using SmolVLM-2 backbone with layer skipping (using only first N=L/2 layers) and visual token reduction to 64 per frame, combined with a Transformer-based action expert trained via flow matching
Train exclusively on community-driven datasets from affordable robotic platforms using automated VLM-based task annotation and camera viewpoint normalization to handle data heterogeneity
Results: Outperforms larger VLA models on LIBERO and Meta-World benchmarks while using significantly fewer resources, with 78.3% average success rate on real-world SO-100 manipulation tasks versus 48.3% for ACT and 61.7% for π0

Achieves 30% faster task completion through asynchronous inference (completing 19 pick-and-place cycles in 60 seconds versus 9 for synchronous mode) while maintaining comparable success rates and improving adaptability to environmental changes
Takeaways: Interleaving cross-attention and causal self-attention layers in the action expert yields superior performance (85.5% vs 79.0% for cross-attention only) by enabling both VLM feature conditioning and temporal action dependencies

Asynchronous inference with action chunk pre-fetching prevents robot idling and enables higher control rates while maintaining task success rates through observation similarity filtering and queue threshold management

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22159.Title: ForceVLA: Enhancing VLA Models with a Force-aware MoE for Contact-rich Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22159.Summary: ForceVLA enhances Vision-Language-Action models for contact-rich robotic manipulation by integrating 6-axis force feedback through a Force-aware Mixture-of-Experts (FVLMoE) module. This approach improves average task success rates by 23.2% and demonstrates superior generalization across diverse physical interaction scenarios, including under visual occlusion.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle with contact-rich manipulation tasks due to their reliance on visual information, leading to brittle behavior.
