Current VLA models often fail under visual occlusion or dynamic uncertainty, lacking fine-grained physical control and the ability to adapt to subtle interaction forces.
There is a scarcity of comprehensive datasets that effectively capture synchronized vision, proprioception, and high-fidelity force-torque data for diverse contact-rich tasks.
Method: ForceVLA, an end-to-end multimodal robotic policy, integrates 6-axis force feedback into an established VLA framework by treating force sensing as a "first-class modality."

A novel Force-aware Mixture-of-Experts (FVLMoE) module dynamically fuses real-time force-torque readings with visual-language embeddings, enabling phase-aware action generation and context-aware routing.
The research includes the creation of ForceVLA-Data, a new dataset of 244 trajectories capturing synchronized vision, proprioception, and force-torque signals for five challenging contact-rich tasks.
Results: ForceVLA achieved an average task success rate of 60.5% across five challenging contact-rich tasks, representing a 23.2% improvement over the strong π₀-base model with force feedback (37.3%).

The model demonstrated superior generalization, achieving 90% success under partial visual occlusion and maintaining compliant control to achieve 20% success in highly unstable socket insertion scenarios.

Ablation studies confirmed the FVLMoE's late-fusion strategy and dynamic routing are essential, with the full ForceVLA achieving 80% success in a key task, while simpler force integration methods reached 60% and early fusion methods performed significantly worse.
Takeaways: Integrating force feedback strategically after the initial Vision-Language Model (VLM) encoding is crucial to preserve powerful pretrained VLM representations and significantly improve performance.
The FVLMoE's dynamic gating network enables expert specialization and phase-aware action generation, allowing the robot to adapt to subtle contact dynamics for precise, context-sensitive control.

Sophisticated multimodal fusion, such as the FVLMoE, yields substantial performance gains over simpler force integration methods like concatenation, demonstrating the importance of dynamic interaction between modalities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18719.Title: VLA-RL: Towards Masterful and General Robotic Manipulation with Scalable Reinforcement Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.18719.Summary: Tsinghua University and Nanyang Technological University researchers develop VLA-RL, a reinforcement learning framework that fine-tunes pre-trained vision-language-action models for robotic manipulation, achieving 4.5% performance improvement over supervised fine-tuning baselines on the LIBERO benchmark and matching commercial model performance through trajectory-level RL formulation combined with a robotic process reward model that provides dense rewards for sparse manipulation tasks, while demonstrating test-time scaling benefits where extended training consistently improves robot performance and exhibiting superior action space coverage compared to behavior cloning approaches.
Problem: Imitation learning approaches for robotic manipulation struggle with out-of-distribution generalization when deployed in new environments or tasks
Sparse reward signals in robotic reinforcement learning make training inefficient and unstable
Existing robotic foundation models trained purely on offline datasets lack the exploration capabilities needed for robust real-world performance
Method: Formulate robotic manipulation as multi-modal, multi-turn conversations enabling trajectory-level RL optimization using existing LLM frameworks
Train a vision-language robotic process reward model on automatically extracted task segments to provide dense, informative rewards
Implement systematic improvements including curriculum selection strategy, GPU-balanced vectorized environments, and critic warmup for training stability
Results: VLA-RL achieves 4.5% improvement over supervised fine-tuning baseline on LIBERO benchmark manipulation tasks
Performance matches advanced commercial models like π0-FAST while demonstrating superior action space coverage and robustness
Ablation studies confirm the importance of each framework component, with the robotic process reward model providing the largest performance gains
Takeaways: Reinforcement learning can successfully improve pre-trained robotic foundation models beyond what supervised fine-tuning achieves
Test-time scaling laws appear to apply to robotics, with extended RL training consistently improving performance
Dense process rewards are crucial for enabling effective RL training in sparse-reward robotic manipulation tasks

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17016.Title: Interactive Post-Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17016.Summary: RIPT-VLA introduces a third training stage for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, employing reinforcement interactive post-training to learn from binary success/failure rewards. The method improved success rates on LIBERO-90 to 94.3% for QueST and achieved a 21.2% absolute improvement on LIBERO-LONG, particularly excelling in low-data scenarios where it consistently achieved over 80% success with single demonstrations.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, trained primarily on offline expert demonstrations, suffer from data scarcity, as collecting high-quality demonstrations is expensive and time-consuming.
Models trained solely on offline data exhibit limited generalization capabilities to new environments, object configurations, or task variations not present in the training data.
VLA models lack interactive experience, preventing them from learning from trial and error and adapting to dynamic environments or distribution shifts between training and deployment.
Method: RIPT-VLA introduces a third training stage that allows VLA models to learn through interaction with their environment using simple binary success/failure rewards.
The method integrates reinforcement learning, extending the LOOP framework by combining REINFORCE leave-one-out (RLOO) advantage estimation with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).
The algorithm iteratively collects rollouts, computes advantages using RLOO, and optimizes the policy with PPO, employing dynamic sampling to maintain training stability.
Results: On the LIBERO-90 multi-task benchmark, RIPT-VLA improved QueST's success rate from 88.6% to 94.3%.
For complex long-horizon tasks in LIBERO-LONG, RIPT-VLA achieved a 21.2% absolute improvement in success rate, increasing it from 50.2% to 71.4%.

In extreme low-data regimes with only a single training demonstration, the method consistently attained success rates above 80-90% across various tasks, where supervised fine-tuning alone achieved near-zero performance.
Takeaways: Dynamic rollout sampling constructs uniform batches of non-zero advantage samples, filtering out zero-advantage groups to improve training stability.
The framework supports both tokenized and continuous action representations, allowing compatibility with various VLA architectures.
The method operates without learned critics and requires only binary success/failure feedback, simplifying the training process and reducing supervision needs.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15660.Title: Exploring the Limits of Vision-Language-Action Manipulations in Cross-task Generalization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.15660.Summary: This research introduces AGNOSTOS, a novel benchmark for evaluating zero-shot cross-task generalization in robotic manipulation, and proposes X-ICM, a method that leverages large language models (LLMs) with dynamics-guided in-context learning. X-ICM significantly outperforms existing vision-language-action models on the AGNOSTOS benchmark, achieving an average success rate of 30.1% on unseen tasks.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models struggle with zero-shot generalization to entirely unseen manipulation tasks, despite excelling in within-task variations.
A lack of a rigorous, reproducible benchmark specifically designed to evaluate true zero-shot cross-task generalization for robotic manipulation.
Existing approaches do not effectively leverage the in-context learning capabilities of LLMs to generate action plans for genuinely novel manipulation challenges.
Method: Introduced AGNOSTOS, a novel simulation benchmark on RLBench comprising 23 distinct unseen manipulation tasks, categorized into two difficulty levels, for rigorous evaluation of cross-task generalization.
Proposed Cross-Task In-context Manipulation (X-ICM), a method that uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to predict action sequences for unseen tasks.

X-ICM integrates a dynamics-guided sample selection module, which employs a diffusion model to retrieve the most relevant in-context demonstrations from seen tasks based on predicted future visual states.
Results: Existing VLA models achieved an average success rate of at most 17.5% on AGNOSTOS, with all models failing completely on at least eight of the 23 unseen tasks.
X-ICM (72B) achieved an average success rate of 30.1% on AGNOSTOS, outperforming the best baseline by 12.6% and successfully addressing all 23 unseen tasks.
Real-world experiments with an xArm7 robot demonstrated X-ICM's practical applicability, achieving success rates ranging from 10% to 70% on five zero-shot cross-task manipulation challenges.
Takeaways: Current state-of-the-art VLA models, including foundation models, exhibit severe limitations in zero-shot cross-task generalization, frequently failing on novel manipulation scenarios (0% success on multiple tasks).
Effective cross-task generalization with LLMs heavily relies on selecting highly relevant in-context demonstrations; random selection significantly degrades performance.
Larger LLM backbones generally improve zero-shot cross-task generalization, and an optimal number of in-context demonstrations exists to maximize performance.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12705.Title: DreamGen: Unlocking Generalization in Robot Learning through Video World Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12705.Summary: DREAMGEN introduces a pipeline that repurposes video world models as scalable synthetic data generators for robot learning, effectively mitigating the reliance on extensive human teleoperation. This approach allows robot policies to generalize to 22 novel behaviors and operate successfully in 10 previously unseen environments, starting from a minimal initial real-world dataset.
Problem: The high cost and labor intensity of collecting large-scale, high-quality human teleoperation data hinders the development of generalist robot policies.
Traditional simulation-based synthetic data generation faces challenges of extensive manual engineering for environments and a persistent sim-to-real gap.
Robot policies struggle to generalize effectively to new behaviors and diverse environments when trained on limited, task-specific real-world data.
Method: A 4-stage pipeline that fine-tunes a pre-trained image-to-video generative model on a small set of robot teleoperation data, then uses it to roll out large volumes of photorealistic synthetic robot videos.
Inferring 'pseudo-action sequences' for the generated videos using an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM) or Latent Action Model (LAPA) to create comprehensive 'neural trajectories'.

Training standard visuomotor robot policies on these large-scale, pseudo-labeled neural trajectories, either solely or co-trained with limited real-world data, compatible with various policy architectures.
Results: DREAMGEN scaled synthetic data up to 333 times the original human demonstrations, yielding log-linear improvements in robot policy performance on the RoboCasa benchmark.

Improved average success rates on 9 diverse real-world dexterous tasks across GR1 humanoid, Franka Emika, and SO-100 robots (e.g., GR1 improved from 37% to 46.4%, Franka from 23% to 37%, SO-100 from 21% to 45.5%).

Enabled a GR1 humanoid robot to generalize to 22 entirely new behaviors in seen environments (43.2% success rate vs. 11.2% baseline) and 10 novel behaviors in unseen environments (28.5% success rate vs. 0% baseline) using a video world model fine-tuned on only pick-and-place data.
Takeaways: State-of-the-art video world models can be effectively repurposed as scalable synthetic data generators for robot learning, moving beyond their traditional role as real-time planners.

Leveraging the broad prior knowledge encoded in large generative models (trained on internet videos) enables robots to generalize to novel behaviors and environments from remarkably small initial real-world datasets.

A strong correlation exists between the quality of generated robot videos (assessed by instruction following and physics alignment) and downstream robot policy performance, providing a low-cost diagnostic tool for world model research.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05800.Title: 3D CAVLA: Leveraging Depth and 3D Context to Generalize Vision Language Action Models for Unseen Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.05800.Summary: 3D-CAVLA, developed by NYU researchers, enhances Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by integrating depth, chain-of-thought narratives, and task-aware region of interest detection, achieving an absolute 8.8% improvement in success rate on unseen robotic manipulation tasks compared to OpenVLA-OFT.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit limited generalization capabilities, performing poorly on unseen tasks or environments.
Many VLAs primarily rely on 2D visual data, lacking sufficient spatial or semantic context for complex robotic manipulation.
Current VLAs often learn direct input-output mappings, bypassing explicit intermediate reasoning steps that could improve task decomposition and transfer.
Method: The 3D-CAVLA model enhances OpenVLA-OFT by integrating Chain-of-Thought Narrative Instructions, using GPT-4 to decompose tasks into step-by-step prompts.
It incorporates depth features by converting RGB-D camera data into 3D point clouds, processed by a lightweight, trainable depth encoder.

It implements Task Aware Region of Interest (TA-ROI) Detection to focus visual attention on relevant objects and regions through an offline pipeline of named entity recognition, object detection, and tracking.
Results: 3D-CAVLA achieved an average success rate of 98.1% on in-distribution LIBERO benchmarks with a dual camera setup, outperforming OpenVLA-OFT (97.1%).
On the new LIBERO-Unseen benchmark of novel tasks, 3D-CAVLA demonstrated an absolute improvement of 8.8% over OpenVLA-OFT, achieving a 45.2% success rate.
Ablation studies indicated that the integration of depth maps caused the highest performance improvement, underscoring their critical importance for robust policy learning.
Takeaways: Incorporating 3D spatial information (depth maps) is the most impactful addition for robust VLA policy learning, significantly improving precision.
Explicit intermediate reasoning via chain-of-thought prompts aids VLA generalization, especially for complex, long-horizon tasks.
Task-aware region of interest detection helps focus attention for generalization, though it can sometimes hinder performance on seen tasks by excluding useful context.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04769.Title: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models: Concepts, Progress, Applications and Challenges
https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.04769.Summary: This review paper synthesizes the landscape of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which unify visual perception, natural language understanding, and physical action generation into a single framework for embodied AI. It maps their conceptual foundations, rapid architectural and efficiency advancements, diverse real-world applications across six domains, and critical challenges to robust deployment.
Problem: Traditional AI systems operated in isolated modalities (vision, language, action), leading to a lack of generalization and real-world adaptability.
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) could interpret multimodal inputs but lacked the capability to translate insights into coherent physical actions.
Robotic systems were often brittle, restricted to predefined scenarios, and unable to perform flexible, context-aware tasks in complex environments.
Method: VLA models integrate vision, language, and action into a unified computational framework, enabling embodied agents to perceive, understand, and interact physically.
The approach leverages tokenization to encode vision, language, and action into a shared embedding space, using a hybrid training paradigm of internet-scale datasets and robot trajectory data.
Architectural innovations like early fusion, dual-system architectures (fast-reactive and slow-reasoning modules), and self-correcting frameworks enhance VLA adaptability and robustness.
Results: The review categorizes over 80 VLA models, illustrating a rapid evolution from foundational integration (2022-2023) to specialization and generalization-focused systems (2024-2025).

VLA models demonstrate transformative potential across six key application domains: humanoid robotics, autonomous vehicles, industrial robotics, healthcare, precision agriculture, and interactive AR navigation.

Identified and analyzed critical challenges including real-time inference constraints (autoregressive decoding limits speed to 3-5 Hz), safety concerns (collision prediction accuracy ~82%), and generalization gaps (up to 40% degradation on unseen tasks).
Takeaways: VLA models represent a crucial step towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) by enabling seamless integration of perception, understanding, and physical interaction.

Significant progress in architectural design (e.g., dual-system approaches) and training efficiency (e.g., co-fine-tuning, LoRA, compressed action tokens) is making VLA models more capable and deployable.

Despite rapid advancements and transformative potential across numerous applications (robotics, autonomous vehicles, agriculture), critical challenges remain in real-time inference, robust action representation, generalization, and ethical considerations.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19854.Title: NORA: A Small Open-Sourced Generalist Vision Language Action Model for Embodied Tasks
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19854.Summary: A 3B-parameter Vision-Language-Action model combines Qwen-2.5-VL-3B with FAST+ tokenization to enable real-time robotic control on consumer GPUs, achieving comparable or better performance than larger models across simulation and real-world robot manipulation tasks while reducing computational requirements by 57%.
Problem: Existing VLA models (7B+ parameters) are too computationally intensive for real-time robotics applications
Current approaches struggle with visual encoding and action generation for precise manipulation tasks
Method: Leverage Qwen-2.5-VL-3B's visual-semantic capabilities with augmented action tokens
Implement FAST+ tokenization for efficient action sequence generation
Optimize training with FlashAttention and bf16 precision
Results: Outperforms baseline models on out-of-domain object grasping tasks
Achieves comparable performance to OpenVLA on LIBERO benchmark tasks
Runs effectively on consumer GPUs with 57% lower computational overhead
Demonstrates robust generalization across diverse manipulation scenarios
Takeaways: Action chunking improves performance in simulation but creates challenges in real-world settings
Visual encoding quality significantly impacts manipulation success rates
Model size can be reduced while maintaining task performance through targeted architecture choices

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054.Title: $π_{0.5}$: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054.Summary: A Vision-Language-Action model called π0.5 enables mobile robots to perform complex household tasks in entirely new homes through co-training on heterogeneous data sources including multi-robot demonstrations, web data, and verbal instructions, while using a hierarchical inference approach that combines semantic subtask prediction with low-level action generation.
Problem: Existing robot learning systems struggle to generalize to new, unseen environments outside of controlled laboratory settings
Current approaches lack the ability to effectively combine knowledge from diverse data sources for improved generalization
Method: Co-training framework that leverages multiple data types including mobile manipulator data, cross-embodiment robot data, web data, and verbal instructions
Hierarchical architecture that first predicts semantic subtasks before generating low-level robot actions
Results: Successfully performed long-horizon tasks like cleaning kitchens and bedrooms in previously unseen homes
Significant improvement in generalization compared to previous VLA models
Effective knowledge transfer from heterogeneous data sources demonstrated through ablation studies
Hierarchical inference approach crucial for completing extended multi-stage tasks
Takeaways: Cross-embodiment data from different robots and environments is essential for generalization capabilities
Web data and verbal instruction improve handling of out-of-distribution objects and complex commands
Scaling up the number of training environments directly improves generalization performance

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15369.Title: Solving New Tasks by Adapting Internet Video Knowledge
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15369.Summary: This work explores adapting large-scale pre-trained video generative models to solve robotic tasks specified through natural language. A novel Inverse Probabilistic Adaptation technique is introduced, demonstrating strong generalization and improving task success rates by up to 3x compared to unadapted models.
Problem: Large-scale pre-trained video generative models possess broad knowledge but lack the specific environment understanding crucial for robotic applications.
Traditional robotics learning heavily relies on expensive, in-domain data collection, which limits generalization to novel tasks.
A challenge exists in effectively balancing the broad generalization capabilities of pre-trained models with the specific knowledge required for particular robotic environments.
Method: The research investigates three adaptation techniques: Direct Finetuning, Subject Customization, and Probabilistic Adaptation, to integrate in-domain information into pre-trained text-to-video models.
A novel Inverse Probabilistic Adaptation technique is introduced, which keeps the pre-trained model frozen and subtracts the score of a small 'distractor' model trained on irrelevant content.
Adapted models are evaluated on two downstream robotics tasks: Visual Planning (generating trajectories) and Policy Supervision (training a policy from generated rollouts).
Results: All adaptation techniques improved the ability of pre-trained models to solve novel robotic tasks, with the most successful techniques achieving up to a 3x improvement in task success rates.
The novel Inverse Probabilistic Adaptation technique consistently delivered strong generalization performance across different robotic environments and evaluation methods.
Subject Customization demonstrated substantial performance improvements while requiring only static images for adaptation, making it data-efficient.
Takeaways: Pre-trained video generative models contain valuable motion priors that can be effectively adapted for robotic tasks.
Subtracting irrelevant information from a pre-trained model's score, as in Inverse Probabilistic Adaptation, can be highly effective for generalization.
Visual metrics for video quality (e.g., FVD) do not necessarily correlate with performance on downstream robotic tasks, emphasizing task-specific evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02792.Title: Unified World Models: Coupling Video and Action Diffusion for Pretraining on Large Robotic Datasets
https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.02792.Summary: Unified World Models (UWM), developed by researchers at the University of Washington and Toyota Research Institute, presents a diffusion-based framework that unifies robot policy learning and world modeling within a single transformer, enabling it to learn from both action-labeled robotic data and action-free video datasets. The model demonstrates improved task success rates and robustness on real-world robot manipulation tasks, outperforming existing baselines.
Problem: Scaling imitation learning (IL) for generalist robots is bottlenecked by the high cost and scarcity of high-quality, action-annotated robot demonstration data.

World modeling approaches, while leveraging abundant action-free video data, struggle to effectively translate temporal dynamics knowledge into robust, generalizable robotic controllers for action generation.

The fields of imitation learning (action generation) and world modeling (observation prediction) have largely developed disparately, missing opportunities for joint learning and mutual benefit from shared features.
Method: Introduces Unified World Models (UWM), a diffusion-based framework that integrates an action diffusion process and an image (video) diffusion process into a single Diffusion Transformer architecture.

Employs independent diffusion timesteps for actions and next observations, allowing for flexible inference modes (policy, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, video prediction) by manipulating these timesteps at inference time.
Trains the model on multitask robotic datasets with action labels and co-trains on action-free video data by fixing the action timestep to a fully noised state, effectively masking missing actions.
Results: UWM achieved the highest success rates (up to 20% higher than baselines) on real-world manipulation tasks in the DROID dataset, showing strong performance in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.

Co-training UWM with action-free videos consistently improved its performance, boosting generalization and robustness (e.g., from 0.86 to 0.92 in Stack-Bowls in-distribution and 0.76 to 0.84 in out-of-distribution scenarios).

UWM accurately predicted future image observations, demonstrated effective inverse dynamics by generating actions that adhered more closely to reference trajectories, and scaled more effectively with large pretraining datasets than other methods.
Takeaways: Maintaining independent diffusion timesteps for actions and future observations enables a single model to flexibly infer policies, forward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and perform video prediction from the same trained model.

Co-training with action-free video data, by effectively masking out actions through diffusion timesteps, enhances model generalization and robustness to out-of-distribution conditions without diluting the action learning signal.

The use of 'register tokens' in the Diffusion Transformer architecture improves performance, hypothesized to facilitate information exchange between distinct modalities (actions and latent image patches).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22020.Title: CoT-VLA: Visual Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.22020.Summary: CoT-VLA integrates visual chain-of-thought reasoning into Vision-Language-Action models by having them predict subgoal images before generating actions. This approach leverages large-scale action-less video data for training, enabling the model to outperform state-of-the-art VLA models by 17% in real-world manipulation and 6% in simulation benchmarks.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily use direct end-to-end mapping from observations to actions, lacking explicit intermediate reasoning steps crucial for complex, multi-stage manipulation tasks.
Current VLA models struggle with effective temporal planning and foresight, limiting their performance on tasks requiring a sequence of sub-goals.
Abundant, action-less video data from the internet remains largely underutilized by robot learning models, which often rely exclusively on expensive action-annotated robot demonstrations.
Method: Introduces visual chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning where the VLA model first predicts a future image frame as a visual subgoal, then generates a sequence of actions conditioned on this subgoal.
Leverages a 7B-parameter unified multimodal foundation model, VILA-U, for both understanding visual observations and generating image and action tokens.

Employs a two-stage training approach, using robot demonstrations for both visual and action prediction, and large-scale action-less video datasets (e.g., EPIC-KITCHENS) specifically for training visual subgoal generation.
Results: CoT-VLA surpasses state-of-the-art VLA models, achieving a 17% improvement in real-world manipulation tasks and a 6% improvement in simulation benchmarks.

The model demonstrates superior instruction following on the LIBERO benchmark and robust adaptation to novel environments in Franka-Tabletop experiments, especially for complex multi-instruction tasks.
Ablation studies confirm the individual and combined effectiveness of visual chain-of-thought, action chunking, and a novel hybrid attention mechanism in boosting task performance.
Takeaways: Explicit visual chain-of-thought reasoning, using predicted subgoal images, significantly enhances the reasoning and generalization capabilities of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models.

Large-scale action-less video datasets can effectively be leveraged for pre-training the visual reasoning component of robot policies, reducing reliance on costly action-annotated robot demonstrations.
Improvements in the visual reasoning capabilities of VLA models directly translate to higher robotic task success rates, particularly for challenging out-of-distribution and long-horizon tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20020.Title: Gemini Robotics: Bringing AI into the Physical World
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.20020.Summary: Google DeepMind introduces the Gemini Robotics family of models, which extend the Gemini 2.0 multimodal model to physical robots, enabling them to perform a wide range of dexterous manipulation tasks. This research demonstrates enhanced embodied reasoning, robust generalization to novel conditions, and rapid adaptation to new tasks and robot embodiments through extensive real-world robot data and specialized fine-tuning.
Problem: Bridging the generalist capabilities of large multimodal models (LMMs) from digital domains to practical applications on physical robots.
Overcoming the limitations of traditional, highly specialized robotic systems that lack robust generalization to diverse, unstructured real-world environments.
Developing robotic AI that can acquire robust embodied reasoning (e.g., 3D understanding, intuitive physics) and directly translate this understanding into precise physical actions.
Method: The Gemini Robotics team at Google DeepMind developed the Gemini Robotics family of models, extending the Gemini 2.0 multimodal model to physical robotics.

Gemini Robotics-ER, a Vision-Language Model (VLM), was developed to enhance embodied reasoning capabilities, including open-world 2D/3D perception, trajectory, and grasp prediction, evaluated on a new ERQA benchmark.

Gemini Robotics, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, was built for low-latency real-time robot control, trained on thousands of hours of diverse real-world expert teleoperated robot action data alongside other multimodal data.
Results: Gemini 2.0 and Gemini Robotics-ER achieved state-of-the-art results on embodied reasoning benchmarks, including the newly introduced ERQA, with chain-of-thought prompting significantly boosting performance.
Gemini Robotics demonstrated proficiency on 20 diverse dexterous tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art baselines, and showed robust generalization across visual, instruction, and action variations.

Specialized Gemini Robotics achieved up to 79% average success on six challenging long-horizon dexterous tasks (e.g., 55% for origami fox), and demonstrated rapid adaptation to new tasks (over 70% success with 100 demonstrations) and new robot embodiments (e.g., Apptronik Apollo humanoid).
Takeaways: Enhancing large multimodal models with "embodied reasoning" capabilities is crucial for enabling them to understand and interact with the physical world effectively.

A generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model built on a powerful large multimodal model backbone and trained on diverse robot action data can achieve robust out-of-the-box dexterity and generalize to unseen visual conditions and instructions.
Such foundation models can be specialized and rapidly adapted with limited data for complex long-horizon tasks, new short-horizon tasks, and even completely different robot embodiments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14734.Title: GR00T N1: An Open Foundation Model for Generalist Humanoid Robots
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14734.Summary: NVIDIA researchers developed GR00T N1, an open foundation Vision-Language-Action model for generalist humanoid robots. The model achieves robust performance on real GR-1 humanoid robots and simulation tasks, utilizing a 'data pyramid' strategy for efficient training and strong generalization across diverse robot embodiments and scenarios.
Problem: The lack of scalable, diverse, and high-quality real-world robot data to train generalist foundation models.
The challenge of adapting large language and vision models to generate continuous, high-frequency actions for physical robots.
The need for generalist robots capable of performing diverse tasks in unstructured human environments, moving beyond task-specific policies and handling open-ended objectives for humanoid robots.
Method: A dual-system Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, GR00T N1, combines a reasoning VLM (NVIDIA Eagle-2) for high-level understanding with a high-frequency action-generating Diffusion Transformer for low-level control.
A 'data pyramid' strategy is employed to integrate heterogeneous data sources, including web data, human videos, large-scale synthetic simulation trajectories, and AI-generated neural trajectories.
Pseudo-actions are inferred for action-less video data using Latent Actions (LAPA) and Inverse Dynamics Models (IDM) to provide scalable action labels for diverse visual data.
Results: GR00T N1 outperforms state-of-the-art imitation learning baselines, BC-Transformer and Diffusion Policy, across multiple simulation benchmarks (e.g., 45.0% vs. 33.4% and 26.4% respectively on average).

On real GR-1 humanoid robot tasks, GR00T N1-2B achieves an average success rate of 76.8% with a full dataset, and demonstrates high data efficiency, achieving 42.6% with only 10% of the training data, nearly matching Diffusion Policy's 46.4% with the full dataset.

Co-training with neural trajectories consistently improves performance across both simulation (e.g., +4.2% to +8.8%) and real-world tasks (e.g., +5.8% average for GR-1 humanoid), demonstrating their effectiveness as data augmentation.
Takeaways: A dual-system architecture effectively integrates a high-level vision-language reasoning module with a low-level action generation module for robust control.
Integrating heterogeneous data sources through a 'data pyramid' strategy can effectively mitigate the 'data island' problem in robot learning.
AI-generated 'neural trajectories' and pseudo-action labeling techniques (Latent Actions, Inverse Dynamics Models) are effective methods to scale robot training data beyond real-world collection.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09527.Title: CombatVLA: An Efficient Vision-Language-Action Model for Combat Tasks in 3D Action Role-Playing Games
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.09527.Summary: CombatVLA is an efficient Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model designed for real-time combat tasks in 3D Action Role-Playing Games, which achieves a 50-fold acceleration in inference speed to 1.85 seconds. The model demonstrates superior combat understanding and higher task success rates than human players in complex in-game scenarios, surpassing previous VLM-based agents.
Problem: Existing VLM-based game agents face severe latency (60-90 seconds) for real-time tasks, making them impractical for dynamic combat in ARPGs requiring second-level responses.
There is a lack of high-quality, action-labeled training data and a standardized benchmark specifically for evaluating 'combat understanding' in 3D ARPGs.
Current methods struggle with high-resolution perception, complex tactical reasoning, and generalization under the real-time constraints of dynamic combat environments.
Method: A Python Action Tracker was developed to efficiently collect human gameplay data, capturing screenshots and keyboard/mouse actions with millisecond precision, used to create the Combat Understanding Benchmark (CUBench).

The 3B parameter CombatVLA model, built on Qwen2.5-VL, is trained using a three-stage progressive learning paradigm (Video-AoT, Frames-AoT, Frames-Truncated-AoT) with an adaptive action-weighted loss function.

An action execution framework integrates CombatVLA, utilizing a novel truncated Action-of-Thought (AoT) inference strategy with a `⟨TRUNC⟩` token to significantly reduce latency during real-time gameplay.
Results: CombatVLA achieved the highest average score of 63.61% on the CUBench, outperforming GPT-4o-0513 (57.29%) and Gemini-2.0-flash (57.90%), particularly excelling in the 'Reasoning' category (69.71%).

It demonstrated a 50-fold acceleration in inference speed, requiring only 1.85 seconds of delay per action, a significant improvement over previous VLM-based agents that incurred delays of 60-90 seconds.

The model achieved a higher task success rate than human players in various challenging 'Black Myth: Wukong' and 'Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice' tasks, also showing strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and different games.
Takeaways: Combining a specialized VLA model with a truncated Action-of-Thought inference strategy effectively overcomes the latency barrier, enabling sophisticated reasoning for real-time, dynamic combat scenarios.

Progressive learning from coarse-grained video understanding to fine-grained frame-level decision-making, coupled with adaptive action-weighted losses, significantly enhances both combat understanding and action prediction accuracy.

High-quality human gameplay data, transformed into semantically rich Action-of-Thought sequences, provides crucial guidance for the model to develop robust tactical reasoning and strong generalization capabilities.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06669.Title: AgiBot World Colosseo: A Large-scale Manipulation Platform for Scalable and Intelligent Embodied Systems
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.06669.Summary: AgiBot World Colosseo presents a large-scale platform and dataset, AgiBot World, comprising over 1 million real-world robot manipulation trajectories spanning diverse tasks and environments. The work introduces GO-1, a generalist policy leveraging vision-language models and latent action representations, achieving an average 32% performance improvement over prior generalist policies on complex manipulation tasks.
Problem: The scarcity of high-quality, large-scale, and diverse real-world robot manipulation data limits the development of general-purpose embodied systems.
Existing robot datasets are often small, confined to controlled lab settings, lack task diversity, or suffer from inconsistent data quality.
Current robotic systems struggle to generalize across various environments and scenarios, particularly for complex, long-horizon, bimanual, and dexterous manipulation tasks.
Method: Developed AgiBot World Colosseo, a full-stack, open-source platform including a 4,000-square-meter facility replicating five real-world domains and the versatile dual-arm AgiBot G1 robot.

Curated the AgiBot World dataset with over 1 million trajectories (2976.4 hours) across 217 tasks, 87 skills, and 106 scenes, utilizing a human-in-the-loop collection protocol for high quality and diversity.
Proposed GO-1 (Genie Operator-1), a hierarchical Vision-Language-Latent-Action (ViLLA) generalist policy that integrates web-scale vision-language models with learned latent action representations.
Results: AgiBot World provides over 1 million trajectories (2976.4 hours), covering five diverse real-world domains and over 3,000 unique objects, enabling training for complex, long-horizon manipulation.
Policies pre-trained on AgiBot World demonstrated an average 30% success rate improvement for in-domain scenarios and 29% for out-of-distribution scenarios compared to Open X-Embodiment.

The GO-1 policy achieved over 60% success rate on complex tasks and an average 32% performance improvement over the RDT approach, exhibiting a predictable power-law scaling with dataset size (Pearson r = 0.97).
Takeaways: An order-of-magnitude increase in data scale, coupled with rigorous human-in-the-loop quality assurance and failure recovery data, is essential for training robust, generalist robot policies.

Integrating web-scale vision-language knowledge with robot-specific latent action representations through a hierarchical policy enables better scene understanding and robust control for complex tasks.
The performance of generalist robot policies scales predictably with increased dataset size, underscoring the importance of large-scale, high-quality data for future advancements.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.02881.Title: Reactive Diffusion Policy: Slow-Fast Visual-Tactile Policy Learning for Contact-Rich Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.02881.Summary: This research introduces the Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP), a novel slow-fast visual-tactile learning approach, paired with TactAR, a low-cost augmented reality teleoperation system, to enable precise and reactive robot manipulation in contact-rich environments. RDP achieves over 35% improvement in performance across tasks like peeling and wiping compared to existing baselines, demonstrating human-like reactive behaviors and immediate adaptation to disturbances.
Problem: Existing visual imitation learning policies execute action chunks in an open-loop manner, limiting real-time reaction to environmental changes or precise contact dynamics in complex tasks.
Current teleoperation systems often lack real-time, fine-grained tactile/force feedback, hindering the collection of high-quality human demonstrations for contact-rich manipulation.
Robots struggle to perform dexterous, contact-rich tasks (e.g., peeling, wiping) with human-like precision and adaptability due to insufficient reactive capabilities.
Method: Introduces TactAR, a low-cost, AR-based teleoperation system for collecting visual-tactile demonstration data with real-time, intuitive 3D deformation field feedback.

Proposes Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP), a slow-fast hierarchical imitation learning algorithm that uses a Latent Diffusion Policy for high-level planning and an Asymmetric Tokenizer for high-frequency, closed-loop reactive control based on tactile/force input.
Utilizes a low-dimensional PCA representation of tactile data and employs relative trajectory prediction combined with latency matching to enhance policy generalizability and robustness.
Results: Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP) outperforms Diffusion Policy baselines by over 35% in overall scores across peeling, wiping, and bimanual lifting tasks, achieving success rates of 0.90-0.95 in peeling and 0.77-0.87 in wiping.

RDP demonstrates immediate reaction to external disturbances, vastly outperforming baselines (e.g., 0.8 vs. 0.15 in perturbation scenarios), by dynamically adjusting trajectories at sub-millimeter scales.

The TactAR teleoperation system improves data quality, leading to significantly better normalized peeling length (0.91 vs. 0.72) and a higher ratio of stable contact force (0.87 vs. 0.58) in collected demonstrations.
Takeaways: Integrating tactile signals directly into action prediction via a high-frequency "fast policy" is crucial for real-time reactivity in contact-rich tasks, unlike merely adding them to observations.
A slow-fast hierarchical policy architecture effectively balances long-horizon action planning with immediate, fine-grained reactive control using tactile feedback.
High-quality, stable tactile/force demonstration data, facilitated by intuitive teleoperation systems, is essential for learning robust and human-like reactive robot behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00200.Title: Unified Video Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.00200.Summary: The Unified Video Action Model (UVA) from Stanford University introduces a general-purpose robotic learning framework that jointly models video and action to achieve high action accuracy and efficient inference. UVA demonstrates competitive or superior performance across multiple simulation and real-world robot tasks, including multi-task scenarios and under visual disturbances, while maintaining fast inference speeds for real-time operation.
Problem: Existing visuomotor policies either prioritize fast action prediction (action-only methods) or robust world understanding through video generation (video-first methods), leading to trade-offs in speed or accuracy and error propagation.
Developing robotic systems often requires multiple specialized models for different functionalities like policy execution, video generation, and dynamics modeling, increasing complexity.
Robot policies frequently struggle with generalization to visual disturbances, out-of-distribution scenarios, and multi-task settings, often failing to effectively leverage longer temporal contexts.
Method: UVA learns a unified latent representation that jointly encodes historical visual observations and action sequences using a Transformer architecture.
It employs decoupled video and action diffusion heads that decode future video observations and action chunks independently, allowing for fast action inference by bypassing video generation.

A masked training framework is used to achieve versatile functionality, enabling a single model to act as a robot policy, video generator, forward dynamics model, or inverse dynamics model by selectively masking inputs and outputs.
Results: UVA achieved competitive or superior policy success rates on single-task benchmarks (e.g., 0.98 on PushT) and notably improved multi-task performance (e.g., 0.88 on PushT-M, 0.90 on Libero10, and up to 40% higher in real-world multi-task OOD scenarios) compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
Maintained inference speeds comparable to action-only policies (e.g., 0.23s vs 0.22s for Diffusion Policy in simulation), making it suitable for real-time robot control.

Demonstrated superior robustness to visual disturbances and effectively utilized longer history lengths, while also outperforming prior methods in video generation quality (lower FVD) and reducing error for inverse dynamics modeling (0.75 cm position error vs. 1.92 cm).
Takeaways: Jointly modeling video and action within a unified latent space enables learning a more comprehensive understanding of scene dynamics, leading to improved action accuracy and robustness.
Decoupling video and action decoding via separate lightweight diffusion heads allows for fast action inference by bypassing computationally intensive video generation during policy execution.

A masked training framework provides a flexible, general-purpose architecture, enabling a single model to perform various robotic functionalities such as policy learning, video generation, and dynamics modeling.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19645.Title: Fine-Tuning Vision-Language-Action Models: Optimizing Speed and Success
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19645.Summary: Researchers at Stanford University developed an Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, substantially increasing their inference speed and task success on new robotic setups, including complex bimanual manipulation, by integrating parallel decoding, action chunking, and L1 regression with continuous actions.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often have slow inference speeds (e.g., 3-5 Hz), making them unsuitable for high-frequency robotic control (25-50+ Hz) required for dexterous manipulation.
Current VLA fine-tuning methods show unsatisfactory performance on complex tasks, particularly in bimanual manipulation scenarios.
There is a lack of clear, empirically-validated guidance on how to effectively fine-tune VLAs for optimal speed and success on novel robot setups and tasks.
Method: A systematic empirical analysis was conducted on OpenVLA, evaluating key design choices for VLA fine-tuning: action generation strategy (autoregressive vs. parallel decoding with action chunking), action representation (discrete vs. continuous), and learning objective (L1 regression vs. diffusion).

An "Optimized Fine-Tuning (OFT) recipe" was developed, integrating parallel decoding, action chunking, continuous action representation, and a simple L1 regression objective for efficient and high-performance VLA adaptation.

Architectural modifications were introduced to support multiple camera views and low-dimensional robot state inputs, with Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) added to the OFT+ variant for enhanced language grounding.
Results: OpenVLA-OFT achieved a new state of the art on the LIBERO simulation benchmark with an average success rate of 97.1% (up from 76.5%) and a 26x speedup in action generation throughput (109.7 Hz).

On a real ALOHA bimanual robot, OpenVLA-OFT+ successfully executed diverse dexterous tasks, consistently outperforming other fine-tuned VLAs and achieving up to 15% higher average success rates, despite being pretrained only on single-arm data.
The inclusion of Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) was essential for robust language grounding on the ALOHA robot, preventing language-dependent task success from plummeting to chance levels.
Takeaways: Combining parallel decoding with action chunking drastically improves both VLA inference efficiency and policy performance, increasing OpenVLA's success rate by 14% on LIBERO.
Using continuous action representations with a simple L1 regression objective yields comparable task performance to diffusion-based methods while offering significantly faster training and inference.
A well-designed fine-tuning strategy enables VLAs pretrained on single-arm data to successfully adapt and even outperform models with bimanual pretraining on complex bimanual manipulation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14795.Title: Humanoid-VLA: Towards Universal Humanoid Control with Visual Integration
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14795.Summary: This paper introduces Humanoid-VLA, the first Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model designed for humanoid robots, enabling autonomous interaction and context-aware motion generation by integrating language, egocentric vision, and control. It addresses data scarcity through a self-supervised data augmentation strategy, outperforming prior text-to-motion models in quality and diversity, and achieving high success rates in real-world object interaction tasks on a Unitree G1 robot.
Problem: Current humanoid control frameworks are largely reactive, responding to explicit external inputs and lacking autonomous interaction capabilities.
Existing methods often rely on third-person observations or lack integrated egocentric visual context, limiting context-aware motion generation from the robot's own perspective.

The development of universal humanoid control models, especially those integrating vision and language, faces significant data scarcity of synchronized first-person visual, textual, and whole-body motion data.
Method: Proposes Humanoid-VLA, the first Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model for humanoids, built on a two-stage framework: Language-Motion Pre-Alignment and Vision-Conditioned Fine-Tuning.
Introduces a self-supervised data augmentation strategy using compositional motion quantization and automatic instructional prompt generation to generate large-scale pseudo-annotated training data.
Integrates the VLA model's generated kinematic motion sequences with a goal-conditioned Reinforcement Learning (RL) policy to control a humanoid robot with physically plausible joint torques.
Results: Humanoid-VLA outperformed baselines in text-to-motion synthesis, achieving an FID of 0.467 on HumanML3D (47.5% improvement over MDM) and 4.466 motion diversity on Humanoid-S (6% better than MDM).
The integrated RL policy achieved robust motion imitation in physics simulations with consistently low errors, including mean position errors below 40mm and pose accuracy at 1.18mm.

Demonstrated strong performance on a real Unitree G1 robot with high success rates (e.g., 10/10 for "Turn to an object," 9/10 for "Hold an object," "Kick a ball") in various real-world object interaction tasks.
Takeaways: A self-supervised data augmentation pipeline is effective in significantly strengthening motion-language alignment and addressing data scarcity for humanoid VLA models.
Integrating egocentric visual perception allows humanoids to move beyond reactive control, enabling autonomous interaction and context-aware motion generation.
Combining large language models for motion generation with a goal-conditioned RL policy for whole-body control leads to robust and physically consistent humanoid behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14420.Title: ChatVLA: Unified Multimodal Understanding and Robot Control with Vision-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14420.Summary: ChatVLA presents a Vision-Language-Action model that successfully unifies multimodal understanding and embodied robot control into a single end-to-end neural network. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance in both visual question answering and 25 real-world robot manipulation tasks by mitigating common training challenges.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lose their multimodal understanding and conversational abilities (spurious forgetting) when fine-tuned for robot control.
Jointly training for robot control and multimodal understanding leads to task interference, where optimizing one capability degrades the performance of the other.
The challenge of creating a truly unified AI agent capable of seamless perception, comprehension, and physical interaction with the environment.
Method: A Phased Alignment Training strategy, a two-stage curriculum that first focuses on robot control mastery and then incrementally integrates visual-text data to reactivate multimodal understanding.

A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture implemented on the MLP layers of the transformer backbone, featuring distinct 'Control-Expert' and 'Understanding-Expert' components with shared self-attention layers.
The model utilizes Qwen2-VL-2B as its Vision-Language Model (VLM) backbone, adapting an action head design from DiVLA for robot control.
Results: ChatVLA achieved significant improvements on VQA benchmarks, scoring 71.2% on TextVQA (a 9.2x relative improvement over ECoT) and 37.4% on MMStar (2.2x over DiVLA), demonstrating robust multimodal understanding.

The model exhibited superior performance across 25 real-world robot manipulation tasks, consistently outperforming baselines like Octo and OpenVLA in long-horizon, compositional, and cross-skill multi-tasking.
These strong results were obtained with greater parameter efficiency, using a 2B parameter VLM backbone, which is 3.5x smaller than some comparable VLA models.
Takeaways: Spurious forgetting and task interference are critical limitations in developing generalist Vision-Language-Action models, and their existence was empirically validated.
A staged training approach (Phased Alignment Training) effectively prevents the degradation of multimodal understanding while acquiring robust robot control skills.

The Mixture-of-Experts architecture, with shared self-attention and dedicated MLP experts, allows for simultaneous high performance in both multimodal understanding and robot control tasks by minimizing interference.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18867.Title: UP-VLA: A Unified Understanding and Prediction Model for Embodied Agent
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.18867.Summary: A unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model, UP-VLA, integrates multi-modal understanding with future visual prediction to enhance robotic control. The model achieved a 33% improvement on the CALVIN benchmark's ABC→D task over previous state-of-the-art and demonstrated improved generalization and precision on real-world robot tasks.
Problem: Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often lack precise low-level visual, spatial, and physical dynamic understanding essential for robotic manipulation.
Visual pre-training methods (e.g., future frame prediction) excel at low-level visual patterns but typically lack the rich semantic and language reasoning capabilities of VLMs.
There is a challenge in developing a single VLA model that can seamlessly handle both high-level semantic comprehension and accurate low-level physical action execution.
Method: UP-VLA proposes a unified autoregressive framework based on an LLM backbone (Phi-1.5), incorporating both continuous vision encoders for multi-modal understanding (MMU) and discrete vision encoders for future visual prediction.
It unifies MMU, future prediction, and action generation tasks into a single sequence modeling problem, using a flexible attention mask and a two-stage training strategy.
Action learning is enhanced through joint future observation prediction and understanding-augmented prompting, where the model's own MMU capabilities describe the scene to guide action generation.
Results: Achieved an average completion length of 4.08 on the CALVIN benchmark's ABC→D task, representing a 33% improvement over the previous state-of-the-art.

Demonstrated improved performance on real-world Franka-Emika Panda robot tasks, particularly in unseen semantic generalization and precise operations requiring detailed visual and spatial understanding.

Ablation studies confirmed that both visual prediction capabilities and multi-modal understanding components are indispensable for achieving superior generalization and precision in embodied AI tasks.
Takeaways: Integrating both high-level multi-modal understanding and low-level future visual prediction is crucial for building robust and generalizable embodied agents.
Future visual prediction provides vital low-level visual and spatial understanding necessary for precise robotic control, while multi-modal understanding enhances semantic generalization.
A unified autoregressive training paradigm can effectively combine these diverse capabilities, leading to superior performance in complex manipulation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15830.Title: SpatialVLA: Exploring Spatial Representations for Visual-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.15830.Summary: Shanghai AI Laboratory's SpatialVLA introduces novel spatial representations for Vision-Language-Action models, equipping them with profound 3D spatial understanding via Ego3D Position Encoding for observations and unifying actions via Adaptive Action Grids. The model achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on diverse real-world robot tasks and demonstrates efficient adaptation to new robot setups, surpassing larger models like RT-2-X with a smaller parameter count.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models primarily rely on 2D observation inputs, lacking precise perception and comprehension of the 3D physical world essential for robot manipulation.
Observations from diverse robot embodiments are heterogeneous due to varying camera placements and calibrations, leading to non-aligned 3D observation spaces.
Learning generalizable spatial actions is challenging across heterogeneous robots due to differing kinematics, degrees of freedom, and motion controllers.
Method: Introduces Ego3D Position Encoding, which integrates 3D spatial context into 2D visual features by estimating depth and encoding egocentric 3D pixel positions, making observations 3D-aware and robot-agnostic.

Proposes Adaptive Action Grids, which discretize continuous robot actions into discrete spatial tokens using parameterized Gaussian distributions for non-uniform, probability-equal binning, enabling generalizable action learning with fewer tokens for faster inference.

Employs a two-stage training scheme: pre-training on 1.1 million real robot demonstrations (Open X-Embodiment and RH20T) followed by efficient post-training using a novel Spatial Embedding Adaption technique for new robot setups.
Results: Achieved state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on SimplerEnv (Google Robot 71.9% Visual Matching, 68.8% Variant Aggregation) and real-world WidowX (highest average success), outperforming larger models like RT-2-X with significantly fewer parameters.

Demonstrated superior adaptation by achieving the highest average success rate (78.1%) on the LIBERO simulation benchmark after fine-tuning and significantly outperforming OpenVLA and Diffusion Policy in Franka instruction-following tasks (+12% improvement).

Consistently showed superior spatial understanding, achieving 73% accuracy in a Franka task requiring spatial prompt understanding and improving manipulation in out-of-distribution tasks involving explicit height changes.
Takeaways: Integrating 3D spatial representations via Ego3D Position Encoding is crucial for Vision-Language-Action models to achieve robust and generalized robot manipulation across varied environments and camera poses.
Discretizing continuous robot actions into 'adaptive' grids based on their statistical distribution significantly improves generalization and convergence compared to uniform discretization.

Freezing pre-trained language embeddings during training preserves general world knowledge, while a novel spatial embedding adaptation method enables efficient transfer of learned action knowledge to new robot embodiments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09747.Title: FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09747.Summary: This paper introduces a novel compression-based tokenization method for converting continuous robot actions into discrete tokens for vision-language-action models
Problem: Current tokenization approaches for robot actions perform poorly on high-frequency, dexterous tasks
Simple per-dimension binning leads to highly correlated tokens that make learning difficult
Existing methods require too many tokens to represent high-frequency action sequences
Method: Introduce FAST (Frequency-space Action Sequence Tokenization) based on discrete cosine transform
Compress action sequences before tokenization to reduce correlations between tokens
Release FAST+, a universal pre-trained tokenizer that works across different robots and action spaces
Results: FAST enables training of autoregressive models on high-frequency dexterous tasks that previous methods failed on
Matches performance of state-of-the-art diffusion models while requiring 5x less training time
Universal tokenizer FAST+ works effectively across diverse robot morphologies and control frequencies
First successful zero-shot evaluation of DROID dataset policies in completely unseen environments
Takeaways: Robot action signals need to be compressed before training to reduce token correlations
Frequency-domain representation via DCT enables effective compression of smooth action trajectories
Simple analytical compression can outperform more complex learned compression methods

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15109.Title: Predictive Inverse Dynamics Models are Scalable Learners for Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15109.Summary: This paper introduces an end-to-end predictive inverse dynamics model that unifies visual prediction and action control for robotic manipulation
Problem: Current approaches either focus solely on behavior cloning from robot data or visual pre-training, but don't effectively combine both
Two-stage approaches that separate visual prediction from action control lack synergy between vision and action
Existing methods struggle with generalization across novel objects, lighting conditions and environments
Method: Proposes Seer, an end-to-end model that integrates conditional visual foresight with inverse dynamics prediction
Uses transformer architecture to process both visual states and actions together
Pre-trains on large-scale robot datasets and fine-tunes on downstream tasks
Employs unidirectional attention to allow action tokens to incorporate both past and future predictive information
Results: Achieves 13% improvement on LIBERO-LONG benchmark
21% improvement on CALVIN ABC-D benchmark
43% improvement on real-world tasks
Shows robust generalization to novel objects, lighting conditions and environments
Demonstrates strong performance even with limited fine-tuning data
Sets new state-of-the-art on CALVIN ABC-D with average length of 4.28
Takeaways: End-to-end training of visual prediction and action control leads to better performance than separated approaches
Future visual state prediction helps guide action selection
Pre-training on large robot datasets improves generalization capabilities
Unidirectional attention enables deep integration of past and future information

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14803.Title: Video Prediction Policy: A Generalist Robot Policy with Predictive Visual Representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14803.Summary: Video Prediction Policy (VPP) introduces a generalist robot policy that leverages predictive visual representations extracted from a fine-tuned video diffusion model in a single forward pass. This approach enables the policy to implicitly learn inverse dynamics from rough future predictions, achieving an average task completion length of 4.33 on the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark and robust generalization across various real-world manipulation tasks with Franka Panda and dexterous hands.
Problem: Existing visual representations for generalist robot policies often focus on static information, neglecting the crucial temporal dynamics necessary for complex, embodied tasks.
Prior methods leveraging future prediction for robot control typically suffer from low control frequencies or sub-optimal prediction quality due to multi-step generative processes.
Developing generalist robot policies that can robustly generalize across a wide array of tasks and environments, including dexterous manipulation and unseen scenarios, remains a challenge.
Method: Develops a two-stage approach: first, fine-tuning an open-sourced large video foundation model (SVD) into a text-guided video prediction (TVP) model using a diverse blend of internet-scale human and robot manipulation videos.
Utilizes the frozen TVP model as a 'predictive visual encoder' by extracting internal representations from a single, efficient forward pass, rather than generating full video sequences.
Employs a Video Former module to condense aggregated multi-layer features from the TVP model and condition a Diffusion Policy head for high-frequency, closed-loop action generation.
Results: Achieves an average task completion length of 4.33 on the CALVIN ABC→D benchmark, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art by 41.5% (over GR-1), and outperforms GR-1 even when trained with only 10% of the data.
Attains an average success rate of 0.682 across 50 MetaWorld tasks, demonstrating a 10.8% absolute improvement over the strongest baseline (GR-1).

Exhibits strong real-world generalization on unseen objects and tasks with a Franka Panda robot (0.73 success rate for unseen tasks) and an Xarm with a 12-degree Xhand dexterous hand (0.68 for challenging tool-use tasks).
Takeaways: Internal representations of video diffusion models (VDMs), even from a single forward pass, implicitly encode rich spatio-temporal dynamics that are highly effective for robot control.
A downstream policy can implicitly learn inverse dynamics by tracking robot movements within these predictive visual representations, simplifying action generation.
Combining large-scale internet video pre-training with diverse robot manipulation datasets enables exceptional generalization and data efficiency for robot policies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14058.Title: What Matters in Building Vision-Language-Action Models for Generalist Robots
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14058.Summary: A detailed empirical study by Tsinghua University, ByteDance Research, and collaborators systematically investigated design principles for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models in generalist robotics. The research identified optimal VLM backbones, architectural structures, and data strategies, achieving state-of-the-art robot manipulation performance on benchmarks and in real-world settings with emergent self-correction.
Problem: Developing generalizable robot policies capable of perceiving, reasoning, and interacting with diverse physical environments remains a grand challenge.

The effective transfer of pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into high-performing robot policies for VLA models is not straightforward, lacking systematic understanding of optimal design choices.
Fundamental questions persist regarding suitable VLM backbones, architectural formulations for action components, and optimal strategies for incorporating diverse robotic datasets.
Method: The researchers developed RoboVLMs, an open-source, flexible framework allowing easy integration of various VLM backbones and configurations of VLA structures.

An extensive empirical investigation was conducted, comprising over 600 experiments across 8 VLM backbones, diverse VLA architectures (e.g., one-step, history modeling, continuous/discrete actions), and data utilization strategies.
The proposed methods were trained and evaluated on simulation benchmarks (CALVIN, SimplerEnv) and a custom real-world dataset from a Kinova robot to assess performance and generalization.
Results: The best RoboVLM achieved new state-of-the-art performance on CALVIN, showing absolute gains of 12.6% for single tasks and 30.3% for 5 consecutive tasks on the unseen split D.

RoboVLMs demonstrated robust real-world effectiveness, generalizing across unseen distractors, backgrounds, target objects, and novel skill descriptions, while exhibiting emergent self-correction abilities.

Specific VLM backbones (KosMos, Paligemma) with extensive vision-language pre-training proved most suitable, and continuous action spaces consistently outperformed discrete actions for robot manipulation tasks.
Takeaways: Vision-language pre-training is essential for achieving strong generalization and high data efficiency in VLA models for robot manipulation tasks.

Continuous action spaces and the incorporation of historical observations via a 'Policy Head' structure significantly enhance VLA performance, particularly with robustly pre-trained VLM backbones like KosMos and Paligemma.
Optimal utilization of large-scale cross-embodiment data is achieved through post-training or by enhancing few-shot learning capabilities, rather than solely through direct co-training.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13877.Title: RoboMIND: Benchmark on Multi-embodiment Intelligence Normative Data for Robot Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.13877.Summary: RoboMIND introduces a large-scale, multi-embodiment dataset for robot manipulation, collected under unified standards across four distinct robot types, including a humanoid. This dataset significantly enhances the performance and generalization capabilities of Vision-Language-Action models, enabling higher success rates on complex real-world tasks and facilitating cross-embodiment policy transfer.
Problem: Existing robotic datasets lack unified data collection standards, leading to inconsistencies and hindering the training of generalizable models across different labs and hardware.

Current datasets offer insufficient diversity in robot embodiments, primarily focusing on single-arm setups, which limits the development of policies for complex multi-arm or dexterous humanoid manipulation.
There is a scarcity of real-world failure data and fine-grained linguistic annotations, which are crucial for developing robust policies that can learn from errors and understand tasks in detail.
Method: Introduced RoboMIND, a large-scale, high-quality, multi-embodiment dataset collected under a unified data collection standard using human teleoperation across single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid robotic platforms.

Provided comprehensive data types for each trajectory, including multi-view RGB-D, proprioceptive states, end-effector information, and linguistic task descriptions, stored in a standardized H5 format.

Included unique data subsets: 5,000 real-world failure demonstrations with detailed causes and 10,000 trajectories with fine-grained, frame-level linguistic annotations, alongside a closely replicated digital twin environment in Nvidia Isaac Sim.
Results: RoboMIND comprises 107,000 demonstration trajectories (305.5 hours) from four robot embodiments (Franka, UR5e, AgileX, Tien Kung humanoid), covering 479 tasks, 96 object classes, 5,000 real-world failure demonstrations, and 10,000 trajectories with frame-level linguistic annotations.

Evaluation showed VLA models like RDT-1B and CrossFormer achieved significantly enhanced performance, with CrossFormer demonstrating near-perfect scores on some dual-arm and humanoid tasks after pre-training on the full RoboMIND dataset, where it previously struggled.

A strong positive correlation (Pearson 0.83-0.91) between real-world and simulation results validated the utility of the digital twin for policy evaluation, though real-world data remains crucial due to persistent sim-to-real gaps, especially for contact-rich interactions.
Takeaways: RoboMIND effectively pre-trains and fine-tunes Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, enabling high success rates and cross-embodiment transfer across diverse robot types and tasks.
The inclusion of multi-embodiment data, particularly from humanoid robots, contributes to better overall policy learning and generalization even for other robot types.

While models show good generalization to unseen objects, generalizing to unseen backgrounds remains a significant challenge, and simulation data, though useful for pre-training, still exhibits sim-to-real gaps for complex contact tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10345.Title: TraceVLA: Visual Trace Prompting Enhances Spatial-Temporal Awareness for Generalist Robotic Policies
https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.10345.Summary: TraceVLA enhances the spatial-temporal awareness of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by introducing visual trace prompting, which overlays historical multi-point movement trajectories onto current visual observations. This approach improves performance by 7.5% in simulation and shows superior generalization across diverse manipulation tasks on a physical robot compared to OpenVLA.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models exhibit limited spatial-temporal awareness, often making decisions based on instantaneous visual inputs.
This lack of historical context hinders their performance in complex robotic manipulation tasks requiring understanding continuous motion, object trajectories, or effects of prior actions.
Naive concatenation of raw historical frames as input is inefficient and can be distracting due to redundancy.
Method: Introduces visual trace prompting where multi-point historical trajectories, extracted using Co-Tracker, are visually overlaid onto the current observation image.
The VLA model receives this trace-augmented image alongside the original observation, informed by an adjusted language prompt.
A new dataset of 150K trajectories with visual traces was created to fine-tune state-of-the-art VLA models like OpenVLA and Phi-3-Vision.
Results: TraceVLA achieved an average success rate of 47.7% in SimplerEnv simulations, an absolute gain of 7.5% over OpenVLA, and demonstrated robustness to environmental variations.

In real-world experiments on a WidowX-250 robot, TraceVLA consistently outperformed OpenVLA across diverse manipulation tasks, including achieving 6/10 successes on unseen generalization tasks like "Pickplace Banana" where OpenVLA failed.
The method also showed superior multitask performance on LIBERO benchmarks, with an average success rate of 74.8%, and incurs minimal inference overhead (approx. 0.03 seconds per step).
Takeaways: Visual trace prompting is the main factor contributing to performance improvements, significantly outperforming simple finetuning or historical frame concatenation.
Explicitly encoding spatial-temporal information visually is more effective than textual descriptions of movements or raw historical image inputs for VLA models.
The length of the visual trace window (e.g., 6 steps) is critical, with optimal performance achieved at intermediate lengths.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19650.Title: CogACT: A Foundational Vision-Language-Action Model for Synergizing Cognition and Action in Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19650.Summary: CogACT is a Vision-Language-Action model that improves robotic manipulation by adopting a componentized architecture and a specialized diffusion-based action module. This approach directly models continuous and multimodal robotic actions, leading to significantly higher success rates across diverse simulation and real-world tasks compared to existing VLA models.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often quantize continuous action spaces into discrete bins, leading to imprecise robotic control.
These models struggle to capture the inherent temporal correlation between successive robot actions and represent multimodal action distributions (multiple valid ways to complete a task).
VLA models often face challenges in generalizing to new robots, environments, and objects in real-world scenarios.
Method: CogACT introduces a componentized Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architecture that separates task understanding (cognition) from execution (action) through distinct vision, language, and action modules.

It employs a specialized action module based on a diffusion transformer (DiT) that directly models continuous and multimodal robotic action distributions, conditioned by cognitive features from the VLM.
The model integrates an adaptive action ensemble algorithm during inference to generate and combine multiple action predictions, enhancing robustness and smoothing action trajectories.
Results: CogACT achieved a 61.3% success rate on variant aggregation tasks and 74.8% on visual matching tasks in SIMPLER simulation with Google Robot, outperforming RT-2-X (54.4% and 46.3%).

In real-world tests, CogACT demonstrated superior performance, including a 71.2% success rate on seen environments and 61.5% on unseen environments with the Realman robot, and 61.4% with unseen objects on the Franka robot.
The research showed that scaling up the specialized action module, even modestly, leads to significant performance improvements, with the large action module achieving a 65.7% average success rate.
Takeaways: Treating robotic action generation as distinct from language generation, requiring specialized modeling approaches for continuous, multimodal, and temporally correlated actions.

A componentized architecture where a dedicated diffusion transformer action module, conditioned by cognitive features from a VLM, effectively models complex action distributions without discretization.
Adaptive action ensemble during inference can smooth action trajectories and improve robustness by combining multiple predictions based on similarity.
