https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19309.Title: GRAPE: Generalizing Robot Policy via Preference Alignment
https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19309.Summary: GRAPE introduces a framework that enhances the generalizability and objective alignment of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) robot policies. It leverages trajectory-wise preference optimization with automatically generated preference data, achieving substantial improvements in success rates and out-of-distribution performance compared to supervised fine-tuning baselines.
Problem: Current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models trained via behavior cloning struggle with generalizability to unseen environments and tasks, often leading to "behavior collapse."
Supervised fine-tuning datasets are often uncurated, leading to suboptimal trajectories because models implicitly learn from mixed and undefined objectives.
Traditional reinforcement learning is impractical for VLA model training due to high costs of online data collection and difficulties in defining explicit reward functions for complex tasks.
Method: GRAPE employs Trajectory-wise Preference Optimization (TPO) to fine-tune VLA policies by learning from comparisons of chosen (preferred) and rejected trajectories.

Guided-Cost Preference Generation (GCPG) automatically synthesizes high-quality preference data by decomposing trajectories into stages, generating cost functions with an LLM, and aggregating them with self-evaluated and success-indicating rewards.
An iterative online training loop continuously refines the VLA policy using these generated preference pairs, progressively enhancing alignment and generalization.
Results: Achieved substantial gains in success rates across simulated and real-world tasks, outperforming supervised fine-tuning baselines by an average of 131.72% in Simpler-Env and 11% in real-world settings over OpenVLA-DPO.
Demonstrated robust generalization to various out-of-distribution scenarios, including unseen objects, different sizes, and modified instructions, validating improved adaptability.

Successfully aligned robot policies with specific objectives, such as GRAPE-Safety reducing collision rates by 37.44% in real-world scenarios and GRAPE-Efficiency reducing rollout step-length by 11.15%, while maintaining high success rates.
Takeaways: Learning from both successful and failure trajectories via trajectory-wise preference optimization provides a more comprehensive understanding of task goals and pitfalls, improving robustness.
Automating preference data generation through multi-modal models (VLMs, LLMs) for defining stage-specific costs and aggregating rewards reduces reliance on costly human annotation.
Policy alignment through preference optimization enables flexible customization of robot behavior to diverse objectives such as safety and efficiency, moving beyond mere task completion.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164.Title: $π_0$: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164.Summary: π0 introduces a vision-language-action flow model that combines a pre-trained VLM with a flow matching action expert for general robot control. The model, trained on over 10,000 hours of diverse robot data, achieves state-of-the-art performance on complex dexterous and multi-stage tasks across various robot platforms.
Problem: Robot learning systems face challenges in data scarcity, generalization, and robustness, leading to specialized and brittle solutions.
Achieving versatile, generalist robot policies that can perform diverse and complex dexterous tasks in varied environments remains an open problem.
Prior Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models often struggle with generating continuous, high-frequency actions crucial for precise manipulation.
Method: Developed π0, a vision-language-action model integrating a pre-trained PaliGemma VLM backbone with a novel action expert based on conditional flow matching.
The action expert generates continuous, high-frequency action chunks (up to 50 Hz) for precise robot control, addressing limitations of autoregressive action modeling.
Employed a multi-stage training paradigm, pre-training on over 10,000 hours of diverse, cross-embodiment robot data from multiple platforms, followed by task-specific fine-tuning.
Results: The pre-trained π0 model achieved superior out-of-box performance across various tasks compared to state-of-the-art baselines like OpenVLA and Octo.
Fine-tuned π0 demonstrated enhanced language following capabilities, leading to improved task success when guided by human or high-level VLM policies.
The model showed significant data efficiency for new dexterous tasks, often doubling performance with limited fine-tuning data compared to training from scratch or other methods.

π0 successfully completed complex, multi-stage dexterous tasks, such as laundry folding and table bussing with novel objects, achieving over 50% of the maximum score and setting a new performance benchmark.
Takeaways: Integrating a pre-trained VLM backbone with a specialized action expert enables robots to leverage internet-scale semantic knowledge for high-level understanding and robust language following.
Conditional flow matching effectively models the continuous, high-frequency action distributions necessary for dexterous and precise physical interaction.
A multi-stage pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm, analogous to large language models, significantly enhances generalization, robustness, and data efficiency for robot policies.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11758.Title: Latent Action Pretraining from Videos
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11758.Summary: Latent Action Pretraining (LAPA), developed by researchers from KAIST, University of Washington, Microsoft Research, NVIDIA, and Allen Institute for AI, enables unsupervised pretraining of Vision-Language-Action models from actionless videos, including human manipulation footage. This approach allows for learning generalizable robot policies from abundant, unlabeled web data and demonstrates superior performance and pretraining efficiency compared to current state-of-the-art methods that rely on extensive labeled robot datasets.
Problem: Developing generalist robotic policies is constrained by the scarcity and high cost of collecting large, diverse, action-labeled robot datasets via human teleoperation.
Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models still largely depend on labeled robot action data, limiting scalability and diversity.
Utilizing abundant, unlabeled internet videos is challenging due to the lack of explicit robot action annotations and the embodiment gap between human and robot movements.
Method: An unsupervised, multi-stage method called Latent Action Pretraining (LAPA) is introduced, which first learns discrete "latent actions" from raw video frames using a VQ-VAE based encoder-decoder model.
A pre-trained Vision-Language Model is then trained to predict these pseudo-labeled discrete latent actions from observations and language instructions.
The LAPA model is fine-tuned on a small dataset of robot trajectories with ground-truth actions to map the learned latent actions to continuous robot control commands.
Results: LAPA, when pretrained on Open-X, surpassed the state-of-the-art OpenVLA (trained on 970k action-labeled trajectories) in real-world tabletop manipulation tasks with a 50.09% average success rate (vs. 43.87%).

Pretraining LAPA solely on human manipulation videos (Something-Something V2) successfully enabled positive transfer to robot manipulation tasks, outperforming OpenVLA (Bridge) in real-world scenarios.
Achieved significantly higher pretraining efficiency, requiring approximately 272 H100-hours for its best model compared to OpenVLA's 21,500 A100-hours (estimated 30-40x more efficient).
Takeaways: Learning discrete latent actions from raw video observations allows for unsupervised pretraining without explicit action labels or pre-defined action priors.
A shared, discrete latent action space can be learned that is robust across different robot embodiments and can transfer from human manipulation videos to robot tasks.
Leveraging a pre-trained Vision-Language Model as a backbone and learning a small, discrete latent action space significantly improves pretraining efficiency (30-40x faster than prior methods).

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07864.Title: RDT-1B: a Diffusion Foundation Model for Bimanual Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.07864.Summary: Researchers at Tsinghua University developed RDT-1B, the first diffusion-based foundation model for bimanual robotic manipulation, featuring 1.2 billion parameters. This model achieved an average 56% improvement in success rates over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse bimanual tasks, showcasing strong zero-shot generalization to unseen objects and scenes, and few-shot learning capabilities.
Problem: Developing generalizable bimanual manipulation policies is challenging due to the inherent complexity of coordinating two arms for diverse tasks.
Data scarcity for dual-arm robot systems hinders the training of data-hungry foundation models.
Bimanual tasks often exhibit multi-modal action distributions, which traditional imitation learning struggles to capture, potentially leading to physically infeasible "average" actions.
Method: Introduces RDT-1B, a 1.2-billion-parameter Diffusion Transformer (DiT) model, adapted with QKNorm, RMSNorm, MLP Decoder, and Alternating Condition Injection for stable large-scale training on robotic data.
Employs a "Physically Interpretable Unified Action Space" to map heterogeneous robot actions into a common 128-dimensional representation, enabling extensive cross-robot pre-training.

Utilizes a pre-training and fine-tuning pipeline: pre-trains on over 1 million trajectories from 46 diverse multi-robot datasets, then fine-tunes on a self-collected bimanual dataset of 6,000 trajectories.
Results: RDT-1B achieved an average 56% improvement in success rates compared to state-of-the-art baselines across a wide range of challenging bimanual tasks on a real ALOHA dual-arm robot.

The model demonstrated exceptional zero-shot generalization, successfully performing tasks with unseen objects, scenes, and novel language instructions (e.g., precise pouring volumes) without prior exposure.
RDT-1B exhibited strong few-shot learning, adapting to complex new skills from as few as 1-5 demonstrations, significantly outperforming baselines which failed.
Takeaways: Diffusion models are effective for capturing and sampling from multi-modal action distributions in complex bimanual tasks, avoiding "average" and infeasible actions.
Large-scale cross-robot pre-training on diverse datasets, combined with a unified action space, is crucial for overcoming data scarcity and enabling robust generalization in bimanual manipulation.

Architectural adaptations to Diffusion Transformers (e.g., QKNorm, RMSNorm, non-linear MLP decoder, alternating condition injection) are essential for stable scaling and handling the unique, high-frequency, and non-linear properties of robotic data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06158.Title: GR-2: A Generative Video-Language-Action Model with Web-Scale Knowledge for Robot Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06158.Summary: Researchers at ByteDance Research developed GR-2, a generalist robot agent that combines large-scale video pre-training with robot action generation using a GPT-style transformer model. The system achieved a 97.7% success rate on multi-task tabletop manipulation, an average of 79.0% on industrial bin-picking, and established new state-of-the-art on the CALVIN benchmark for language-conditioned tasks.
Problem: Developing robotic systems capable of understanding natural language instructions and performing a wide range of manipulation tasks.
Enabling robots to generalize effectively to unseen environments, novel objects, and new tasks with limited specific training data.
Addressing the challenge of generating precise robot action trajectories from observations, where multiple valid actions may exist for a given state.
Method: A GPT-style transformer architecture that processes tokenized representations of text instructions, video frames, and robot actions.
A two-stage training process involving large-scale video-language pre-training on 38 million diverse video clips, followed by fine-tuning on robot-specific video-language-action data.
Integration of a conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE) within the fine-tuning stage to generate diverse and robust action trajectories.
Results: Achieved a 97.7% success rate on simple multi-task tabletop manipulation and maintained 75% success with only 50 demonstrations per task, showing data efficiency.

Demonstrated an average success rate of 79.0% on industrial bin-picking tasks, a significant improvement over its predecessor GR-1 (35.9%), including with unseen objects and in cluttered environments.
Established a new state-of-the-art on the CALVIN benchmark, achieving 98.6% success for completing one task and an average task completion length of 4.64 for longer sequences.
Takeaways: Large-scale video pre-training on diverse human activity data enables strong generalization capabilities for subsequent robot manipulation tasks.
A unified GPT-style transformer architecture can effectively integrate language, video, and robot action modalities for complex control.
The use of a conditional Variational Autoencoder (cVAE) helps in generating robust action trajectories by addressing the one-to-many mapping inherent in robot control.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.20537.Title: Scaling Proprioceptive-Visual Learning with Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.20537.Summary: Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers (HPT) introduces a modular architecture for robotic policy learning that integrates diverse data from multiple robot embodiments and sources. It demonstrates consistent performance improvements with increased data quantity and diversity, model size, and compute, achieving 10-30% higher success rates in simulations and 20%+ in real-world tasks compared to training from scratch.
Problem: Traditional robotic learning approaches require collecting task-specific data for each robot embodiment, leading to high costs and time consumption.
Policies trained on one robot often fail to transfer to different embodiments due to variations in morphology, sensors, and action spaces.
The heterogeneity of robotic data, including diverse camera configurations, proprioceptive sensors, and action representations, makes it difficult to train unified generalist models.
Method: Introduces Heterogeneous Pre-trained Transformers (HPT), a modular 'stem-trunk-head' architecture designed to process diverse robotic inputs and learn shared representations.
Embodiment-specific stems tokenize proprioceptive and visual inputs from various robots, feeding them into a shared Transformer trunk that uses cross-attention to fuse information.

The model is pre-trained on a diverse mixture of real robot data, simulation data, human videos, and multi-embodiment data, enabling it to learn generalizable patterns across different robotic systems.
Results: HPT consistently outperforms baselines in transfer learning across multiple simulation benchmarks, achieving 10-30% higher success rates compared to training from scratch.
In real robot experiments, pre-trained HPT policies achieve over 20% improvements in success rates on four diverse manipulation tasks compared to training from scratch.

Experiments demonstrate clear scaling behaviors, showing lower validation loss with increased data quantity and diversity, larger model sizes (up to over 1 billion parameters), and more training compute.
Takeaways: Robotic learning exhibits clear scaling laws, with performance improving consistently as dataset size, data diversity, model parameters, and training compute increase.
Joint training on both proprioceptive and visual data is more effective than training on either modality alone or sequentially.
Incorporating diverse data sources, including simulation data and human videos, significantly improves the transferability and final performance of robotic policies across embodiments.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12514.Title: TinyVLA: Towards Fast, Data-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models for Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12514.Summary: TinyVLA introduces a Vision-Language-Action model that achieves robust robotic manipulation performance while being significantly faster and more data-efficient than prior VLA models. It demonstrates that strong VLA capabilities can emerge without extensive pre-training on massive robotic datasets, leveraging compact pre-trained VLMs and a diffusion policy for action generation.
Problem: Existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as RT-2 and OpenVLA, suffer from slow inference speeds due to their reliance on large Vision-Language Models (often 7+ billion parameters) and autoregressive action token generation.
These VLA models require extensive pre-training on massive robotic datasets (e.g., 970K samples for OpenVLA), which is computationally expensive and resource-intensive.
Current VLA approaches face challenges in real-time, responsive robotic control and accessibility for researchers or applications with limited computational resources or data collection capabilities.
Method: Utilizes compact, pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ranging from 70 million to 1.4 billion parameters as the policy backbone, pre-trained on general vision-language data.
Employs Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning on robotic manipulation data, freezing most of the VLM's pre-trained weights to preserve knowledge and enhance data efficiency.
Integrates a Diffusion Policy (DP) as the policy head for direct, continuous robot action generation, departing from slow autoregressive token prediction.
Results: TinyVLA-H achieved a 94.0% average success rate in real-world single-arm manipulation tasks, outperforming OpenVLA's 68.3%. It also achieved 44.5% in bimanual tasks where OpenVLA failed (0%).

TinyVLA operates 20 times faster than OpenVLA (14 ms vs. 292 ms per action prediction) while using 5.5 times fewer parameters, and eliminates the need for extensive pre-training on large robotic datasets like OpenX.
The model demonstrated robust generalization capabilities across various scenarios, including novel instructions, camera viewpoints, backgrounds, illumination, distractors, and spatial variations.
Takeaways: Robust Vision-Language-Action (VLA) capabilities can be achieved without extensive pre-training on massive robot-specific datasets, by effectively leveraging knowledge from general vision-language data.

The combination of compact, pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and a diffusion policy decoder provides a method for achieving both high inference speed and data efficiency in robotic manipulation.
VLM size scales with performance in TinyVLA, with larger VLMs (e.g., TinyVLA-H) mitigating issues such as instruction misinterpretation and inaccurate positioning.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01652.Title: ReKep: Spatio-Temporal Reasoning of Relational Keypoint Constraints for Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01652.Summary: ReKep enables robots to perform diverse, multi-stage manipulation tasks in unstructured environments by automatically generating visually-grounded relational keypoint constraints from language instructions using foundation models. The system demonstrates robust real-time execution and zero-shot generalization across various complex behaviors, outperforming baseline methods on real-world robot platforms.
Problem: Existing constraint formulations for robotic manipulation often lack versatility for diverse, complex tasks, including multi-stage, in-the-wild, and bimanual operations.
Manually specifying constraints, object models, or annotating keypoints for every new task is time-consuming and does not scale.
Generated constraints must be in a format that allows off-the-shelf optimization solvers to produce real-time robot actions for continuous, closed-loop control.
Method: Introduces Relational Keypoint Constraints (ReKep), defined as Python functions encoding spatial relationships between 3D keypoints, which are used as cost functions for manipulation.
Employs a hierarchical optimization procedure, decomposing tasks into 'sub-goal' and 'path' problems, solved in real-time (10 Hz) using off-the-shelf numerical solvers.
Automates keypoint proposal using DINOv2 and SAM from RGB-D inputs, and leverages GPT-4o to generate the ReKep Python functions directly from free-form language instructions and visual prompts.
Results: Achieved a 44.3% total success rate across seven diverse real-world manipulation tasks, outperforming a VLM-based baseline (VoxPoser, 10.0%) and demonstrating robustness to disturbances.
Successfully generalized to novel manipulation strategies for 8 unique garment categories, achieving a 73.8% execution success rate when the VLM generated a feasible strategy.
Identified point tracking inaccuracies (due to occlusions) as the primary source of system failures, while the optimization module proved relatively robust.
Takeaways: Visually-grounded keypoint constraints, automatically generated by VLMs, offer a versatile and scalable representation for complex robotic manipulation tasks.
A hierarchical, receding-horizon optimization framework enables real-time, reactive control, allowing robots to adapt to disturbances and execute multi-stage behaviors.

Leveraging foundation models (DINOv2 for keypoints, GPT-4o for constraint generation) automates the traditionally manual process of constraint specification, significantly reducing engineering effort.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.05996.Title: Multimodal Diffusion Transformer: Learning Versatile Behavior from Multimodal Goals
https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.05996.Summary: The Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MDT) enables robots to learn versatile behaviors from multimodal goal specifications using only sparse language annotations. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks like CALVIN and LIBERO, particularly with limited language data, and demonstrates successful transfer to real-world kitchen manipulation tasks.
Problem: Robot learning from multimodal goals (language, images) is difficult when datasets are sparsely labeled.
Most existing robot learning approaches require fully annotated data, which is expensive and time-consuming to create.
The challenge of training robots efficiently from 'play data' with limited language annotations limits broader applicability.
Method: Introduces the Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MDT), an architecture combining a transformer encoder with a diffusion-based policy decoder.
The encoder processes visual observations and multimodal goals (language or image) through specialized encoders and a transformer block.
Incorporates two self-supervised learning techniques: Masked Generative Foresight (MGF) for future state prediction and Contrastive Latent Alignment (CLA) for goal modality alignment.
Results: Achieved approximately 85% success on the CALVIN benchmark for executing 5 consecutive instructions, outperforming previous methods, especially with limited language annotations.
Demonstrated a 65% success rate on the LIBERO benchmark with only 2 labeled demonstrations out of 20, competitive with methods trained on fully labeled datasets.
Successfully transferred to real-world scenarios, enabling a robotic arm to complete various kitchen manipulation tasks based on natural language instructions.
Takeaways: Masked Generative Foresight (MGF) improves learning by training the model to reconstruct masked future image patches, enabling robust latent feature learning.
Contrastive Latent Alignment (CLA) ensures consistency across latent representations conditioned on different goal modalities (language and image) for the same desired behavior.
The combination of a multimodal transformer encoder, a diffusion-based policy, and these self-supervised objectives enables effective robot learning from sparsely annotated multimodal play data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09246.Title: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09246.Summary: OpenVLA introduces a fully open-source, 7B-parameter Vision-Language-Action model that sets a new state of the art for generalist robot manipulation, outperforming larger closed-source models by 16.5% absolute success rate. The model also demonstrates effective and efficient fine-tuning strategies for adapting to new robot setups and tasks on commodity hardware.
Problem: Traditional robotic manipulation policies were task-specific and struggled with generalization to novel objects, scenes, or unseen instructions.
Existing state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models were largely closed-source, limiting accessibility, transparency, and collaborative community development.
There was a lack of established, efficient methods for fine-tuning large VLA models to new robot embodiments and tasks, particularly for deployment on more accessible, commodity hardware.
Method: Develops and releases OpenVLA, a 7B-parameter, fully open-source Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model based on a Llama 2 LLM combined with a fused DINOv2 and SigLIP visual encoder.
Trains OpenVLA on 970k real-world robot demonstrations from the Open X-Embodiment dataset, formulating robot action prediction as a next-token prediction task by tokenizing continuous actions.

Investigates and validates efficient fine-tuning methodologies, including parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) and 4-bit quantization, to enable practical adaptation and inference on commodity hardware.
Results: OpenVLA, a 7B-parameter model, established a new state of the art for generalist robot manipulation, outperforming the 55B-parameter RT-2-X by 16.5% absolute success rate across 29 tasks on WidowX and Google Robot embodiments.

The model demonstrated effective and data-efficient adaptation to new real-world robot setups with small datasets (10-150 demonstrations), outperforming from-scratch imitation learning methods by 20.4% on diverse multi-instruction tasks.

LoRA fine-tuning achieved performance comparable to full fine-tuning while training only 1.4% of parameters, reducing compute by 8x, and 4-bit quantization maintained performance while halving GPU memory footprint to 7.0 GB for inference at ~6Hz on consumer GPUs.
Takeaways: Fine-tuning the vision encoder is crucial for achieving high performance in robot control, suggesting pretrained vision backbones need adaptation for precise spatial details.
Extensive training over many epochs (27) with a fixed learning rate is essential for maximizing action token accuracy and real-world robot performance.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) and 4-bit quantization enable significant reductions in computational requirements and memory footprint, making VLA model adaptation and deployment practical on commodity hardware without substantial performance degradation, provided vision encoder adaptation is included.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02523.Title: RoboCasa: Large-Scale Simulation of Everyday Tasks for Generalist Robots
https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.02523.Summary: RoboCasa is a simulation framework designed to address the data scarcity challenge in robot learning by providing diverse, large-scale datasets for household tasks. The project, building on RoboSuite, includes varied kitchen environments, an extensive object repository, and a benchmark of 100 tasks, demonstrating that increasing training data significantly improves robot policy performance and facilitates sim-to-real transfer.
Problem: Robotics faces a critical bottleneck due to the lack of large-scale, diverse, and realistic datasets for training generalist robots.
Collecting real-world robot data is expensive, time-consuming, and often lacks the diversity needed for generalization.
The 'sim-to-real gap' makes transferring skills learned in simulation to real-world robots challenging.
Method: RoboCasa provides a comprehensive simulation framework built on RoboSuite, supporting room-scale environments, mobile manipulation, realistic physics, and high-quality rendering.
It features a systematically created environment with 120 unique kitchen scenes across 10 floor plans and 12 styles, alongside an asset library of over 2,500 objects.

A benchmark of 100 tasks (25 atomic, 75 composite) was designed, with composite tasks generated using large language models, and large-scale demonstration data created using both human teleoperation and automated methods like MimicGen.
Results: Visuomotor policies trained on RoboCasa data showed significant performance improvements as the amount of training data increased.
Machine-generated data from MimicGen led to better generalization compared to training solely on human demonstrations.
Policies trained in RoboCasa successfully transferred to a real Franka Emika Panda robot, with co-training on simulation data improving real-world task success.
Takeaways: Robot learning benefits significantly from larger datasets, similar to other AI domains.
Machine-generated demonstrations can be more effective for generalization than human demonstrations alone.
Training across diverse scenes, objects, and task variations is crucial for improving robot robustness and generalization.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14093.Title: A Survey on Vision-Language-Action Models for Embodied AI
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14093.Summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, crucial for embodied AI, are comprehensively organized in this survey, detailing their architectures, training methodologies, and essential resources for language-conditioned robotic tasks. The work presents a novel taxonomy classifying VLAs by hierarchical control (low-level policies and high-level planners), identifying key components and future research opportunities.
Problem: The rapidly evolving landscape of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models lacked a comprehensive and structured overview.
Researchers faced challenges in understanding and categorizing the diverse architectures and approaches emerging in embodied AI for language-conditioned robotic tasks.
A need existed to bridge the gap between advanced vision-language understanding and the generation of actionable outputs for physical robots.
Method: A structured methodology was employed to systematically review, categorize, and synthesize existing research on VLA models.
A novel hierarchical taxonomy was developed, segmenting models into low-level control policies and high-level task planners based on their function in robotic systems.
Comprehensive summaries of datasets, simulators, benchmarks, and data collection methods were aggregated to provide a resource hub for the community.
Results: The survey defines VLAs and Large VLAs (LVLAs), identifying their distinct role in enabling language-conditioned robotic tasks.
Analysis revealed that VLA systems predominantly utilize a hierarchical control paradigm, with distinct low-level control policies and high-level task planners.

Key components like Pretrained Visual Representations (PVRs), dynamics learning, and world models were identified as crucial for VLA functionality, alongside trends towards Transformer-based architectures and diffusion models for action generation.
Persistent challenges include significant data scarcity for real-world robot interactions, the sim-to-real gap, and the need for more comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation benchmarks.
Takeaways: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models represent a critical and emerging category of multimodal AI for embodied systems, directly linking perception, language, and physical action.
The hierarchical control framework, comprising high-level task planners and low-level control policies, is a prevalent and effective approach for managing complexity in VLA systems.
The integration of large language models (LLMs) and large vision-language models (VLMs) as core components provides enhanced versatility and generalizability for VLA models.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12213.Title: Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12213.Summary: Octo introduces an open-source, transformer-based generalist robot policy that achieves strong zero-shot control and state-of-the-art data-efficient finetuning across diverse robot embodiments and tasks. It is trained on the largest available robot manipulation dataset (800k trajectories from Open X-Embodiment), supporting flexible task and observation definitions.
Problem: Existing generalist robot policies often lack flexibility in input observations, constraining users to predefined sensory inputs.
Many prior generalist models offer ineffective finetuning support, limiting their adaptation to entirely new domains or observation/action spaces.
The most capable generalist robot policies are typically proprietary and not publicly accessible, hindering widespread research and deployment.
Method: Octo employs a modular, transformer-first architecture with a conditional denoising diffusion process for action prediction, enabling flexible input observations (language, goal images, various cameras) and action spaces.
It is pretrained on 800,000 trajectories from the Open X-Embodiment dataset, carefully curated and augmented for diversity and scale.
The entire framework, including pretrained model checkpoints (Octo-Small, Octo-Base), training pipelines, and data loaders, is released as open-source.
Results: Octo (93M parameters) achieved a 29% higher average success rate than RT-1-X on language-conditioned tasks across multiple robot platforms, performing competitively with the much larger RT-2-X (55 billion parameters).
It significantly outperformed training from scratch and state-of-the-art visual representation finetuning (VC-1) by an average of 52% across six diverse finetuning setups.
Finetuning to new domains (e.g., force-torque inputs, joint position control, bimanual robots) required only ~100 in-domain demonstrations and less than 5 hours on a single NVIDIA A5000 GPU.
Takeaways: A "transformer-first" ViT architecture substantially outperforms ResNet-based models when trained on large, diverse robot data mixtures.
Performance of generalist policies directly scales with the diversity and quantity of the training data, with broader data leading to better generalization.
Conditional diffusion decoding is superior to MSE or discretized action prediction for continuous control, effectively modeling multi-modal action distributions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05941.Title: Evaluating Real-World Robot Manipulation Policies in Simulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.05941.Summary: SIMPLER is an open-source framework designed for reliable evaluation of real-world robot manipulation policies within simulation. It demonstrates strong correlation with real-world performance across diverse tasks and policies by addressing control and visual disparities between simulated and physical environments.
Problem: Evaluating robot manipulation policies on real hardware is expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce across different research labs.
Traditional simulated evaluations often fail to accurately predict real-world policy performance due to significant control and visual disparities between simulation and reality.
Existing metrics like Pearson correlation do not fully capture whether a simulation correctly ranks policies according to their real-world performance.
Method: The SIMPLER framework provides open-source simulated environments that faithfully replicate common real robot manipulation setups, including Google Robot and BridgeData V2.
It addresses the control gap by using system identification to fine-tune simulated robot controller parameters to match real-world trajectories.

The visual gap is mitigated through techniques like 'green screening' real backgrounds onto simulated scenes, 'baking' real object textures onto simulated assets, and aggregating results from varied visual environments.
Results: SIMPLER achieves strong Pearson correlation coefficients (r > 0.85 for Google Robot tasks, r = 0.890 overall for BridgeData V2 tasks) between simulated and real-world success rates across various policies.
The framework demonstrates low Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) values, indicating accurate ranking of policies by their real-world performance.

SIMPLER accurately predicts a policy's robustness and performance drops when subjected to various distribution shifts, including changes in camera pose, table texture, distractor objects, lighting, and background.
Takeaways: System identification and visual adaptation techniques, such as green screening and texture matching, are crucial for bridging the control and visual gaps between simulation and reality for reliable policy evaluation.
Physics simulation provides a more accurate prediction of a robot policy's real-world performance than the commonly used validation action Mean Squared Error (MSE).
The Mean Maximum Rank Violation (MMRV) metric effectively quantifies the reliability of policy ranking in simulation, offering a robust measure of simulation fidelity beyond simple correlation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12945.Title: DROID: A Large-Scale In-The-Wild Robot Manipulation Dataset
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12945.Summary: The DROID project introduces a large-scale robot manipulation dataset collected "in-the-wild" across 16 institutions, featuring unprecedented diversity in scenes, tasks, and objects. Policies co-trained with DROID show an average 20% increase in success rate and enhanced robustness to out-of-distribution variations, outperforming existing dataset aggregations.
Problem: Existing robot manipulation datasets lack diversity in scenes, tasks, and objects, limiting the generalization capabilities of learned policies.
Data collection for physical robots is complex due to logistical, safety, and hardware constraints, leading to a scarcity of high-quality, real-world data.
Robot learning algorithms struggle to generalize beyond controlled laboratory environments, hindering real-world deployment.
Method: Over 80 authors from 16 institutions collaboratively collected data using 18 standardized robot platforms across diverse real-world environments.
A rigorous data collection protocol encouraged scene augmentations, random task selection, and systematic introduction of variations to maximize diversity.
Post-processing included crowdsourced natural language annotations and automatic camera calibration refinement using deep learning methods to enhance data quality and geometric accuracy.
Results: DROID consists of 76,000 successful trajectories (350 hours) with an order of magnitude more unique scenes (564) and tasks (86) than prior datasets.
Policies co-trained with DROID achieved a 20% average increase in success rate and significantly improved robustness on out-of-distribution tasks compared to in-domain baselines.

DROID co-training outperformed co-training with the Open X-Embodiment (OXE) dataset, demonstrating that DROID's unique 'in-the-wild' diversity is more impactful than combining existing less diverse datasets.
Takeaways: Unprecedented scene diversity (564 unique scenes across 52 buildings) is a crucial factor for improving robot policy robustness and generalization to novel environments.
A distributed, multi-institutional data collection effort using standardized hardware effectively overcomes traditional bottlenecks in acquiring large-scale, 'in-the-wild' robot data.
High-quality natural language annotations and refined camera calibration are essential components for maximizing the utility of large-scale robot manipulation datasets.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09631.Title: 3D-VLA: A 3D Vision-Language-Action Generative World Model
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09631.Summary: 3D-VLA introduces a generative world model that integrates 3D scene understanding with language and action generation, enabling embodied AI systems to predict future states and plan actions in 3D environments. It leverages a new 3D embodied instruction dataset and demonstrates improved performance in 3D reasoning, goal generation, and action planning compared to 2D vision-language models.
Problem: Current embodied AI systems primarily rely on 2D visual inputs, which limits their understanding of the intrinsically 3D nature of physical environments.
This 2D limitation hinders robots' ability to accurately understand spatial relationships, reason about occlusions, and plan precise actions for navigation and object manipulation.

Existing vision-language models (VLMs) operate on 2D images, reducing their effectiveness in robotics applications that require a deep understanding of 3D environmental structure and action consequences.
Method: Introduces 3D-VLA, a framework that integrates a 3D vision encoder with a Large Language Model (LLM) backbone, leveraging special interaction tokens to process 3D scene and object information.

Develops a large-scale 3D embodied instruction dataset by supplementing existing robotics datasets with RGBD images, 3D point clouds, bounding boxes, and natural language instructions paired with actions.

Incorporates a generative world model, built using diffusion models aligned with the LLM, to predict future RGBD images and goal point clouds, enabling reasoning about action consequences and goal imagination.
Results: 3D-VLA demonstrated superior performance in 3D reasoning and grounding, showing improved object localization accuracy compared to 2D VLM baselines.
The model effectively generated multimodal goal states, producing RGBD images and point clouds that accurately represented the expected outcomes of requested actions.
3D-VLA showed promising zero-shot generalization to novel environments and objects, demonstrating the ability to plan appropriate action sequences for robot manipulation tasks.
Takeaways: Explicitly integrating 3D perception with language understanding and action generation enhances embodied AI capabilities by enabling a more complete understanding of physical environments.
A generative world model capable of predicting future 3D states (e.g., RGBD images, point clouds) is crucial for effective planning and reasoning about action consequences in embodied tasks.
Training on a large-scale, 3D-annotated instruction dataset is essential for developing models that can effectively learn and understand 3D relationships, language commands, and embodied actions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08321.Title: ManiGaussian: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting for Multi-task Robotic Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.08321.Summary: A novel framework, ManiGaussian, extends Gaussian Splatting to predict future scene states conditioned on robot actions, improving language-conditioned robotic manipulation. This approach enables agents to learn and leverage scene-level spatiotemporal dynamics for more robust task completion.
Problem: Perceptive robotic manipulation methods often struggle with comprehensive 3D scene understanding, especially in unstructured environments with occlusions or limited camera views.
Generative methods, like NeRFs, reconstruct static 3D scenes but largely ignore spatiotemporal dynamics, failing to model how objects interact or move during manipulation.
Robots lack an explicit understanding of scene-level dynamics, which is crucial for accurately predicting action outcomes and successfully completing complex human-specified manipulation tasks.
Method: Introduces a Dynamic Gaussian Splatting (DGS) framework that models the propagation of geometric (position, rotation) and semantic features of objects in an embedding space over time.

Develops a Gaussian World Model with a Deformation Predictor to infer changes in Gaussian parameters (positions, rotations) for each primitive based on current scene state and robot actions, effectively predicting future scene states.

Utilizes a comprehensive set of learning objectives including future scene consistency loss, which forces the model to learn and embed scene-level spatiotemporal dynamics by comparing predicted and actual future scenes.
Results: Achieved an average success rate of 44.8% across 10 challenging RLBench tasks, outperforming the previous state-of-the-art generative method (GNFactor) by 13.1% absolute (41.3% relative).
Ablation studies confirmed that the dynamic modeling component (deformation predictor and future scene consistency loss) significantly boosted performance by 4.4%.
Demonstrated superior training efficiency, being 2.29 times faster than GNFactor, while also showcasing improved novel view synthesis and accurate future state prediction qualitatively.
Takeaways: Explicitly learning scene-level spatiotemporal dynamics through action-conditioned future scene reconstruction in a Gaussian embedding space is crucial for robust robotic manipulation.
Gaussian Splatting, known for its efficiency in 3D representation, can be effectively extended to model dynamic, interactive scenes for predictive control in robotics.
Distilling high-level semantic features from pre-trained foundation models into the Gaussian representation enhances contextual understanding for complex manipulation tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03954.Title: 3D Diffusion Policy: Generalizable Visuomotor Policy Learning via Simple 3D Representations
https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03954.Summary: DP3, developed by researchers at Shanghai Qi Zhi Institute, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and Tsinghua University, introduces a 3D Diffusion Policy that learns robust robotic skills from significantly fewer demonstrations by integrating compact 3D representations with diffusion models, achieving higher success rates and generalization across varied scenes and objects while enhancing deployment safety.
Problem: State-of-the-art visual imitation learning methods require large volumes of human demonstrations, creating a significant data collection bottleneck.
2D image-based policies lack explicit spatial understanding, hindering generalization across varying viewpoints and object instances, and leading to unsafe behaviors.
Prior 3D-based methods for robotics often suffer from slow inference speeds or are ill-suited for continuous, high-dimensional control tasks.
Method: A two-module architecture, comprising a Perception module for 3D representations and a Decision module using a conditional diffusion model, is trained end-to-end.
The Perception module utilizes single-view depth images, converting them to cropped and downsampled point clouds, then processed by a lightweight MLP-based encoder.
The Decision module, built on Diffusion Policy, generates action sequences conditioned on 3D visual features and robot poses, optimized via a conditional denoising process.
Results: Achieves an average 74.4% success rate in 72 simulated tasks (24.2% relative improvement over baseline Diffusion Policy) with only 10 demonstrations per task.
Demonstrates high real-world success rates (average 85%) across 4 challenging dexterous manipulation tasks using only 40 demonstrations.
Exhibits exceptional generalization abilities across spatial, appearance, instance, and viewpoint variations, along with near-zero safety violations in real-world deployment, surpassing baselines.
Takeaways: Simple, lightweight MLP encoders for point clouds, rather than complex pre-trained models, are highly effective for visuomotor control tasks.
Explicit 3D representations, specifically point clouds processed without color information, inherently lead to superior generalization across spatial, appearance, instance, and view variations.
Integrating compact 3D representations with diffusion policies enables significantly higher data efficiency and enhanced safety, reducing erratic behaviors in real-world robot deployment.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13139.Title: Unleashing Large-Scale Video Generative Pre-training for Visual Robot Manipulation
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.13139.Summary: ByteDance Research introduced GR-1, a GPT-style transformer that leverages large-scale video generative pre-training on egocentric videos to achieve enhanced generalization and data efficiency in multi-task visual robot manipulation. The model outperforms baselines on benchmarks and real-world tasks, demonstrating robust performance in unseen scene and language generalization, as well as with limited robot data.
Problem: Robot learning traditionally faces data scarcity, as robot data collection is expensive, time-consuming, and often requires costly human demonstrations.
Existing robot policies often struggle with generalization to challenging, out-of-distribution scenarios, including unseen scenes, novel object instances, or synonymous language instructions.

Many current robot manipulation approaches are not unified, relying on separate modules for visual processing, high-level planning, and low-level control, often requiring sparse keypoint predictions rather than end-to-end action generation.
Method: ByteDance Research introduced GR-1, a unified GPT-style (decoder-only) transformer for multi-task language-conditioned visual robot manipulation.

The approach uses a two-phase training strategy: large-scale language-conditioned video generative pre-training on 800,000 clips from the Ego4D dataset, followed by finetuning on robot data from the CALVIN benchmark and custom real robot data.

GR-1 leverages frozen CLIP text and MAE ViT image encoders for input, and jointly predicts continuous robot actions and future video frames through learnable [ACT] and [OBS] tokens, with a combined loss for finetuning.
Results: GR-1 achieved a 94.9% success rate on the CALVIN benchmark for multi-task learning, outperforming the best baseline (HULC) at 88.9%, and demonstrated substantial improvement in zero-shot generalization to unseen scenes (85.4% vs. 53.3%).
The model showed strong data efficiency, maintaining a 77.8% success rate when trained on only 10% of the robot data, compared to the best baseline at 66.8%.

In real robot experiments, GR-1 achieved a 0.79 success rate for seen object transportation (vs. 0.27 for RT-1) and 0.75 for articulated object manipulation, demonstrating robust performance and generalization to unseen object instances (0.73) and categories (0.30).
Takeaways: Video generative pre-training on large-scale non-robotics data, such as Ego4D, effectively transfers visual-textual understanding to robot manipulation tasks.

A unified GPT-style transformer architecture can seamlessly bridge the gap between large-scale video prediction and multi-modal robot control, providing visual foresight that guides action generation.
The joint objective of predicting future video frames alongside robot actions significantly improves policy learning, enhancing generalization and data efficiency for robotic tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01378.Title: Vision-Language Foundation Models as Effective Robot Imitators
https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.01378.Summary: RoboFlamingo presents a framework that adapts publicly available vision-language models for robot manipulation by employing an efficient fine-tuning strategy. The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN benchmark, demonstrating superior generalization while significantly reducing computational requirements.
Problem: Integrating large vision-language models (VLMs) directly into low-level robot control often requires extensive, costly co-fine-tuning on vast, often proprietary, datasets and models (e.g., RT-2).
Existing VLMs are primarily trained on static image-language pairs, making it challenging to adapt them efficiently for dynamic, sequential robot observations and continuous action prediction.

Many state-of-the-art VLM-driven robotics solutions are not widely accessible due to their high computational demands and reliance on private models and resources, hindering broader research and adoption.
Method: RoboFlamingo leverages publicly accessible pre-trained VLMs (specifically OpenFlamingo) as a backbone for vision-language comprehension.

It employs a decoupled architecture with a VLM backbone for single-step multimodal understanding and a separate, explicit policy head (e.g., LSTM) to model sequential decision-making and generate robot actions.

The framework uses a highly efficient fine-tuning strategy, freezing the majority of the VLM backbone and only updating specific components (perceiver resampler, cross-attention layers) and the policy head using only language-conditioned manipulation datasets.
Results: RoboFlamingo significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods on the CALVIN benchmark, demonstrating a 2x performance improvement in average successful task sequence length.
It exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to novel visual environments and diverse linguistic variations (e.g., GPT-4 enriched instructions), improving robustness for real-world scenarios.
Ablation studies confirm the critical role of an explicit policy head for temporal modeling and the necessity of both VLM pre-training and targeted fine-tuning for effective robot imitation.
Takeaways: An explicit policy head (like LSTM or Transformer) dedicated to modeling sequential history is crucial for robot manipulation, as simply feeding historical frames into the VLM backbone is insufficient for robust temporal modeling.
Both strong vision-language representations from pre-training and targeted fine-tuning on robotic data are indispensable for high performance in imitation learning.
Instruction fine-tuning (IFT) in the underlying Large Language Models (LLMs) consistently improves policy performance, enhancing the robot's ability to follow diverse instructions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10625.Title: Video Language Planning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10625.Summary: The VIDEO LANGUAGE PLANNING (VLP) algorithm enables long-horizon visual planning for robotic tasks by combining vision-language models (VLMs) with text-to-video models in a tree-search framework. This approach substantially improves task completion rates on complex multi-step tasks across simulated and physical robot platforms.
Problem: Existing robotic planning methods struggle with complex, long-horizon tasks in variable real-world environments.
Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) provide abstract planning but lack an intrinsic understanding of physical dynamics and how objects interact over time.
Text-to-video models can learn dynamics for short sequences but cannot generate long-horizon plans or perform high-level abstract reasoning.
Method: A Video Language Planning (VLP) algorithm orchestrates vision-language models (VLMs) and text-to-video models within a parallel hill climbing tree-search framework.
VLMs serve as both policy generators for abstract text actions and heuristic functions to evaluate the favorability of future visual states.

Text-to-video models function as dynamic simulators, predicting detailed short video sequences showing the outcome of proposed actions. Synthesized video plans are translated into robot actions using a goal-conditioned policy that targets intermediate frames, coupled with a receding horizon control strategy for execution.
Results: VLP achieved up to 98% success rate in synthesizing long-horizon video plans for tasks like "Group Color" in simulation, significantly outperforming baselines (2-64%).
On robot execution, VLP completed tasks such as "Group Color" in simulation at 92%, substantially exceeding baseline performance (0-4% for challenging long-horizon tasks).
The framework generalized to new objects, lighting conditions, and novel instructions, and was demonstrated on 7DoF mobile and 14DoF bi-manual robot manipulators.
Takeaways: Combining large generative foundation models—specifically VLMs for abstract reasoning and text-to-video models for dynamics—via a planning algorithm enables emergent capabilities for long-horizon visual tasks.
A VLM can effectively serve as a heuristic function within a tree search, guiding the generation of physically plausible and goal-directed video plans.
Synthesizing detailed, multimodal video plans that link high-level language instructions to specific visual states provides a robust representation for robot execution.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08864.Title: Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08864.Summary: The OpenX-Embodiment Collaboration released the Open X-Embodiment (OXE) Dataset, a consolidated collection of over 1 million real robot trajectories from 22 embodiments. This work demonstrates that large RT-X models trained on such diverse data achieve positive transfer and emergent skills across different robot platforms.
Problem: Robotics lacks large-scale, diverse datasets comparable to those in NLP and computer vision, limiting the development of general-purpose, pre-trained models.
Existing robotics datasets are typically small, specialized, and narrow in scope, which hinders generalization and requires extensive retraining for new applications.
The 'embodiment gap' makes data transfer difficult between different robot platforms due to variations in kinematics, sensors, and action spaces.
Method: Consolidating 60 existing robot datasets from 21 institutions into the Open X-Embodiment (OXE) Dataset, comprising over 1 million real robot trajectories from 22 distinct embodiments.
Standardizing all aggregated data into a consistent RLDS data format to enable unified training.
Training high-capacity Transformer-based RT-X policies (RT-1-X and RT-2-X) on this combined dataset, with a focus on standardizing action and observation spaces.
Results: RT-1-X achieved notable positive transfer, outperforming original methods on 4 out of 5 small-scale datasets.
The larger RT-2-X model (55B parameters) outperformed original methods and baselines even on data-rich domains, demonstrating the importance of model capacity for large-scale data utilization.
RT-2-X showed approximately 3x higher success rates in emergent skills, demonstrating robust knowledge transfer and the ability to perform tasks previously unseen by a specific robot.
Takeaways: Pooling and standardizing diverse, large-scale robotics data is crucial for developing generalizable robot policies, mirroring successes in NLP and CV.
High-capacity models, like RT-2-X, are necessary to effectively leverage vast and heterogeneous robotics datasets for positive transfer.
Co-training on multi-embodiment data facilitates the emergence of novel skills and knowledge transfer across different robot platforms.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08576.Title: Learning to Act from Actionless Videos through Dense Correspondences
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08576.Summary: The Actions from Video Dense Correspondences (AVDC) framework enables robots to learn and execute tasks solely from actionless video demonstrations by synthesizing future video plans using a conditional diffusion model and inferring 3D robot actions from the dense optical flow between synthesized frames and initial depth information. This approach achieves 43.1% average success across 11 Meta-World manipulation tasks and demonstrates successful zero-shot transfer from human videos to robot control, all while significantly reducing computational training costs.
Problem: Robot learning methods traditionally rely on expensive, robot-specific action labels, even for video-based approaches, hindering scalability and data efficiency.
Current robot policies struggle with generalizability across diverse tasks, robot embodiments, and environments due to varying state and action representations.
State-of-the-art video generation models for robot learning demand immense computational resources, creating a high barrier to entry for research and adoption.
Method: A three-stage pipeline (video generation, flow prediction, action regression) is introduced to infer robot actions directly from synthesized future video plans without explicit action labels.

An efficient conditional diffusion model, utilizing factorized spatial-temporal convolutions, generates high-fidelity future video frames from initial RGBD observations and text prompts on commodity hardware.
3D rigid body transformations for objects or the robot are regressed by lifting 2D optical flow from synthesized videos and initial depth, incorporating a replanning strategy for closed-loop control.
Results: Achieved an average success rate of 43.1% across 11 Meta-World manipulation tasks, outperforming behavioral cloning baselines (15.4-16.2%) and prior methods like UniPi (6.1%).
Demonstrated successful zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, with a model trained on human videos achieving 90% success controlling a simulated robot in a pushing task.
Successfully deployed on a real-world Franka Emika Panda robot for tabletop manipulation, generalizing from a large dataset to a new setup with minimal fine-tuning.
Takeaways: Inferring 3D actions from 2D optical flow between synthesized video frames and initial depth allows for policy learning and execution without requiring explicit action labels.
Factorized spatial-temporal convolutions in diffusion models enable training high-fidelity video generation models on 4 GPUs in a single day, dramatically improving computational accessibility.
A replanning strategy that re-synthesizes video plans based on current observations is critical for achieving robust, closed-loop control and mitigating accumulated errors in long-horizon tasks.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06114.Title: Learning Interactive Real-World Simulators
https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06114.Summary: UniSim is a universal simulator learning real-world interaction via video diffusion models that orchestrates heterogeneous datasets. It generates action-rich, long-horizon, and consistent simulations, and can train vision-language policies and reinforcement learning agents with zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
Problem: Bridging the sim-to-real gap for embodied AI, where policies trained in simplified simulations struggle to transfer to complex real-world environments.
Addressing the scarcity and high cost of collecting diverse, action-rich real-world data, particularly for robotics.
Unifying disparate data sources (e.g., static images, human videos, robot logs) that individually lack comprehensive interactive dynamics.
Method: Formulating real-world simulation as a conditional video generation problem using a 5.6-billion-parameter video diffusion model.
Orchestrating diverse, heterogeneous datasets (robotics, human activity, panoramas, internet image/text/video) into a unified format for training.
Creating a unified action space by converting high-level language instructions and low-level robot controls into consistent T5 embeddings and normalized values.
Results: UniSim generates action-rich, long-horizon, and temporally consistent simulations of human and robot interactions from diverse inputs.

Policies trained solely in UniSim demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to physical robots, achieving 3-4 times better goal reduction for vision-language models and improved success rates for RL policies.
Using UniSim-generated data for finetuning a video captioning model improved its CIDEr score from 15.2 to 46.23 on ActivityNet, and enhanced generalization to other datasets.
Takeaways: A learned simulator can effectively generalize across diverse real-world interactive data by integrating various modalities and action types.
Conditioning on past frames and a broad mixture of datasets is critical for generating high visual quality and action fidelity in simulations.
Learned world models can bridge the sim-to-real gap, allowing policies trained entirely in simulation to transfer to physical robots.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13037.Title: GELLO: A General, Low-Cost, and Intuitive Teleoperation Framework for Robot Manipulators
https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.13037.Summary: Researchers from UC Berkeley developed GELLO, a low-cost, intuitive teleoperation framework for robot manipulators that uses a scaled, 3D-printed kinematically equivalent controller. This system enables efficient collection of high-quality human demonstration data, achieving superior task success rates and faster completion times compared to other low-cost teleoperation methods.
Problem: Collecting large, high-quality human demonstration data is a bottleneck for training robust, data-driven robot learning policies, especially in imitation learning.
Existing high-fidelity teleoperation systems are prohibitively expensive, limiting accessibility and scalability for widespread data collection.
Low-cost teleoperation devices often abstract robot kinematics, leading to unintuitive control, increased operator errors (e.g., self-collisions), and lower quality demonstration data.
Method: GELLO introduces a low-cost teleoperation framework utilizing a scaled, 3D-printed, kinematically isomorphic replica of the target robot arm as a controller.

It employs inexpensive backdrivable servo motors primarily for their integrated high-resolution encoder functionality, alongside passive joint regularizers to manage arm posture and provide subtle tactile feedback.

The entire system, including hardware designs and software stack, is open-sourced with a bill of materials under $300 per device, ensuring ease of build and replication for various robot manipulators.
Results: GELLO achieved an average 92% task success rate across five bi-manual manipulation tasks, substantially outperforming 3D mouses (63%) and VR controllers (72%).
Human operators using GELLO completed tasks faster and experienced significantly fewer failures, including a notable reduction in self-collisions, compared to other low-cost teleoperation devices.

The framework was successfully implemented and demonstrated on three different robot arms (UR5, xArm7, Franka Panda), enabling complex, contact-rich, and bi-manual manipulation tasks with a total bill of materials under $300 per device.
Takeaways: A scaled, kinematically isomorphic controller built from economical components can provide highly intuitive and precise robot teleoperation, significantly reducing operator errors like self-collisions.
Inexpensive servo motors can effectively function as high-resolution encoders, offering a cost-effective alternative to expensive haptic devices or full robot-to-robot teleoperation.

Simple passive joint regularization, using components like springs, can enhance user experience by providing natural damping and maintaining arm posture without requiring complex active force feedback systems.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15818.Title: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15818.Summary: Google DeepMind's RT-2 directly transfers knowledge from internet-scale vision-language models to robotic control systems, enabling robots to leverage extensive semantic understanding for low-level actions. This Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model demonstrates improved generalization across unseen objects, backgrounds, and environments, and exhibits emergent reasoning capabilities.
Problem: Translating the vast web-scale knowledge of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to robotic control systems has remained challenging.
Traditional robot learning often requires extensive, costly, and task-specific training data, limiting generalization to new environments or tasks.
Previous approaches using VLMs for high-level planning created a disconnect with low-level execution, preventing robots from directly leveraging semantic understanding for actions.
Method: Google DeepMind's RT-2 introduces Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, directly extending VLMs (PaLI-X and PaLM-E) to output tokenized robot actions.
Robot actions are discretized into tokens that the VLM can predict, treating robot control as a continuation of the language modeling task.
The model is simultaneously co-fine-tuned on a combination of robot demonstration data and internet-scale vision-language data to integrate general knowledge with robotic capabilities.
Results: RT-2 significantly outperformed previous approaches (RT-1, VC-1, R3M) in generalization across unseen objects, backgrounds, and environments.

The model demonstrated emergent capabilities not explicitly trained, including reasoning (e.g., interpreting abstract numerical commands), symbol understanding (e.g., brand logos), and human recognition.
RT-2 successfully executed sequential tasks and followed complex instructions, leveraging its semantic understanding to plan appropriate actions.
Takeaways: Web-scale Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can directly transfer knowledge to robotic control, enabling robots to leverage extensive semantic understanding.
Co-fine-tuning on both robot demonstration data and internet-scale vision-language data is crucial for maintaining general knowledge while learning robotic actions.
Scaling up the VLM, as seen with the 55B parameter model, significantly improves a robot's generalization capabilities and enables emergent behaviors.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.05973.Title: VoxPoser: Composable 3D Value Maps for Robotic Manipulation with Language Models
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.05973.Summary: VoxPoser enables robotic manipulators to execute open-set natural language instructions by having Large Language Models (LLMs) generate 3D value maps that guide a motion planner. This approach achieved an 88.0% success rate on real-world tasks and demonstrated superior zero-shot generalization compared to primitive-based approaches, addressing limitations in robot versatility and skill acquisition.
Problem: Existing language-guided robotic manipulation systems often rely on a rigid, pre-defined library of motion primitives, which limits versatility and requires extensive, task-specific data collection.

Bridging the gap between high-level, abstract natural language instructions from LLMs and the fine-grained, continuous 6-DoF control signals required for robot end-effector trajectories remains a significant challenge.

Traditional LLM-robot interfaces struggle with spatial-level composition of actions, meaning they can plan sequences but not precisely define spatial goals and constraints (e.g., 'grasp the top of the handle while avoiding the vase').
Method: VoxPoser prompts a Large Language Model (LLM) to generate Python code that orchestrates the creation of 3D value maps from visual observations and language instructions.

The LLM-generated code invokes Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for object detection and segmentation, then uses NumPy operations to compose various 3D value maps (affordance, avoidance, velocity, rotation, gripper action) in the robot's observation space.

A model-based planner utilizes these dynamically generated 3D value maps as objective functions within an MPC framework to synthesize full 6-DoF end-effector trajectories for zero-shot task execution.
Results: Achieved an 88.0% average success rate for 5 representative everyday manipulation tasks in static real-world environments and maintained a 70.0% success rate under dynamic disturbances, significantly outperforming a primitives-based baseline (24.0% static, 0.0% disturbed).

Demonstrated superior zero-shot generalization to unseen instructions and object attributes in simulation, consistently achieving higher success rates across various generalization categories compared to learning-based and primitives-based baselines.

Accelerated learning for complex, contact-rich tasks by using zero-shot trajectories as priors for exploration, enabling high success rates (80.0-91.7%) with less than 3 minutes of online interaction, where unguided learning often failed to converge within 12 hours.
Takeaways: Large Language Models (LLMs) can be leveraged to infer language-conditioned affordances and constraints and express them as executable code.
Composing spatial objectives via dynamic 3D value maps offers greater flexibility and zero-shot generalization for robot manipulation than relying on a fixed library of pre-defined motion primitives.
Combining LLM-generated code with Vision-Language Models (VLMs) allows abstract language to be grounded into continuous 3D robot observation space, enabling direct trajectory synthesis.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.00595.Title: RH20T: A Comprehensive Robotic Dataset for Learning Diverse Skills in One-Shot
https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.00595.Summary: A comprehensive real-world robotic manipulation dataset, RH20T, comprising over 110,000 multi-modal sequences across 147 diverse tasks, has been collected by researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. This dataset enables robotic policies to achieve improved few-shot learning and generalization capabilities compared to non-pretrained models.
Problem: Robotics lacked large, diverse real-world datasets for complex, contact-rich manipulation tasks, hindering the development of generalizable robotic policies.
Existing robot learning methods often relied solely on visual input, overlooking crucial multi-modal sensory data like tactile or force feedback for intricate interactions.
Traditional tele-operation methods for data collection were inefficient and unsafe for capturing intricate contact-rich interactions, limiting data quality and scale.
Method: Developed RH20T, a dataset of over 110,000 real-world robotic manipulation sequences featuring 147 tasks and 42 skills, emphasizing complex, contact-rich interactions.
Employed an advanced tele-operation system utilizing haptic devices and force-torque sensors for precise, safe, and intuitive data collection.

Captured multi-modal sensory information, including visual (RGB, depth, IR), tactile, force-torque, audio, and proprioceptive data, alongside paired human demonstration videos and language descriptions.
Results: Pre-training robot learning models on RH20T consistently improved task success rates and accelerated model convergence for various manipulation tasks.
Models pre-trained on RH20T demonstrated superior few-shot learning capabilities, achieving higher performance with significantly fewer new demonstrations compared to non-pretrained models.
The dataset enabled improved generalization, allowing pre-trained models to perform effectively with novel objects and environmental variations not seen during initial training.
Takeaways: Collecting real-world, large-scale, and multi-modal robotic manipulation data, particularly for contact-rich tasks, requires an advanced and intuitive tele-operation system.
Exposure to a wide variety of tasks, robot embodiments, and environmental conditions during pre-training is critical for enabling few-shot learning and generalization in robotic policies.
Integrating diverse sensory inputs (visual, tactile, force, audio, proprioception) allows for learning more robust and versatile manipulation skills, especially for complex interactions.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10007.Title: Robot Learning with Sensorimotor Pre-training
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.10007.Summary: Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley developed Robot Pre-Training (RPT), a self-supervised sensorimotor pre-training model that learns general and transferable representations from real-world multimodal robot interaction data through a masked prediction task. RPT consistently outperforms training from scratch with up to a 2x increase in success rate on manipulation tasks, scales effectively, and enables robust transfer across tasks, environments, and different robot platforms.
Problem: Current robot learning approaches do not fully exploit the rich multimodal data (visuals, proprioception, actions) present in robotic interaction trajectories for self-supervised pre-training.
Existing self-supervised methods often learn task-specific policies, failing to produce general sensorimotor representations transferable across diverse robot manipulation tasks.
Developing robust models of the physical world requires foundational learning that goes beyond task-specific supervision and integrates dynamic relationships between sensory inputs and motor outputs.
Method: A two-stage approach involving self-supervised pre-training of a Transformer-based model (RPT) on unlabeled sensorimotor trajectories, followed by fine-tuning for downstream tasks.
The RPT model processes interleaved sequences of latent visual features, proprioceptive states, and actions, encoded into tokens with positional embeddings.
Pre-training utilizes a masked prediction objective, where the model predicts randomly masked sensorimotor content across all modalities and time steps using an MSE loss.
Results: RPT consistently surpassed training from scratch, achieving up to a 2x increase in success rate on tasks such as block stacking.
The model demonstrated strong transferability, with significant performance improvements (e.g., 68.8% success in cross-lab, 50.0% in cross-robot transfer) over scratch baselines.

Performance scaled positively with larger pre-trained vision encoders, longer sensorimotor context lengths, and increased pre-training data, while maintaining a 10 Hz inference speed on a physical robot.
A high masking ratio (0.7-0.9) and independent token masking were critical for optimal performance, and the model sometimes exhibited emergent self-correction behaviors.
Takeaways: Learning to predict masked sensorimotor content across modalities in robot trajectories can build robust models of the physical world, forming a basis for intelligent robot action.
Operating on latent visual representations derived from pre-trained vision encoders makes the prediction task tractable and allows for scalable, real-time inference on physical robots.
Generalizable sensorimotor representations can be learned directly from raw, unlabeled real-world robot interactions, reducing reliance on extensive task-specific or human-labeled data.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03310.Title: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.03310.Summary: Researchers from The University of Texas at Austin, Sony AI, and Tsinghua University introduce LIBERO, a procedurally generated benchmark for lifelong robot manipulation designed to evaluate knowledge transfer of both declarative and procedural skills. Their experiments show policy architecture's importance, surprising effectiveness of sequential finetuning for forward transfer, and unexpected negative impacts of naive pretraining.
Problem: Lifelong learning research traditionally focuses on supervised tasks (e.g., image classification, NLP), emphasizing declarative knowledge and overlooking decision-making domains.
Existing robot learning benchmarks for multi-task and meta-learning often lack explicit focus on sequential lifelong learning paradigms.
There was a gap in systematically analyzing the complex interplay and transfer of both declarative (what) and procedural (how) knowledge in robot manipulation.
Method: Introduces LIBERO, a novel benchmark built on Robosuite for lifelong learning in robot manipulation, focusing on decision-making tasks.
Employs a procedural generation pipeline using human activity templates (Ego4D) and PDDL to create a scalable and diverse set of manipulation tasks with varying knowledge transfer requirements.
Curates 130 tasks into four distinct suites (LIBERO-SPATIAL, -OBJECT, -GOAL, -100) and provides 50 human-teleoperated demonstrations per task to enable efficient learning.
Results: Transformer-based temporal backbones (RESNET-T, VIT-T) consistently outperformed RNNs, and ViT excelled on visually diverse tasks.
